item.title: [SCMP] China challenges Western ‘tribute system’ theory in push to control its narrative power
item.description:
Beijing is stepping up efforts to challenge the Western concept of the “tribute system”, arguing that foreign frameworks distort ancient Chinese diplomacy and misrepresent the country’s contemporary global rise.

China is redoubling efforts to define its own practices, experiences and ideas through original, home-grown social science language rather than through what it says are Western conceptual lenses.

The theory was forged and made popular in the US decades ago as a means to interpret both ancient and contemporary Chinese diplomacy. China’s push for narrative power to win over a broader overseas audience continues to be tested, including among foreign perceptions of Chinese history and practices.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing is stepping up efforts to challenge the Western concept of the “tribute system”, arguing that foreign frameworks distort ancient Chinese diplomacy and misrepresent the country’s contemporary global rise.

China is redoubling efforts to define its own practices, experiences and ideas through original, home-grown social science language rather than through what it says are Western conceptual lenses.

The theory was forged and made popular in the US decades ago as a means to interpret both ancient and contemporary Chinese diplomacy. China’s push for narrative power to win over a broader overseas audience continues to be tested, including among foreign perceptions of Chinese history and practices.

In a recent example, American billionaire investor Ray Dalio wrote in an article published on his Substack on June 19 that “we are in the very early stage of a shift to a tribute system-type order in the Asia region and even beyond”.

He argued in the article “The Tribute System: The New World Order” that while China’s economic and financial powers were growing rapidly, the US handling of Iran’s seizure of the Strait of Hormuz had convinced others that Washington “doesn’t have what it takes to fight to maintain its empire”, prompting a change in thinking by global leaders.

The founder of Bridgewater Associates, one of the world’s biggest hedge funds, said the dynamic was reflected in the many visits by foreign heads of state and their delegations to Beijing since late last year, which Dalio characterised as efforts “to build tribute-type relationships” with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The “tribute system” is a term coined in the 1940s by John King Fairbank, a Harvard historian credited with founding the academic field of modern Chinese studies in the US, and his collaborator Ssu-yu Teng, for a Sinocentric, hierarchical model of international relations that prevailed before unravelling in the second half of the 19th century.

As China’s global standing has risen, analysts and policymakers in many countries have repeatedly revisited the more than 80-year-old term to assess Beijing’s foreign policy and potential strategic calculations, despite broad objection to the concept within academia.

Even Fairbank had reservations about its use, writing that “tribute” was a “very rough and often misleading” translation borrowed from European vocabulary.

Its use led to views that China could be leveraging its Belt and Road Initiative to build a so-called new tribute system centred around it to extend increasing influence and power across the neighbourhood and beyond, prompting rebuttals from Chinese scholars.

Mention of the notion by Dalio – who has long been seen as a bridge between China and the United States and a frequent visitor to senior Chinese officials – did not appear to strike a chord with officials in Beijing.

“The so-called tribute system is a false image projected by the Western hegemonic logic onto Chinese diplomacy,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said on July 16, responding to a question apparently about Dalio’s argument, even though he was not identified by name.

That was two days after a social media channel named Chaoyang Shaoxia – which is widely believed to be affiliated with the ministry – published a long critique of the concept.

“Using the negatively loaded English word ‘tribute’ to describe the ancient Chinese concept of chao gong is highly misleading to international audiences unfamiliar with Chinese culture,” it said.

According to the tribute system theory, which is called “the Chinese world order”, China’s historical dynasties were considered the centre of civilisation, culturally and morally superior to outsiders, who would naturally come bringing “tributes” – usually produce from their native lands – to pay homage.

In return, Chinese emperors would reward them with fine objects, formally invest their rulers as native kings or chieftains, and grant them access to trade with the Middle Kingdom.

According to Dalio’s post, relations in the tribute system were not between equals but between superiors and subordinates who should treat each other well to preserve harmony.

On the surface, this appears to be a translation issue, but in essence it is a question of who has the power to define

Ding Gang, People’s Daily

If an inferior power treated a stronger one inappropriately, the latter would typically punish it through pressure and deception, although also occasionally by violence, he added.

But Chaoyang Shaoxia noted that the term tribute was “born with the attributes of coercion, violent plunder and one-way exploitation”, as it was derived from a Latin word that originally referred to Roman imperial taxes on provincial populations, and later forced medieval payments from vassals to feudal lords in Europe.

It stated that the formulation did not correspond to chao gong, a term it said was intended to denote “voluntary” acts of reaching out to others based on appreciation and “spontaneous” behaviours of presenting gifts to express goodwill.

The channel said ancient China had followed the principle of hou wang bo lai, or giving generously and taking little. This meant it returned goods to so-called tributary states worth far more than what they had been offered, making the arrangement economically lucrative for them.

It also argued that while modern China had inherited the traditional philosophy of “valuing harmony above all”, it had “completely” abandoned the hierarchical world view of imperial times and firmly upheld that all countries, regardless of their size, wealth or strength, were equal.

The mismatch between “the tribute system” and China’s historical practice “effectively reflects a deeper question of who has the final say and who sets the definitions in the international public opinion sphere”, Chaoyang Shaoxia said.

“For years, China’s ideas and image have faced a problem of being shaped by others rather than by itself. The West has always projected its own historical experience onto China and measured China by its own value standards.

“For cultural concepts unique to China that lack direct English equivalents, or for existing Western translations that carry colonial, exoticising or prejudicial connotations, we can definitely forge a new path.”

The critique comes as Beijing steps up its push to build a “Chinese intellectual system in philosophy and social sciences”, reiterated by Xi in May in a directive urging the development of indigenous, independent theories and knowledge that can explain China’s practices to the outside world without being allegedly monopolised or distorted by Western concepts and narratives.

The effort has extended beyond contemporary Chinese politics, diplomacy and law, to scrutinising foreign origin theories about China’s history, as those interpretations are increasingly seen as relevant to the country’s current domestic governance and foreign policy.

For example, Chinese scholars and officials in recent years have taken aim at the “New Qing History” school of thought that emerged in the US, saying it misreads China’s past and inherently threatens the country’s national unity today by providing historical ammunition for separatism in border regions.

Zheng Yongnian, a Chinese political scientist, cautioned that historical experiences in China were often used as case studies for Western concepts and theories, which would not help the world understand the country accurately.

He said the term “tribute system” was the result of Fairbank imposing Western frameworks on China because he could not find an exact equivalent in the English lexicon.

Zheng said the way ancient Chinese states organised their external relations more closely resembled what would today be described as China’s policy of unilateral opening-up.

Liu Wenming, a history professor at Capital Normal University in Beijing, has also called for re-examining the tribute system as a “foreign concept” to help “eliminate misunderstandings of Chinese history … and to better appreciate the peaceful and friendly nature of the regional order in ancient East and Southeast Asia”.

“Until a more appropriate translation is found, transliteration remains a viable option, namely using chao gong in English,” he wrote in an article published in July last year in Historical Review, a bimonthly journal supervised by the state-run Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

In its article on July 14, Chaoyang Shaoxia suggested that “the tribute system” could be replaced with “jade-silk covenant” or “treasure ship model”, referring to Ming dynasty admiral Zheng He’s seven voyages into the Indian Ocean in the 15th century. Beijing has long portrayed the historical episode as a symbol of China’s peaceful rise, win-win diplomacy and openness to the world.

However, those alternative translations could also run into headwinds from competing narratives abroad, with many foreign scholars noting that the Chinese mariner’s “treasure ships” were heavily armed. Some also cited records pointing to coercion and conflict when local rulers failed to pay due respect, with others framing Zheng’s expeditions as “power projection” or “proto-maritime colonialism”.

A similar challenge to external messaging has surfaced in discussions surrounding China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which took effect last month.

While Chinese officials may use the term “unity” to convey that the legislation emphasises interaction, exchange and blending among ethnic groups in China on an equal footing – premised on the coexistence of differences – overseas media use terms such as “integrate” or “assimilate”.

“On the surface, this appears to be a translation issue, but in essence it is a question of who has the power to define,” Ding Gang, a senior editor with the official People’s Daily, wrote in an article on social media on July 7.

“The public debate surrounding this law is ultimately not just about the legislation itself, but about who has the authority to interpret a particular development path,” added Ding, who is also a senior fellow with the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University in Beijing.

He said that in the English-speaking world, the word “unity” had never been used to describe how different ethnic groups coexist amid their differences.

Because of differences in knowledge, foreign audiences would “naturally” substitute it with concepts more familiar to them and “automatically” link China’s ethnic policies to their historical memory of Western colonisers’ cultural and racial oppression of indigenous peoples, he argued.

Ding added that the association of “China’s ethnic policy” with “assimilation” had become a common sense-style default perception in Western coverage of China-related issues.

He called for greater attention to the “concepts” that could allow China’s “stories” to properly land with the foreign audience.

“Without conceptual intermediaries that can be recognised within the other side’s cognitive system while accurately corresponding to Chinese practice, even the most compelling stories will remain floating outside their framework of understanding, ultimately to be recompiled and redefined by their own concepts,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China, India and Pakistan’s dangerous nuclear triangle just became more complicated
item.description:
The China-India-Pakistan triangle has never been short on danger, but Islamabad’s new defensive alliance has added another variable to an already volatile situation.

Last week, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia signed a pact in Mecca in which they agreed to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all. The three governments have described it as defensive and not directed at any particular state.

Analysts said its main significance for India lay less in whether it would be invoked, but in how it could alter Pakistan’s strategic position as well as the balance between the three nuclear powers.
item.content:encoded:
The China-India-Pakistan triangle has never been short on danger, but Islamabad’s new defensive alliance has added another variable to an already volatile situation.

Last week, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia signed a pact in Mecca in which they agreed to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all. The three governments have described it as defensive and not directed at any particular state.

Analysts said its main significance for India lay less in whether it would be invoked, but in how it could alter Pakistan’s strategic position as well as the balance between the three nuclear powers.

For several decades their relationship has been marked by intermittent deadly flare-ups, most recently the 2020 Galwan clashes between Indian and Chinese troops and last year’s India-Pakistan conflict.

“The agreement institutionalises a trilateral framework combining Saudi capital, Turkish defence technology and Pakistan’s strategic geography,” according to Brahma Chellaney, a New Delhi-based strategic analyst.

“Regardless of whether such provisions are ever invoked [the pact’s] existence could nonetheless complicate India’s strategic calculus by introducing additional uncertainty into crisis planning and deterrence,” he wrote in a social media post.

That uncertainty is important because India already faces two major security challenges from its long-running border disputes with both Pakistan to its west and China to the north.

It has fought four wars with Pakistan since 1947, in addition to last year’s conflict, and one full-scale war with China in 1962.

There have also been a series of deadly border confrontations with the latter along their Himalayan frontier, most recently the Galwan Valley clash in 2020 that killed 20 Indian and four Chinese troops.

Chellaney linked the Mecca agreement to the fallout from India’s military operation against Pakistan last year.

In the conflict, which started after an attack on tourists in Indian-held Kashmir that New Delhi blamed on its neighbour, Pakistan said it had downed a number of Indian warplanes.

New Delhi’s decision to end hostilities after just 3½ days, Chellaney argued, “helped revive Pakistan’s international image, particularly in the Islamic world”.

He said that perception had raised Islamabad’s strategic importance and helped pave the way for a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia last year and then its recent expansion to include Turkey.

With the new deal, Pakistan, China’s closest strategic partner, gains further diplomatic weight and possibly access to more diverse military equipment from Turkey, a Nato member.

A relatively stronger Pakistan would also keep Indian attention divided between its western and northern fronts, an outcome that has long suited Chinese interests.

The agreement “does embolden Pakistan further”, according to Farwa Aamer from the Asia Society Policy Institute, a think tank in New York.

“Pakistan’s further embedded in the wider regional security architecture ... it’s of interest to Beijing to have Pakistan in a more secure and stable position.

“It serves both its economic investment interests as well as geopolitical interests in the region”, she said.

India now has “to deal with a higher political and security profile of Pakistan in the region where we have major interests”, said Kanwal Sibal, India’s former foreign secretary.

“[Pakistan] will feel more emboldened to pursue its combative diplomacy against India and could take risks on the terrorism front,” he added.

“Pakistan has gained a formal security framework with two states that possess deep financial resources, technology and diplomatic influence,” Saira Bano, from Thompson Rivers University in Canada, wrote in an analysis for the Lowy Institute think tank.

“This sits alongside Pakistan’s deeper strategic and defence relationship with China, transforming what India once viewed mainly as a bilateral rivalry into a wider network of alignments.”

The Mecca agreement does not create an automatic anti-India bloc or give China an unconstrained advantage, she added.

But Bano argued its most “consequential feature” was not the resemblance to Nato, whose members also treat an attack on one as an attack on all, but the way it “collapses the strategic distance between the Gulf, the eastern Mediterranean and South Asia”.

She added: “It is an experiment in regional self-reliance that joins three strategic theatres usually analysed separately.”

Saima Afzal, a researcher specialising in South Asian security, wrote in an analysis for US-based platform Counter Punch that Pakistan’s presence meant a defensive network centred on the Gulf “now reaches into an environment shaped by India-Pakistan rivalry, China’s regional role and nuclear deterrence”.

For India the risks are multilayered and its room for manoeuvre is constrained by the added uncertainty caused by the risk Pakistan’s new allies could join any conflict, the need to protect its Gulf interests and the prospect of closer alignment with Israel.

Its large diaspora in the Gulf is vital to both its economy, in the form of remittances, and energy security strategy.

Any future India-Pakistan crisis might risk deeper involvement from the Gulf states or threaten those interests.

Chellaney observed that all three members of the new pact sit along critical sea lanes, giving India “fresh reason to prioritise naval expansion”.

Bano said: “During a future India-Pakistan crisis, uncertainty over what constitutes an ‘attack’ on Pakistan could complicate India’s calculations even if Riyadh and Ankara have no intention of becoming involved.”

Aamer said India had already been widening its defence partnerships, including those with Israel, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates, and “will also continue to engage Saudi Arabia for commercial opportunities”.

Countries were increasingly pursuing “wider diversification and hedging strategies” by building broader partnership networks as buffers against future economic and security risks, she added.

The key question is whether the Mecca pact changes the balance of power or simply changes the strategic calculation.

Husain Haqqani of the Hudson Institute described it as “more symbolic than substantive”.

He added: “A shared enemy is the first element of a mutual defence agreement and that is absent here.”

Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have also proved reluctant to get involved in each other’s conflicts, such as those involving Afghanistan, Iran or the Houthis in Yemen.

Bano said India’s priority should be to “preserve [its] influence in Riyadh” and strengthen its defensive partnerships, while Pakistan’s role in the new framework “cannot be separated entirely from Chinese weapons, technology and infrastructure”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Taiwan is conducting its first-ever mobile network throttling exercise
item.description:
Taiwan is conducting its first-ever mobile network throttling exercise this week to test how the public responds to wartime communications disruptions, a new civil defence measure that has sparked criticism over the government’s preparedness.

The exercise, held in central Taiwan on Monday and planned for northern Taiwan on Thursday, will simulate severe mobile network congestion by reducing 4G and 5G bandwidth for 30 minutes.

About 17 million people, or 73 per cent of the island’s population, are expected to be affected, according to the National Communications Commission (NCC).
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan is conducting its first-ever mobile network throttling exercise this week to test how the public responds to wartime communications disruptions, a new civil defence measure that has sparked criticism over the government’s preparedness.

The exercise, held in central Taiwan on Monday and planned for northern Taiwan on Thursday, will simulate severe mobile network congestion by reducing 4G and 5G bandwidth for 30 minutes.

About 17 million people, or 73 per cent of the island’s population, are expected to be affected, according to the National Communications Commission (NCC).

Rather than a complete internet shutdown, authorities said voice calls, SMS messages and emergency cell broadcasts would continue to function.

Services relying on mobile data, including video streaming, video calls, mobile payments, online banking, e-ticketing, food delivery, QR code verification, cloud synchronisation and app authentication, may become temporarily unavailable.

The first phase of the exercise in central Taiwan on Monday prompted complaints from users who said the throttling had effectively left them without mobile internet access.

Some reported that 4G and 5G connections had slowed to the point where they could not send messages online or even load a browser homepage.

“What throttling? It’s basically a complete shutdown,” one user in Taichung said, while others described having “a signal but no internet speed”, saying the disruption felt more like an internet blackout than reduced speeds.

The drill is part of this year’s expanded Urban Resilience exercises, which replace the long-running Wan An air-raid drills and reflect Taiwan’s growing focus on preparing civilians for network outages caused by war, cyberattacks or natural disasters, according to the defence ministry.

The NCC said northern and central Taiwan were chosen because they had the island’s highest population density and telecommunications traffic, adding that the exercise would eventually be extended island-wide.

Before the tests, Premier Cho Jung-tai stressed that the exercise would be “network throttling, not an internet shutdown”.

He said it drew on the experience of democracies – including Japan, South Korea and the Nordic countries – to test the government’s ability to operate under degraded communications while encouraging people to prepare alternative means of staying connected.

“We hope this exercise will help the public build the ability to cope with communications disruptions through backup measures,” Cho said at a cabinet meeting late last month.

He described communications as a critical pillar of resilience, saying natural disasters, large-scale cyberattacks and other emergencies could all disrupt telecoms networks.

The exercise has nevertheless drawn criticism online and from opposition lawmakers.

Many internet users questioned the practicality of the government’s civil defence handbook, which directs readers to scan QR codes for additional information.

“If the internet is unavailable during wartime, what exactly are we supposed to scan?” one widely shared comment asked.

Others criticised the NCC’s advice to postpone important online activities or switch to fixed broadband during the drill, arguing such recommendations were unrealistic for commuters, street vendors and people working outdoors.

Ko Ju-chun, a legislator from Taiwan’s main opposition Kuomintang (KMT), said reducing mobile bandwidth to about 1 per cent of normal capacity amounted to a large-scale internet shutdown.

Ko disputed the government’s claim that the drill followed international practice, arguing that countries such as Japan and South Korea generally conducted smaller-scale or scenario-based exercises.

“Real communications resilience means backup systems immediately take over when the primary network fails,” he said. “The exercise should test whether backup systems work, not whether the government can cut off people’s internet.”

Fellow KMT legislator Weng Hsiao-ling said the government should compensate the public for any financial losses or damage caused by the exercise.

Ruling Democratic Progressive Party legislator Chen Kuan-ting defended the drill, arguing that a real attack could disrupt communications for an entire day rather than the 30 minutes being simulated.

However, he warned Beijing could exploit the exercise through a false-flag operation by blaming any simultaneous cyberattack or communications disruption on technical failures by Taiwan’s authorities.

Beijing has dismissed the exercise, saying that no matter how many drills the island’s authorities conduct, in the face of the People’s Liberation Army they were “little more than political theatre and an attempt to bolster morale”.

“They cannot alter the doomed fate of ‘Taiwan independence’ or stop the historical trend towards inevitable reunification of Taiwan with the motherland,” Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, told a press conference last month.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries – including the United States, Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take it by force.

Analysts also offered mixed assessments of the tests.

Su Tzu-yun, a senior analyst at the government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research, said the exercise reflected lessons from recent natural disasters as well as overseas resilience drills that simulate communications congestion.

“It gives people an opportunity during the 30-minute exercise to think about how they would stay in contact with family members if internet access became unavailable,” Su said.

He suggested future exercises could recruit volunteers for closed trials, minimising disruption while allowing authorities to collect more detailed technical data.

Taipei-based military analyst Lu De-yun, a former defence ministry press secretary, said the government had failed to adequately explain the exercise beforehand, unnecessarily alarming the public.

While agreeing that degraded communications were a realistic scenario during war or major disasters, Lu said the authorities “have focused on telling people to prepare their own backup communications without demonstrating what contingency measures the government itself has in place”.

He also questioned why Taiwan was not making greater use of leased low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications services, such as Britain’s OneWeb, as a backup if terrestrial mobile networks are disrupted.

“The government often talks about developing Taiwan’s LEO satellite capabilities but none of that seems to benefit ordinary people. Instead, people are simply told to fend for themselves,” Lu said.

item.title: [SCMP] As US marks 75 years of defence pact with Philippines, can it stay the course?
item.description:
The Philippines and the United States are marking the 75th anniversary of their defence alliance with a renewed pledge to step up joint drills as geopolitical tensions in the region continue to simmer.

While the allies are moving towards more frequent planning for maritime security cooperation and deterrence, there are still questions about Washington’s long-term commitment towards the security of the Philippines and the broader region, according to analysts.

At an annual meeting to strengthen security engagement in Manila on Saturday, Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the US Indo-Pacific Command, and Armed Forces of the Philippines chief of staff General Antonio Nafarrete reaffirmed their commitment to the mutual defence treaty signed in 1951 and signed a memorandum to map out the next phase of cooperation.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines and the United States are marking the 75th anniversary of their defence alliance with a renewed pledge to step up joint drills as geopolitical tensions in the region continue to simmer.

While the allies are moving towards more frequent planning for maritime security cooperation and deterrence, there are still questions about Washington’s long-term commitment towards the security of the Philippines and the broader region, according to analysts.

At an annual meeting to strengthen security engagement in Manila on Saturday, Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the US Indo-Pacific Command, and Armed Forces of the Philippines chief of staff General Antonio Nafarrete reaffirmed their commitment to the mutual defence treaty signed in 1951 and signed a memorandum to map out the next phase of cooperation.

While Paparo and Nafarrete did not disclose details, US Pacific Command said the plans included expanding on large-scale military exercises and specialist exchanges.

In recent years, the US and the Philippines have taken part in joint and multilateral military drills with partners such as Japan, Australia and New Zealand, including in contested waters near the Southeast Asian country.

Expanding ties with other allies

The alliance is stepping up such cooperation as the Philippines sits at the intersection of the South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait – two theatres that could spark a potential conflict between major powers, according to analysts.

Developments near Taiwan would have major implications for Philippine security and US regional planning, said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and chief executive of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a Canadian foreign policy think tank.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

“The next phase should be about networked deterrence: stronger Philippine defence capabilities, deeper US-Philippines planning and closer cooperation with Japan, Australia and other partners,” Nadjibulla said.

“The objective should be to make coercion more difficult and give Manila more strategic options, not fewer,” she said.

Nadjibulla noted the increasing sophistication of the joint drills through bilateral planning and real-time information sharing in areas such as air and missile defence, maritime offence, unmanned systems and cyber cooperation.

As such, the treaty between Manila and Washington is becoming “less of a passive insurance policy and more of an active deterrence architecture”.

China’s growing military capabilities and aggressive activities in the South China Sea had accelerated cooperation between the two allies, Nadjibulla said, citing Beijing’s use of water cannons and dangerous manoeuvres during confrontations around Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal.

“For Washington, the Philippines now matters not only because of the South China Sea disputes but because its geography is increasingly consequential to preserving deterrence across the first island chain,” she added.

Washington’s island chain strategy dates back to the Cold War. The first island chain stretches from the Kuril Islands through Japan, Taiwan, and the Philippines down to Borneo, with the second island chain including the major US base at Guam further east, extending through the Marianas to Palau and New Guinea.

Next stage of alliance

Muhammad Faizal Bin Abdul Rahman, a research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said the evolution of the Manila-Washington alliance reflected a shift in the geopolitical landscape.

“While it was important to the US during the Cold War as part of the strategic competition between the Western and communist blocs, it has now become a key strategic and operational frontline in the competition between the US and China,” Faizal said.

Sylwia Monika Gorska, a political analyst at the University of Central Lancashire, said the alliance had moved from the Americans having a large permanent military presence in the Philippines during the Cold War to rotational deployments and counterterrorism cooperation followed by cooperation focused on maritime and territorial defence.

Gorska cited the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement signed by the allies to rotate US troops in the Philippines for longer stays and deploy American equipment in Philippine territories, such as northern Luzon, as central to the shift in defence cooperation.

To further enhance the alliance, Washington and Manila should build resilience in the areas of logistics, communications and command-and-control networks, according to Gorska.

“The next stage of the alliance is therefore not simply geographical expansion of access, but whether distributed forces can remain supplied, connected and operational when the network supporting them is under pressure,” she added.

Chris Gardiner, chief executive of the Institute for Regional Security, said that while the memorandum was another step in strengthening the bilateral partnership, the alliance should be further enhanced by expanding defence cooperation with Japan and Australia.

“The treaty is strong and strengthening because there is a clear strategic confluence of interests,” Gardiner said, adding that the Trump administration viewed closer alignment with the Philippines as more important than its strategy over Taiwan.

However, doubts still linger about Washington’s commitment to the long-term security of the Philippines and the region, according to analysts.

Faizal cited the US aversion towards being drawn into another conflict amid the ongoing war against Iran and signs of Gulf allies reassessing their security ties with Washington.

“This makes it necessary for the Philippines and other US allies to work more closely to ensure that the hub-and-spokes alliance system continues to function by strengthening the spokes [allies] to compensate for the hub [US] becoming less credible,” he explained.

Gorska said while Manila’s other regional allies were stepping up to the plate, they would not be able to replace the US as the anchor of regional security.

“Japan and Australia already give Manila additional sources of surveillance, logistics, equipment, training and operational support, reducing its reliance on Washington for some functions,” Gorska explained.

“What they cannot substitute is the treaty guarantee itself, or the scale of high-end military capability that sits behind it,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why India’s new Himalayan border map threatens a fragile thaw in China ties
item.description:
New Delhi has issued names for 27 locations in Arunachal Pradesh on its official maps, including sensitive sites near the disputed border with China, in a move that an analyst warned could complicate efforts to repair bilateral ties.

The Indian government announced the move on Friday, just a day after officials from the two countries held a working-level consultation in New Delhi to discuss border management and reaffirm the need for peace along the Line of Actual Control.

Beijing has long referred to the northeastern border state as Zangnan, or southern Tibet.
item.content:encoded:
New Delhi has issued names for 27 locations in Arunachal Pradesh on its official maps, including sensitive sites near the disputed border with China, in a move that an analyst warned could complicate efforts to repair bilateral ties.

The Indian government announced the move on Friday, just a day after officials from the two countries held a working-level consultation in New Delhi to discuss border management and reaffirm the need for peace along the Line of Actual Control.

Beijing has long referred to the northeastern border state as Zangnan, or southern Tibet.

In a statement, India’s Ministry of Home Affairs said the Survey of India had issued standard names for the locations to ensure “accurate recognition” and improve public awareness of their geographical and historical significance.

The list includes 21 land areas, four mountain passes, a high-altitude lake and a memorial. The names have been added to official Survey of India maps.

Among them are Longju, a village that was the scene of a 1959 border confrontation, as well as the nearby villages of Maja and Bisa and the high-altitude Thag La, the strategic pass where the 1962 border war between India and China erupted.

The list also includes the Sher-e-Thapa Memorial, which commemorates an Indian soldier who fought in that conflict, and Sambho Sarovar, a high-altitude lake.

Indian media described the step as a response to Beijing’s own mapping campaign since 2017 to assign standardised names to places in Arunachal Pradesh.

According to the state-owned Global Times, China’s Ministry of Civil Affairs has issued six lists of names covering 112 locations, including villages, mountain passes, rivers and peaks.

In essence, India is using maps and place names to construct a narrative of expansion, relying on its own mythology rather than established international norms

Liu Zongyi, Shanghai Institutes for International Studies

New Delhi has consistently rejected China’s renaming exercises, with Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesman Randhir Jaiswal on Saturday describing them as “vain and preposterous”.

“Arunachal Pradesh was, is, and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of India. Assigning invented names will not alter this reality,” he said.

Beijing rejects Indian sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China’s Tibet autonomous region, and claims the area as historically part of China. Three of the areas included in India’s list of names – Longju, Maja and Bisa – are under Chinese control.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun defended Beijing’s naming campaign in April, saying the “Zangnan region is China’s territory” and that China did not recognise the “so-called Arunachal Pradesh illegally set up by India”. He said issuing standard names for locations in the region fell within China’s sovereign rights.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said India’s latest move was “primarily aimed at reinforcing its territorial claims” and creating the impression that its sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh was already settled.

He said the naming exercise was based on what Beijing considered the “illegal McMahon Line” and built on India’s 1987 establishment of the “so-called Arunachal Pradesh”.

According to Liu, the move served both external and domestic purposes.

“By issuing these names, New Delhi seeks both to declare sovereignty externally, including over some sites under China’s actual control, to demonstrate continuity of its claims, and to foster a domestic perception that the territory is beyond dispute,” he said.

He said several of the chosen locations carried “clear military and strategic significance”, such as mountain passes and logistical hubs that could support future Indian deployments and infrastructure projects in the region.

He added that the inclusion of a war memorial reflected an element of “political education and nationalist messaging”.

“In essence, India is using maps and place names to construct a narrative of expansion, relying on its own mythology rather than established international norms,” Liu said.

He contrasted this with China’s approach, which he argued was rooted in sovereignty and historical legitimacy, and in Beijing’s rejection of the British colonial-era McMahon Line, which India regards as the basis of its eastern boundary with China.

“By publishing standardised names, China reaffirms its sovereignty over Zangnan to the international community and underscores its right to exercise lawful authority there in the future,” Liu said.

Pending a comprehensive border settlement, the two countries have fought a war and several deadly clashes over their competing perceptions of the Line of Actual Control.

Liu described the latest naming controversy as evidence that New Delhi’s position on the territorial dispute remained entrenched despite recent efforts to improve relations.

“Rather than seeking resolution through negotiation, it attempts to legitimise its occupation by asserting ‘possession itself equals sovereignty’. This shows that, despite outward gestures of easing relations, India’s stance on fundamental questions remains unchanged,” Liu said.

New Delhi and Beijing have been trying to sustain a cautious improvement in ties after years of tension along the Himalayan frontier.

India is preparing to host next month’s summit for Brics, the bloc of emerging economies that also includes China. Meanwhile, special representatives from the two countries are expected to hold their 25th round of boundary talks in Beijing in the coming months.

There have also been limited signs of practical engagement. Border trade through Nathu La resumed on August 1 after a six-year suspension, while Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Indian Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar pledged at a July 22 meeting in Manila to consolidate positive momentum in bilateral ties.

On Thursday, senior diplomats co-chaired the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs in New Delhi, joined by representatives from defence, home affairs and immigration agencies.

According to China’s foreign ministry, the two sides discussed border management, cross-border cooperation and official demarcation. They agreed to prepare for the next round of special representative talks and to maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels.

At the New Delhi talks, India also urged China to resume sharing hydrological data amid concerns over Beijing’s construction of a massive dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra) River about 50km (31 miles) from the Arunachal Pradesh border, according to Bloomberg.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia seeks to deepen trade ties with South Korea in chips, AI, halal sector
item.description:
Malaysia is seeking to elevate its economic partnership with South Korea beyond traditional manufacturing and trade by positioning itself as a long-term strategic partner in high-value industries, ranging from semiconductors and AI to electric vehicles, renewable energy and the fast-growing global halal economy.

In an interview with The Korea Times, Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) director Redzuan Abd Rahman and Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) trade commissioner Mohamad Termizi HJ Piee said the two countries’ economic relationship had entered a new phase, with growing opportunities for South Korean companies to leverage Malaysia as both an investment destination and a gateway to the wider Asean market.

“Malaysia and South Korea have built a strong and enduring economic partnership over the past several decades,” Redzuan said. “We believe the greatest opportunities lie in deepening collaboration in industries that are shaping the future of our economies.”
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia is seeking to elevate its economic partnership with South Korea beyond traditional manufacturing and trade by positioning itself as a long-term strategic partner in high-value industries, ranging from semiconductors and AI to electric vehicles, renewable energy and the fast-growing global halal economy.

In an interview with The Korea Times, Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) director Redzuan Abd Rahman and Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) trade commissioner Mohamad Termizi HJ Piee said the two countries’ economic relationship had entered a new phase, with growing opportunities for South Korean companies to leverage Malaysia as both an investment destination and a gateway to the wider Asean market.

“Malaysia and South Korea have built a strong and enduring economic partnership over the past several decades,” Redzuan said. “We believe the greatest opportunities lie in deepening collaboration in industries that are shaping the future of our economies.”

According to MIDA, South Korean companies have implemented investments totalling US$11.7 billion across more than 400 projects in Malaysia as of 2025, creating nearly 50,000 jobs. Those investments span chemicals, transport equipment, electrical and electronic products, petroleum products and basic metals.

Redzuan highlighted that the two countries’ respective national development strategies were highly complementary, explaining that while South Korea continued to advance its leadership in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, mobility, batteries and green technologies, Malaysia was implementing the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, the National Semiconductor Strategy and the National Energy Transition Roadmap “to accelerate industrial transformation towards higher-value, innovation-driven and sustainable industries”.

This strong strategic alignment presents significant opportunities for deeper Malaysia-South Korea collaboration in investment, technology and industrial partnerships, reinforcing Malaysia’s position as a strategic destination for South Korean companies seeking regional growth.

Termizi echoed that assessment from the trade perspective, pointing to rapidly expanding bilateral commerce between both countries.

“Malaysia and the Republic of Korea have built a strong and resilient economic partnership, supported by growing trade, complementary industries and close cooperation through Asean and regional trade agreements,” he said.

From January through June this year, bilateral trade increased a whopping 52.3 per cent year on year to US$19 billion, with Malaysia’s exports to South Korea rising 44.2 per cent and imports from South Korea climbing 58.9 per cent.

“From MATRADE’s perspective, the next phase should focus on diversifying trade into emerging sectors such as AI, robotics, medical devices, green technology, digital services and the halal economy, while helping more Malaysian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) participate in South Korean supply chains,” he said. “Ultimately, our priority is to transform conventional buyer-seller relationships into long-term partnerships involving technology, innovation, joint product development and access to wider regional and global markets.”

As South Korean companies continue diversifying their supply chains across Southeast Asia, both officials highlighted Malaysia’s advantages beyond competitive production costs. Redzuan said Malaysia combined “industrial maturity, strategic location and policy stability” with more than five decades of experience in electrical and electronics manufacturing.

“Malaysia handles roughly 13 per cent of global semiconductor packaging and testing, providing an established supplier ecosystem that significantly lowers market entry risks,” he said.

He also stressed the country’s multilingual, English-proficient workforce, strong intellectual property protection and long-term industrial policy frameworks.

“Unlike markets that compete solely on low labour costs, Malaysia offers South Korean investors an ecosystem capable of supporting capital-intensive, hi-tech and ESG-compliant manufacturing from day 1,” Redzuan said.

Termizi similarly described Malaysia as “a strategic gateway to Asean,” citing its participation in major trade agreements including the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the free trade agreement between South Korea and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, in addition to its multilingual business environment. He added that the coming Malaysia-South Korea FTA was expected to further strengthen bilateral trade and investment, enhance market access and create new opportunities for businesses in both countries.

“These strengths make Malaysia an ideal sourcing partner for South Korean companies seeking to build resilient and diversified supply chains,” Termizi said.

Asked where bilateral cooperation could expand most significantly over the coming years, both officials identified advanced technology industries as priority areas. Redzuan said Malaysia aimed to deepen collaboration with South Korea in advanced electronics, electric vehicles (EV), renewable energy and digital infrastructure, in tandem with the Southeast Asian country’s acceleration of its dual transition towards a hi-tech and low-carbon economy.

“We see South Korean firms not merely as foreign investors, but as long-term strategic partners that co-develop intellectual property, upskill local engineering talent and integrate Malaysian suppliers into global value chains,” Redzuan said.

Termizi likewise pointed to opportunities in semiconductors, AI, robotics, smart manufacturing, medical devices, green technology and digital services.

“Malaysia is already a key player in the global semiconductor ecosystem, while South Korea is recognised for its leadership in advanced technologies and industrial innovation,” he said. “These complementary strengths create opportunities for greater collaboration in supply chains, technology partnerships and regional market expansion.”

Redzuan cited South Korean conglomerates including SK Nexilis, Samsung, POSCO, OCI and Lotte as examples of successful investments in Malaysia, highlighting SK Nexilis’ US$540 million EV copper foil manufacturing facility in Sabah as the company’s largest overseas investment.

He said MIDA supported investors through end-to-end facilitation, including manufacturing licences, tax incentives and expatriate services, while MATRADE connected South Korean companies with Malaysian suppliers through business-matching programmes.

“Together, MIDA Seoul and MATRADE Seoul handhold investors from the initial site selection and regulatory approvals all the way through to commercial operations and supply chain localisation,” he said.

Both officials reaffirmed their commitment to supporting South Korean companies seeking opportunities in Malaysia, noting that MIDA Seoul and MATRADE Seoul were conveniently co-located at the Malaysian Trade and Investment Centre near Jonggak station in central Seoul. That arrangement, they said, gave South Korean businesses a single point of contact for investment- and trade-related inquiries, reflecting Malaysia’s commitment to delivering seamless support throughout every stage of the investment journey.

On sustainability, Redzuan said both countries’ shared commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 would create significant room for collaboration in renewable energy, hydrogen, carbon capture and storage, solar manufacturing and the circular economy.

Termizi noted that MATRADE launched its Sustainability Action Values for Exporters (SAVE) initiative back in 2019 to help Malaysian exporters strengthen environmental, social and corporate governance practices and remain competitive in global supply chains.

“By combining South Korean technology with Malaysian manufacturing, engineering and market-access capabilities, companies from both countries can jointly develop and commercialise sustainable solutions for Malaysia, Asean and wider global markets,” he said.

Both officials also highlighted the halal economy as an area with particularly strong growth potential.

Redzuan said combining South Korea’s advanced biotechnology and pharmaceutical capabilities with Malaysia’s internationally recognised halal certification system could unlock major opportunities in halal pharmaceuticals, functional foods and cosmetics.

Termizi emphasised that halal had evolved well beyond food: “Another misconception is that halal is only relevant to food,” he said. “In reality, the halal economy now covers cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, logistics, tourism and many other sectors, representing one of the world’s fastest-growing consumer markets.”

He encouraged South Korean businesses to leverage Malaysia’s well-established halal ecosystem to expand into Muslim markets across Asean, the Middle East, South Asia and Africa, while also pointing to the MIHAS as a platform for building international partnerships.

This article was first published by The Korea Times

item.title: [SCMP] China waits in wings as Mecca pact signals Gulf shift away from US security umbrella
item.description:
The grand security bargain between the United States and Gulf countries is widely perceived to be fraying, creating what analysts see as an opening for Beijing to expand its presence in the region.

For decades, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states relied on Washington’s defensive shield, while it in turn relied on them for access, energy and influence.

Riyadh’s decision to sign a mutual defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan is the clearest sign yet of that shift.
item.content:encoded:
The grand security bargain between the United States and Gulf countries is widely perceived to be fraying, creating what analysts see as an opening for Beijing to expand its presence in the region.

For decades, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states relied on Washington’s defensive shield, while it in turn relied on them for access, energy and influence.

Riyadh’s decision to sign a mutual defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan is the clearest sign yet of that shift.

Signed this week in Mecca, the pact declares that an armed attack on one will be treated as an attack on all three, in an echo of Nato’s Article 5.

But the significance of the Mecca pact goes beyond a new regional security arrangement. Three middle powers – a Gulf energy giant, a Nato member and nuclear-armed South Asian state – are taking steps to reduce their reliance on US-dominated security architecture and build their own collective defence framework.

Such independent alliances among middle powers have been rare since the early Cold War, making the pact a potential model for other countries.

It could also complicate matters for countries such as India and prompt them to reassess their own security partnerships.

“For Riyadh, this agreement bolsters the country’s leverage as it both copes with an emboldened Iran and confronts the limits of US deterrence in the region,” Allison Minor from the Atlantic Council think tank wrote in a recent analysis.

She described the pact as “further evidence that Riyadh is abandoning its quest for an Article 5-like security guarantee from Washington.”

Rich Outzen, a former military and civilian adviser at the US State Department who is now with the Atlantic Council, argued that the agreement marked “an inflection point in the emerging multipolar order in the Middle East and South Asia.”

The pact also brings together countries with very different strategic relationships with China.

John Spencer from the Madison Policy Forum, a New York think tank, said Pakistan was “dependent on China with a military heavily equipped by Beijing”.

Highlighting Pakistan’s fragile economy and reliance on international bailouts, he added: “This is the last country a Nato member should be entering into an Article 5-style mutual defence commitment with.”

For China, however, the new arrangement could create an opening.

As Imran Khurshid from the US-based Middle East Forum wrote in an analysis published last month: “China is using Pakistan for weapons promotion as a gateway to enter the region’s defence landscape.

“Moreover, if the potential ‘Islamic Nato’ that many of these countries, including Pakistan and Turkey, discuss takes shape, China might believe it has an augmented market.”

Khurshid added that China had “aggressively advertised its weapon platforms and builds narratives around its defence systems in the region”, including claims about the success of the JF-17 fighter jet and other Chinese weapons during last year’s India-Pakistan conflict.

That military relationship could become more significant as Saudi Arabia deepens its ties with Pakistan.

According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, more than 80 per cent of Pakistan’s arms imports between 2021 and 2024 came from China.

Under the Saudi-Pakistan mutual defence pact signed last year, Pakistan sent JF-17 fighter jets and other Chinese-made systems to Saudi Arabia, giving them greater visibility and operational experience.

Khurshid said such deals created lasting partnerships because they “typically involve long-term commitments related to maintenance, spare parts, training and logistical support,” embedding Chinese systems more deeply into the recipient’s military structure.

Ali Chishti, from the New Pakistan Foundation, an Islamabad-based think tank, wrote recently that China was “ecstatic” about the Mecca pact and pointed to Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan’s recent visit to Beijing as evidence of Riyadh “deepening ties beyond the West”.

However, Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council, pointed out that the three signatories “have gone to great lengths not to cast this as a Nato-style alliance”, adding that it suggested they would want to “avoid the optics of enthusiastically pooling their resources to purchase Chinese arms”.

“Such transactions would therefore be done quietly and also not at great volume ... Turkey may be able to provide to Pakistan and Saudi Arabia what China could, and at a better price,” he said.

The combination of China’s close relationship with Pakistan and its broader strategic ambitions in the Middle East could therefore give Beijing an indirect route into the Gulf’s defence architecture.

The three-way pact also complicates India’s strategic calculus. New Delhi has moved closer to Washington in recent years, but ties have soured sharply during Donald Trump’s second term.

Meanwhile, the US has moved closer to Pakistan, which is trying to help mediate a deal to end the war with Iran.

Any future Indian military conflict with Pakistan could be framed by Islamabad as an attack that triggers the pact’s collective defence clause – a possibility that may push India and Israel closer together.

India’s former foreign secretary Kanwal Sibal described the situation as “on the face of it, a very negative development for Indian interests”.

The country needed to “explore more options with the United Arab Emirates, Israel, Greece and Cyprus. And Afghanistan”, he added. “We should consult Iran. All this is a fallout from the disastrous US aggression against Iran.”

The Mecca pact followed by months of Iranian missile and drone strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure and sustained Houthi attacks.

Despite the extensive US military presence in the region, American forces were unable to intercept every attack.

The US-Israel war against Iran has also led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas supplies, further reinforcing concerns in Gulf capitals about relying exclusively on Washington for security.

Those concerns have been compounded by reports the war has used up significant stocks of key US weapons.

Around 65 per cent of Patriot air defence interceptors and a substantial share of Terminal High Altitude Area Defence interceptors have reportedly been used up, according to multiple reports citing senior officials, as well as assessments by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

Stocks of long-range precision weapons have also been heavily depleted, including virtually all available ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, while Tomahawk cruise missile inventories have fallen by nearly half.

Restocking will take years, partly because of global supply chain constraints, and the Pentagon has already been forced to delay weapons deliveries to allies and partners.

For Gulf states, the lesson may be less about abandoning the US than about reducing their dependence on it.

Rebeccah Heinrichs of the Hudson Institute pointed to the close ties between Islamabad and Beijing, saying: “It is not in US interests for the Pakistanis to be aligning closer with Saudi and Turkey and our approach towards Iran should keep that in mind.”

But Kugelman said that the new pact, with its “emphasis on burden sharing and implied objective of deterring Iran, should go down well in Trump’s Washington”.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Europe stay united in China trade battle? Ceuta migrant crisis offers a warning
item.description:
The European Union’s traditional August break was supposed to provide officials with some respite ahead of a potentially bruising autumn when it will try to set its fiery trade relationship with China on a new course.

Instead, a border crisis on its southern flank has created turmoil and division among its 27 members, raising questions over how prepared the bloc is for a dust-up with one of the world’s economic superpowers.

“We had a real-time test of what happens when one member state was under coercion,” said Alberto Rizzi, a Rome-based policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, specialising in geoeconomics. “Everybody was very quick to jump on that.”
item.content:encoded:
The European Union’s traditional August break was supposed to provide officials with some respite ahead of a potentially bruising autumn when it will try to set its fiery trade relationship with China on a new course.

Instead, a border crisis on its southern flank has created turmoil and division among its 27 members, raising questions over how prepared the bloc is for a dust-up with one of the world’s economic superpowers.

“We had a real-time test of what happens when one member state was under coercion,” said Alberto Rizzi, a Rome-based policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, specialising in geoeconomics. “Everybody was very quick to jump on that.”

The crisis was sparked on July 30, when an estimated 72,000 mainly Moroccan migrants surged into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in North Africa, after Moroccan border controls appeared to collapse. At least 75 people died, mostly at sea, with the Spanish authorities estimating more than 100 died.

The surge raised suspicions that the Moroccan authorities had weaponised migrant flows in response to Spanish efforts to improve ties with its neighbour and rival Algeria.

In the immediate aftermath, however, many EU members placed the blame squarely on Madrid, whose openness to welcoming migrants is an outlier in a Europe that is becoming increasingly hawkish on the issue.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said Spain’s “uncontrolled immigration” policy was a security threat and suspended the Schengen freedom of movement agreement with Madrid, even though Ceuta is not part of the Schengen area.

Finland and Denmark fell in behind Meloni, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen agreement.

A day later, they were among the 22 EU members signing a letter to the European Commission expressing concern over the Ceuta crisis.

While member states later toned down their criticisms of Madrid, the dispute flared up again over the weekend – ensuring the EU’s dirty laundry remained on full public display for a third week – after Spain imposed its own border checks on air and sea travel from Italy.

The episode may seem far removed from the EU’s trade tensions with China, but the question of solidarity will underpin Brussels’ ability to confront Beijing this autumn – particularly once China starts retaliating.

After national leaders discussed how to move forward under the weight of a China shock to European industry in June, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen praised their “clear support for a European response based on unity among member states”.

The Ceuta crisis, however, is a reminder of how easily the capitals can be divided when one comes under attack.

“The reaction was not as united as we would expect from a union of states that aims to become a geoeconomic actor,” Rizzi said. “China doesn’t have to win 27 of them over to weaken the negotiating position.”

A central figure in the Ceuta crisis, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is also likely to be a major player in any contest with China.

One of Europe’s few remaining socialist leaders, his open-border policies, embrace of renewable energy, and willingness to stand up to US President Donald Trump have made him a poster boy for the global left.

He also stands out for his embrace of Beijing, making an annual visit to China for the last four years. He is also seeking Chinese investment in Spain’s electric vehicle supply chain and was the sole dissenting voice last October, when national leaders called for a tougher EU policy towards China.

“Sanchez was already the outlier arguing China should be seen as a partner, with repeated visits to Beijing, while France pushes ‘European preference’ and Germany remains the pivotal swing state,” said Sari Arho Havren, a China specialist at the Royal United Services Institute.

This, in turn, made it less likely that Sanchez would quietly fall in behind the Brussels-led push for a tougher China policy, she said.

He already has some history in such matters.

In 2024, the Spanish government flipped its vote in favour of EU tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles to an abstention, reportedly after Beijing warned investments could stall and threatened tariffs on the country’s pork exports.

“Madrid has just learned that European solidarity is conditional and retrospective. The rational lesson for a government that expects retaliation from China against its exposed sectors in any trade confrontation is to hedge bilaterally,” Arho Havren said.

The Ceuta episode was, she added, “a stress test” for the expected collision with Beijing, which would “depend on whether member states were ready to absorb costs for each other”.

“The answer we received was certainly discouraging,” she said. “When costs land asymmetrically, the majority’s instinct is to declare the exposed state the author of its own misfortune.”

Commission trade officials are trying to convince nervous capitals not to let the fear of consequences block EU-wide action, and they are already working on a “solidarity mechanism” that would compensate any companies targeted in a tit-for-tat trade war.

China has previously shown its willingness to respond asymmetrically to EU gambits.

When Brussels launched an investigation into EV subsidies in 2023, Beijing went after EU pork, brandy and dairy products, while state media carried copious threats of investigations into the aircraft and automotive sectors.

Frenzied lobbying from threatened industries led Germany to vote against the EV duties, but it failed to convince others to join it.

With the commission preparing new instruments and broader trade investigations to deal with what it sees as unfair trade policies, Beijing has once again vowed to respond in kind.

Matters may come to a head in October, when the two sides’ trade chiefs are due to meet and EU national leaders will meet to thrash out a plan.

Analysts believe the member states are more aligned on the need to act – but the Ceuta crisis has diluted belief that they can follow through.

“Being a geopolitical actor means being able to speak and to present yourself as one, and making it understood from the outside that if you attack any one of us, it’s an attack against all of us. If you coerce one of us, we’re going to respond with an entire EU marketwide response,” said Rizzi.

Cracks have appeared with increasing frequency of late, however, as national interest runs up against abstract notions of pan-European solidarity.

For example, when the EU lined up retaliatory tariffs against Trump’s “Liberation Day” duties last year, France – the most vocal supporter of EU strategic autonomy – quickly lobbied for alcohol to be removed to protect its wine and brandy makers.

Beijing’s promised retaliation will examine again whether Europe is willing to pay the price of unity – but the Ceuta affair provides an uncomfortable preview.

“The lack of solidarity towards a member under hybrid attack does not bode well as the EU stands on the brink of a trade war with Beijing,” said Arho Havren.

item.title: [SCMP] How China’s ‘magic’ rice seeds are transforming the fortunes of Nigerian farmers
item.description:
Just outside the Nigerian capital Abuja, where Green Agriculture West Africa Limited (Gawal) is based, locals do not refer to the company by name, instead as the place where the Chinese supply “magic” rice seeds.

Ahmed Yusuf, 42, credits the seeds with turning around his rice business for good. Before Gawal, Yusuf’s yields averaged just 2 tonnes per hectare, putting him on the verge of forsaking farming after more than a decade of toiling.

“Each year I was making losses, and I couldn’t meet the needs of my family, so I thought, ‘what was the point?’” he recalled.
item.content:encoded:
Just outside the Nigerian capital Abuja, where Green Agriculture West Africa Limited (Gawal) is based, locals do not refer to the company by name, instead as the place where the Chinese supply “magic” rice seeds.

Ahmed Yusuf, 42, credits the seeds with turning around his rice business for good. Before Gawal, Yusuf’s yields averaged just 2 tonnes per hectare, putting him on the verge of forsaking farming after more than a decade of toiling.

“Each year I was making losses, and I couldn’t meet the needs of my family, so I thought, ‘what was the point?’” he recalled.

Yusuf’s fortunes changed after he was introduced to Gawal’s R1 rice strain.

“With this new variety I have been able to stay in business by increasing my yield more than threefold on basically the same effort,” he said.

Yusuf’s success is part of a broader China-backed push to transform African subsistence farming into a highly productive mechanised powerhouse. But this agricultural diplomacy is about more than food security.

Beijing’s hands-off, state-backed approach is directly challenging traditional Western aid models, prompting Washington to counter with its own multimillion-dollar agribusiness interventions to maintain influence on the continent.

Gawal is among a growing number of Chinese companies finding business opportunities in African agriculture, which smallholder farmers dominate.

According to officials, the companies are deploying new techniques, using demonstration farms to accelerate local adoption and help build value chains linking the farms to markets.

Gawal is a joint venture between Yuan Longping High-Tech Agriculture, which is headquartered in Changsha in China’s central Hunan province, and state-owned Beijing-based CGCOC Group.

Founded in 2006, Gawal has spearheaded China’s agricultural diplomacy in Africa, producing new seeds and offering machinery, field expertise and processing capacity.

Its 2,000-hectare (4,900-acre) demonstration farm in Nigeria’s northwestern Kebbi state provides seeds and training to more than 5,000 smallholder rice farmers who also have access to modern technologies under a programme linked to the Nigerian government.

“Seeing is believing,” said Godfrey Ngwoke, an agricultural development programme manager with Nigeria’s agriculture ministry, of the demonstration farm.

“These demonstrations showcase the superiority of new crop varieties and techniques, helping farmers make informed decisions.”

Gawal’s R1 rice variety is among its most popular products. Introduced in 2017 for its resistance to disease and ability to grow on diverse terrain, it yields between 7.5 and 8 tonnes per hectare and became popular with local farmers like Yusuf.

Other varieties, such as Faro 69 and Faro 70, have even greater yield capabilities that range from 11 to 13 tonnes per hectare. Their widespread acceptance has helped boost Nigeria’s rice output by as much as 2 million tonnes a year, according to the company.

Nigeria now consumes an estimated 10.5 million tonnes of rice every year while producing about 7 million tonnes, according to data from the central bank.

Xu Guoxin is part of a team comprising six Chinese and two Nigerians who developed Gawal’s R1.

Holding a bachelor’s degree in agriculture and postgraduate specialisation in crop genetics and breeding, Xu came to Nigeria in 2014, encouraged by the country’s sizeable arable land and large population.

“My professional work focuses on crop variety development, seed systems, agricultural technology promotion and international agricultural cooperation,” Xu said.

“I chose to work in Nigeria because agriculture here has huge development potential and significant opportunities for impact.”

Despite Nigeria’s considerable natural resources and strong workforce, there is still a significant “need for improved technologies, quality seeds and modern farming systems”, Xu added.

This is where Gawal is asserting its presence. Aside from rice, the company supplies improved varieties of maize, millet, peanuts, sorghum and other local staples.

The project falls under a Beijing-backed programme touting “China aid for a shared future” for Africa, emphasising the benefits of shared development.

Xu said Nigeria was chosen for its “leading role in West Africa” and for being “an important hub for regional agricultural cooperation and food security initiatives”.

Beyond Nigeria, CGCOC Group is involved in agricultural cooperation initiatives in Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Guinea and Zimbabwe.

In addition, China is currently engaged in major agricultural projects in more than a dozen countries across Africa, including what it describes as “friendship farms” in Mozambique and Tanzania.

According to rice farmer Chieke Agu, who gets his seeds from Gawal: “It is packaged as aid, but it is also showing us the Chinese way and encouraging us to use their agricultural technology.”

“We can say that Western aid does the same thing.”

The company’s demonstration farm in Abuja boasts hundreds of newly imported tractor engines for supply to Nigerian farmers and serves as a showroom for Chinese equipment and technology.

Still, Xu cited winning the support and trust of the government and local communities as Gawal’s major achievement.

“Government agencies appreciate the company’s contributions to seed development, agricultural technology transfer and farmer capacity building,” he said.

“Farmers have also responded positively because improved seeds and better cultivation practices have helped increase yields and incomes.”

In support of Chinese efforts, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), a United Nations agency, started a programme in March to accelerate the mechanisation of African agriculture through the exchange of information in collaboration with the UN Office for South-South Cooperation in China.

The objective was to create a platform to exchange information on best practices in agricultural mechanisation among researchers, entrepreneurs, government officials and farmers from Africa and Asia, as well as other regions.

“Agriculture mechanisation is an essential pillar in the African transformation agenda,” said Meshack Malo, the FAO’s deputy regional director for Africa. “Scalable mechanisation is not an option but urgent.”

To counter China’s perceived influence in Africa’s agribusiness, the US has weighed in with its own interventions.

While Beijing favours big agricultural projects, Washington has focused on private-sector support, mostly aimed at mitigating risk and improving access to finance.

For instance, the US Department of Agriculture provides commercial credit guarantees under its GSM 102 programme to back exports of American agricultural products and the Facility Guarantee Programme for related equipment.

It also provides inputs such as special seeds and fertiliser to support crops such as maize, rice, cowpea and wheat.

China’s agricultural objectives in Africa, as articulated by its Ministry of Foreign Affairs, are to support the African Union’s Agenda 2063.

The main goal is to achieve continental food security by transforming subsistence farming into highly productive mechanised agriculture.

Nigeria appeared to endorse this approach when it announced a US$900 million deal with China in March to establish six giant poultry farms across the country.

Located on farms measuring 7,000 to 10,000 hectares, each will have the capacity to produce a million eggs daily. They will also be supported by feed mills and power stations, as well as feature maize and soybean farms to generate the feed.

Beijing’s decision to implement a zero-tariff regime for African exports means that a significant amount of product surpluses will have the opportunity to be exported to China, given its position as a major destination of African agricultural exports, according to a study led by Zhao Wenjie of China Agricultural University in Beijing.

Published in the peer-reviewed journal Sustainability in March, the study said the contrasting approaches adopted by Western countries and China had influenced project outcomes.

Western aid often comes with exacting conditions involving human rights, good governance and environmental protection.

“While these standards are important, they can sometimes be perceived as intrusive or paternalistic by African nations,” wrote Zhao and his colleagues.

“In contrast, China’s non-conditional approach provides a sense of relief to these countries, allowing for more flexible and pragmatic cooperation agreements.”

item.title: [SCMP] Historian Wang Gungwu on US credibility and why Xi thinks ‘only the party can save China’
item.description:
Professor Wang Gungwu is regarded internationally as an authority on Chinese history. The 95-year-old is best known for his explorations of Chinese history in the long view, and for his writings on the Chinese diaspora. He has been a professor at the National University of Singapore since 2007 and emeritus professor at the Australian National University since 1988. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong from 1986 to 1995.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The US-China rivalry is now quite prominent on the world stage. Do you think these two countries are facing the Thucydides Trap? How do you see their rivalry unfolding?
item.content:encoded:
Professor Wang Gungwu is regarded internationally as an authority on Chinese history. The 95-year-old is best known for his explorations of Chinese history in the long view, and for his writings on the Chinese diaspora. He has been a professor at the National University of Singapore since 2007 and emeritus professor at the Australian National University since 1988. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong from 1986 to 1995.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The US-China rivalry is now quite prominent on the world stage. Do you think these two countries are facing the Thucydides Trap? How do you see their rivalry unfolding?

At one level, it is really similar to the United States and Soviet Union Cold War because both have nuclear weapons.

The question of having to fight one another and the possibility of using nuclear weapons makes it unlikely that they will fight each other. Fighting through proxies would be the same as during the Cold War.

I think military strategists would think that the way to deal with the situation when there’s US and China rivalry is to have another Cold War, and for the US to use the same methods that they used to destroy the Soviet Union.
