Syed responded that politics was “not a Hollywood movie”, sparking a heated public exchange between him and the Johor royal.

Harding said political fragmentation since 2018 had created greater room for the monarchy to exercise and extend its established constitutional functions, including in the appointment of governments and decisions over whether to dissolve legislatures.

“It is true that politics abhors a vacuum,” he said.

Nine crowns

The public clashes only showcase one dimension of Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy.

The debate is complicated by the fact that Malaysia does not have a single uniform monarchy.

Each royal state has its own constitution, succession rules and historical relationship between palace, government and traditional authorities. Johor’s royal house has long maintained a highly visible place in the state’s public life, while Negeri Sembilan follows a distinctive system drawn from Minangkabau custom.

There, the Yang di-Pertuan Besar is selected from eligible princes by four territorial chieftains known as the undang. The system amounts to an elective state monarchy nested within Malaysia’s elective federal monarchy.

Its complexity burst into national view this year when a succession dispute involving Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, several chieftains and a rival claimant spilled into public declarations, court proceedings and competing interpretations of the state constitution.

The palace consolidated its position following the Negeri Sembilan polls on August 1, with Tuanku Muhriz dismissing the undang of Jelebu and revoking the royal titles of several figures linked to the succession dispute, clearing the way for the swearing-in of the new state government and Barisan Nasional’s Ismail Lasim as the new menteri besar the following day.

BN secured a win in the state polls, taking 18 of the 36 seats, defeating PH’s 11 and ultimately forming the state government with a supermajority of 25 through electoral cooperation with opposition Perikatan Nasional.

Tuanku Muhriz urged freshly elected assemblymen to ensure the interests of the state and its people are put above political or personal considerations.

“To the candidates who were unsuccessful in this election, I hope that all of you will continue to serve the people with dedication and contribute to the well-being of society and the progress of Negeri Sembilan,” the ruler said during the swearing-in ceremony at Istana Besar Seri Menanti.

His remarks followed months of political and royal uncertainty that strained Negeri Sembilan’s unique constitutional system, underscoring that the state constitution remains intertwined with state governance even as the broader royal dispute continues through the courts.

A rare postponement of the Conference of Rulers’ meeting set for June 23-25 had pushed the Negeri Sembilan succession dispute into politics. The next meeting is yet to be determined.

In June, Prime Minister Anwar said the federal government continued to recognise Tuanku Muhriz, after Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar was proclaimed as the new ruler at a hotel in neighbouring Melaka.

The dispute remained entangled in litigation and arguments over the authority of the undang and the state’s royal council.

Wan Ahmad Fauzi said the controversy exposed a widespread misunderstanding of Negeri Sembilan’s royal structure.

“The ruler of Negeri Sembilan is not the Yang di-Pertuan Besar alone,” he said, arguing that the constitutional duties of the ruling chieftains should not be dismissed as merely customary positions.

The episode differed sharply from the 2022 federal deadlock, but both forced Malaysians to confront the architecture beneath their monarchy, including powers and traditions that usually remain distant from everyday political debate.

Historian Milner said the central question was whether the monarchy could continue supplying stability when elected institutions faltered.

“Monarchy, on the face of it, is an outdated institution,” he said. “In recent times, however, it may be gaining new support, especially as people look at other types of constitution.”

Constitutionally, Malaysia’s political upheavals stemming from its democratic process have shown that the monarch has played a decisive role, exercising some level of discretion on who leads the nation based on parliamentary majority and support.

Lim, the constitutional lawyer, said decisions made by the palace had gone beyond what was widely deemed as a ceremonial role previously.

“So when political parties are not as strong as they used to be, the monarchs invariably fill that power vacuum and play a much more influential role in governance, at least compared to pre-2018,” he told This Week in Asia.

According to Lim, rulers’ constitutional powers are enumerated in the federal constitution and have the force of law which is not open to question while the constitutional convention acts as a long-standing practice derived from the UK which Malaysia’s system is largely based on.

From legal observations, Lim said monarchs were not overstepping their constitutional powers. “I think the constitution is working as intended for now.”

However, he said constitutional convention might evolve, stemming from any instability of political coalitions.

“For example, it may now be a constitutional convention for the king to be consulted on the annual budget or on major public policies before they are rolled out, which I definitely see happening unlike before,” Lim said. “The monarchs will no doubt be playing a larger role in governance due to the instability of political coalitions.”

New normal

Awang Azman Awang Pawi, a political analyst at the University of Malaya, said Malaysia appeared to be entering a form of conditional new normal as long as politics remained fragmented.

He said the monarchy was likely to remain more visible in matters involving government formation, legislation dissolution and determination of majority support.

“The healthiest constitutional model is one in which the monarchy remains influential but firmly bound by the constitution; respected but not politicised; and committed to safeguarding the democratic process rather than competing with the elected government.”

That prominence carries advantages and risks. Royal intervention can help break a deadlock when no political leader commands a majority, but sustained dependence on the palace may allow political parties to avoid the harder task of rebuilding durable coalitions and settling disputes through parliament.

The institution’s legitimacy also rests partly on remaining above partisan combat, even as political actors increasingly appeal to rulers, invoke palace relationships or portray royal approval as a source of authority.

For Darwisy, those arguments remain beyond the purpose of his portraits. His focus is the cultural language surrounding the institution and how it can reach a generation more familiar with short videos than royal archives.

“Not everyone reads history books, but today many people connect with art on social media,” he said. “My hope is that people don’t just see a royal portrait, but also discover and appreciate the beauty of Malaysian culture through the artwork.”

item.title: [SCMP] Myanmar touts economic potential but is it pie in the sky with it still at war?
item.description:
Rina left Myanmar shortly after the 2021 coup as military violence escalated against pro-democracy protesters like herself and the economy of her country, once a Southeast Asian frontier that had flickered with promise, ground to a virtual halt.

Now in Bangkok, the 21-year-old has found work in a cafe, a regular, albeit low-salaried income, the minimum required by the millions of her age group forced to survive outside a domestic economy in ruins, where civil war has killed an estimated 100,000 people in five years.

But her thoughts on who is to blame for the destruction of her country remain unchanged: Min Aung Hlaing, the junta chief who became civilian president this year after elections in the parts of the country the military controls.
item.content:encoded:
Rina left Myanmar shortly after the 2021 coup as military violence escalated against pro-democracy protesters like herself and the economy of her country, once a Southeast Asian frontier that had flickered with promise, ground to a virtual halt.

Now in Bangkok, the 21-year-old has found work in a cafe, a regular, albeit low-salaried income, the minimum required by the millions of her age group forced to survive outside a domestic economy in ruins, where civil war has killed an estimated 100,000 people in five years.

But her thoughts on who is to blame for the destruction of her country remain unchanged: Min Aung Hlaing, the junta chief who became civilian president this year after elections in the parts of the country the military controls.

He is currently in the Thai capital basking in the welcome of an official visit to Thailand, following trips to China and India that have offered a diplomatic ladder out from isolation since the coup.

In Bangkok, the welcome included a red carpet, honour guard, gala dinner and a chance to offer business leaders a vision of his civil-war-torn nation as a future regional infrastructure and investment hub – rather than the regional basket case his coup created.

“Min Aung Hlaing is the reason we are living here outside our country. The day he is gone – and the military is defeated – we will go back and we will build our country again,” she told This Week in Asia, giving her nickname to avoid any recriminations.

“But we will have to wait. Who knows how long? Maybe it will be three, five or 10 years?”

The realisation that the former army chief – wanted for war crimes at The Hague and sanctioned from the United Kingdom to the United States – is firmly at the helm of an albeit fractured country, has also shaped Thailand’s diplomatic outreach.

Thailand has embarked on what it calls a “calibrated re-engagement’’ with Myanmar, a position it says is inevitable given the long shared border and interests that involve close cooperation, no matter who is in charge in Naypyidaw.

“We have issues every day and need to cooperate … so bilaterally we need to talk, we need to cooperate particularly on issues of border security: the border itself, how to work together to suppress the transnational crimes, scams, drugs,’’ Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told reporters on Thursday evening, adding that air and cross-boundary water pollution were the most pressing issues, referencing toxic run-off that had hit river communities along the Mekong and its tributaries in northwestern Thailand.

While emphasising that Thailand wanted to keep Myanmar pegged to outcomes of a five-point consensus – an Asean bloc peace deal to end violence against civilians and ensure aid gets to the millions of displaced since the coup – Sihasak said there were also economic reasons to extend a hand to Myanmar’s government.

“It’s not just the immediate opportunities,” he told reporters. “Many of the private sector are looking long-term. If Myanmar returns to peace and stability there will be a lot of opportunities, whether in trade and investment.”

While Myanmar’s economy has shown signs of life this year after years of sky-high inflation and negative growth partly caused by a devastating earthquake, experts say it is far from recovering its previous footing which began with political and economic reforms in 2011 – a period of growth abruptly ended by the coup.

“The projects Min Aung Hlaing is pushing with neighbours centre on infrastructure construction, gas development, and energy,” said Htwe Htwe Thein, an associate professor of international business at Curtin University in Australia.

Min Aung Hlaing’s economic plans pivot on highways, railways, dams and power projects, she added, to remodel the war-shattered but strategically important country – pinned between India, China and Thailand – as a manufacturing hub in the heart of Asia’s supply chains.

But “serious obstacles’’ stand in the way of that bright vision, Htwe Htwe Thein added, in a country where the United Nations say 16 million people – nearly a third of the population – need humanitarian relief and foreign investment has collapsed as the war has deepened.

“For one, how do you build infrastructure corridors through active war zones? No serious investor is going to commit capital to projects running through contested territory the government doesn’t fully control,” she said.

“Layer sanctions and the banking restrictions that follow on top of that, and any financing tied to Myanmar comes under heavy scrutiny at every step.”

That leaves economic drivers of jade and gems, tin, copper and rare earths operated by military cronies and shadowy tycoons rather than creating a wider economic base as the likely outcome, she added.

“Real investment has narrowed to resource extraction carried out with little proper due diligence, and also murky financial flows. None of that is capital that builds a manufacturing base or delivers broad-based development.

“It’s extraction and survival financing, not growth.”

While the economic picture uneven at best, Thailand’s renewal of relations has come under scrutiny.

The militaries of Myanmar and Thailand share good relations that have stretched back decades, according to Paul Chambers, an analyst of Thai politics at the University of Oklahoma in the US, adding that Myanmar’s “abominable human rights record’’ has rarely been the deciding factor in their diplomacy.

Myanmar’s diplomatic reintegration in its Asian neighbourhood owed more to military gains of the last 18 months, he said, that were secured in part with Chinese and Russian military aid that had pulled back the patchwork of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic armed groups that at one point threatened to overwhelm the military.

Still, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is yet to fully readmit Myanmar to its main summits until the five-point consensus is firmly back on track.

Instead, Myanmar’s tip-toe back into the diplomatic fold, represented by this week’s Bangkok trip – after Beijing and New Delhi – reflects the national interests of its neighbouring countries, according to Richard Horsey, Crisis Group’s senior Asia adviser.

“China, India, and Thailand are taking on real reputational risk by doing so, and the rest of the world is watching,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] For China’s aspiring foreign workers, getting a job is only half the battle
item.description:
Even as an undergraduate in his native Barcelona, Aitor knew he wanted to work in China.

The young finance major reckoned an economy of such scale and speed had more to offer someone with his skill set than the market waiting for him closer to home.

After moving to Shanghai to complete a master’s degree, he had what he came for: a supply-chain job in the bustling financial centre. What Aitor – a nickname, requested to protect the identity of his employer – did not expect was that getting a job would be the easy part.
item.content:encoded:
Even as an undergraduate in his native Barcelona, Aitor knew he wanted to work in China.

The young finance major reckoned an economy of such scale and speed had more to offer someone with his skill set than the market waiting for him closer to home.

After moving to Shanghai to complete a master’s degree, he had what he came for: a supply-chain job in the bustling financial centre. What Aitor – a nickname, requested to protect the identity of his employer – did not expect was that getting a job would be the easy part.

Being hired at firms in China is already difficult for foreign graduates: employers barely give applications a look, given the number of qualified local candidates.

But Aitor’s Chinese language proficiency provided a way around this hurdle. He could search on Boss Zhipin, one of the country’s largest recruitment apps, which Aitor said was “not very friendly for foreigners” and not known to most expats.

Then came the real challenge: the visa. A points-based system for qualification, the overlapping categories and the volume of documentation involved have made obtaining a work permit a longer-running problem than the job search ever was.

“Visa applications are complicated, especially working visas, and I’m still in the process six months after my application,” Aitor said. “The amount of papers needed makes it very complicated.”

Yet as a degree holder from a Chinese university, he said he considered himself lucky, noting that others had it worse.

“I know many valuable and well-educated individuals are struggling to find ways to formalise their work in China, since family reunion visas are not flexible at all and working visas are very hard to get and [it is] hard to be sponsored by local companies; they are caught in between,” he said.

As China’s economy has grown in scale and its influence across global supply chains has expanded, more international graduates and professionals are eyeing opportunities in the world’s second-largest economy.

However, unlike traditional immigration destinations such as the United States and Canada, China has historically relied less on foreign workers to fill labour shortages, leaving the country to build a foreign talent system relatively slowly.

Many foreign workers in China are transferred there by multinational companies, with visa processing, housing and relocation costs typically covered by their employers. This provides a markedly different experience from younger candidates attempting to enter China’s job market independently.

At the same time, the country has been facing rising employment pressure, particularly among young workers, adding another layer of complexity to efforts to attract overseas talent. Its youth unemployment reached 21.3 per cent in June 2023, before the National Bureau of Statistics revised its calculation method. The rate stood at 14.9 per cent in June.

Last year, China introduced the “K visa”, targeting young science and technology professionals as it competes globally for engineers, researchers and innovators.

For most foreign workers, however, the standard “Z visa” remains the main route, requiring employer sponsorship, qualifications, work experience and extensive administrative procedures.

“In reality, we have not yet handled any K visa applications. The visa is still very new and at least from my experience, I have not heard of any successful cases so far,” said Anna Chen, a visa consultant based in Shenzhen.

Chen said the K visa, which attracted significant attention overseas when it was introduced, mainly targets young foreign scientists, engineers and other highly skilled technology professionals.

“The target group is quite narrow. Most foreigners coming to China for work do not meet that threshold,” she said. “And those who do often choose the United States instead, since salaries there are generally more attractive, based on my conversations with clients.”

Meanwhile, the Z visa is divided into three categories: A, which targets high-level talent such as leading researchers, executives and recognised experts; B, which covers most skilled professionals who must meet requirements related to education, work experience and salary; and C, a less common category reserved for seasonal or temporary employees.

“Most of the foreign workers I deal with are still applying for Category B work permits,” Chen said.

The visa agent said that compared with the US, China’s work visa system was generally less competitive for high-skilled applicants, as it did not have a lottery system like the H-1B programme in the US.

“But the process can still be complicated, since China requires employers to sponsor visas and most Chinese companies do not lack workforce domestically anyway, making them less likely to look overseas for talent,” she added.

Unlike China, countries such as the United Kingdom and US offer post-study work routes for international graduates.

In the UK, new degree holders can apply for a graduate visa, allowing them to work without employer sponsorship, usually for two years before switching to a skilled worker visa with an approved employer.

In the US, graduates can seek Optional Practical Training – temporary employment related to their field of study – before seeking employer-sponsored visas such as the H-1B.

China, by contrast, generally does not offer a similar transition route. Foreign graduates typically need to secure a job offer and employer sponsorship before applying for a work visa, even after studying at a Chinese university.

China has not released updated nationwide figures on foreign employment, but data showed that authorities issued 711,000 residence permits to foreign nationals in 2023, about 15 per cent below pre-pandemic levels.

Around 237,000 of these were work-related residence permits, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data.

Chen said China had tightened scrutiny of work visa applications in recent years, following cases in some cities where foreigners obtained permits through fake employment arrangements or shell companies.

“The process now takes longer, employers also face stricter documentation requirements and applicants are asked to provide more financial records. Overall, work visa approvals have slowed,” she added.

Marshall Ma, a former recruiter based in Shanghai, said demand for foreign professionals in the city – widely regarded as China’s largest market for overseas talent – has declined sharply in recent years.

“The last time I heard a company specifically asking to hire foreigners was in 2021,” Ma said. “After the pandemic, competition in Shanghai’s job market intensified.

“Foreign candidates [are] often seen as having higher expectations, not only in terms of salaries but also benefits such as annual leave.”

Ma said demand for foreign workers remained relatively strong mainly in English teaching roles, while many other white-collar positions could now be filled by younger Chinese jobseekers at lower cost and with native language proficiency.

Another factor discouraging companies from hiring foreigners, he said, was the additional administrative burden, including visa applications and social insurance requirements.

“Many that traditionally hired large numbers of foreigners were Asia-Pacific regional headquartered firms, but lots of them began scaling back their China operations since 2023. Naturally, demand for foreign workers declined as well,” Ma added.

China has taken steps to make everyday digital services more accessible for foreigners, initially targeting overseas visitors but also benefiting foreign residents living and working in the country.

Since 2023, authorities have expanded mobile payment options by allowing more international bank cards to link with platforms such as Alipay and WeChat Pay, while simplifying registration and identity verification procedures.

However, challenges remain for some foreigners navigating China’s digital ecosystem.

“Digital and internet services work very well for the most part, but as foreigners, we often encounter small issues with many apps because we need to use our passports or provide other information that can sometimes cause problems,” Aitor said.

“Since I came to China three years ago, I think things have been moving in a positive direction, but there is still work to be done in some internet services so that foreigners can have a smoother experience.”

The reason why I decided to stay in China is because I knew my skill set would be more valuable here

Marcos Sabio, British-Spanish dual citizen

Yet not all foreigners encounter the same visa hurdles. For British-Spanish dual citizen Marcos Sabio, the transition into China’s workforce was relatively smooth. He found his software industry role in Beijing through the career-oriented social media platform LinkedIn, where his employer handled the work permit application.

“Luckily, for the visa applications and all the administration and bureaucracy, everything was handled by the HR team in the company,” he said.

“The reason why I decided to stay in China is because I knew my skill set would be more valuable here. Being able to speak Chinese, English, Spanish and some Russian is a real asset,” said Sabio, who has lived in China for 12 years.

Despite the hurdles, China’s appeal among foreign professionals appears to be recovering. According to a 2025 survey from InterNations – an online platform for people living and working abroad – China ranked sixth out of 46 destinations, with respondents expressing relatively high satisfaction with career opportunities, personal finances and daily convenience.

However, the survey also highlighted persistent challenges, including language barriers, administrative procedures and adaptation to the domestic digital ecosystem.

For Malaysian citizen Jens Lee, his China career journey involved less adaptation than others. His ethnic background and previous study experience in the country meant that adjusting to daily life and workplace culture came relatively naturally. After completing his master’s degree, he moved smoothly into a full-time role at a European-backed consultancy.

But familiarity with China did not necessarily make the bureaucracy easier.

Lee turned to a visa agency to handle the process, but found the experience less than smooth. The agency was relatively inexperienced, partly because he chose a cheaper provider that charged 6,000 yuan (US$886).

He said the intermediary handled most of the application, leaving him with limited understanding of the points-based system and other requirements.

Despite the administrative obstacles, Lee said, “China’s scale, economic dynamism and fast-paced working environment offer significant opportunities for professional learning and personal growth, which is something I value tremendously at the current stage of my career.”

item.title: [SCMP] Chip off the old bloc: Thailand looks to Siam Silica to propel it to top Asean player
item.description:
Thailand launched its Siam Silica framework last week, a national road map that stamps the Southeast Asian country’s stake in the semiconductor race by building a domestic ecosystem and positioning it as a key hub within an integrated supply chain among Asean member states.

However, analysts say that the country will have much ground to cover as it trails behind neighbours Malaysia and Singapore.

At the unveiling by the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation (MHESI) on July 27, minister Yodchanan Wongsawat called semiconductor development “a national priority”.
item.content:encoded:
Thailand launched its Siam Silica framework last week, a national road map that stamps the Southeast Asian country’s stake in the semiconductor race by building a domestic ecosystem and positioning it as a key hub within an integrated supply chain among Asean member states.

However, analysts say that the country will have much ground to cover as it trails behind neighbours Malaysia and Singapore.

At the unveiling by the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation (MHESI) on July 27, minister Yodchanan Wongsawat called semiconductor development “a national priority”.

Siam Silica will target five areas: photonics fabrication, advanced packaging, silicon design, quantum photonics and power devices. Thailand aims to establish eight integrated circuit design companies, one semiconductor fabrication plant, and two advanced semiconductor packaging facilities by 2030.

The MHESI also announced it was launching a Higher Education Sandbox degree programme for universities to fast-track deep-tech expertise and develop advanced competencies.

STEMPlus, the ministry’s human resources development and planning platform, will recruit 152 lecturers and scientists, 950 researchers, experts and senior engineers, 553 highly skilled engineers and 1,330 technicians for the programme.

Bangkok’s ambitions also include creating an Asean Talent Observatory to forecast demand in the workforce, incorporating photonics and printed circuit boards into the Asean Semiconductor Roadmap, and growing its Thailand Skill Bridge platform to collaborate on research and development with other countries in the region.

To achieve that, Thailand should push for closer Association of Southeast Asian Nations integration so the bloc could strengthen its resilience and regional bargaining power amid disruptions in the global supply chain, Surin Khomfoi, vice-president of the Office of the National Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Policy Council, was quoted as saying by the Bangkok Post.

Thailand could also look into producing power control chips, photonics chips and sensor chips, as there is a high market demand and low number of players in this sector, according to Surin.

Appropriately ambitious

The recently unveiled plans reflect Thailand’s long-standing ambitions to move into higher-value segments of the semiconductor manufacturing chain, such as chip design and wafer fabrication.

In 2024, Thailand established the inter-ministry National Semiconductor Board to promote its semiconductor and advanced electronics industries, and deepen its foothold in global value chains.

However, analysts say the Southeast Asian country faces an uphill battle.

“It’s a tall order, for two reasons. First, Thailand is a latecomer to the semiconductor value chain compared with Singapore and Malaysia. Announcing a road map to build, by 2030, an ecosystem that can rival what those two neighbours have spent decades assembling is very different from actually delivering it,” Pavida Pananond, a professor of international business at Thammasat University’s Thammasat Business School, told This Week in Asia.

“Second, Thailand also lags in the breadth of semiconductor activities it can perform.”

In 2024, Thailand’s semiconductor exports reached 436 billion baht (US$13.8 billion). Malaysia’s total that year was US$95.6 billion, nearly seven times that.

“Thailand exports a much smaller value in semiconductors each year than Malaysia and Singapore. It would have to increase exports by orders of magnitude to catch up, which is unrealistic in the near term,” said Robert Walker, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre.

Thailand’s traditional role in the semiconductor chain has largely been confined to back-end work such as assembly, packaging and testing, according to Pavida.

“Expanding into front-end chip manufacturing and design will take a lot more than financial incentives and a government push to attract investment,” she said. “Both design and front-end manufacturing demand highly specialised technology and skills that simply aren’t as readily available in Thailand today as they are in Singapore and Malaysia.”

While Thailand’s policy appeared to be “well-designed” and “appropriately ambitious and realistic”, it would have to be a “decades-long strategy” – particularly if it wanted to become a leading player in the region, Walker said.

“Siam Silica’s focus on skill pipelines, rationalising government support mechanisms, and trying to leverage regional cooperation all look positive. Thailand is unlikely to overtake leaders like Malaysia and Singapore but can still make itself indispensable to regional supply chains,” he said.

Managing expectations

Thailand would have to be realistic in its expectations, Pavida said.

“Thailand is trying to build this ecosystem in 2026, when Singapore and Malaysia already began that journey some 50 years ago – and neither of them is standing still,” she said.

“So there is a lot of catching up, and even leapfrogging, that Thailand will need to do if it wants to become a central player in an integrated regional supply chain.”

Siam Silica’s success will depend on the effectiveness of its implementation, according to Pradittha Werasakun and Piriya Piriyakrit, senior analysts at BowerGroupAsia.

While Thailand has established its strengths in the downstream semiconductor segment, it needs to solve key issues such as limited wafer manufacturing capability, technology transfer, and high-skilled talent to build the ecosystem required to support its goal as a central hub in the region.

The greater challenge might be political rather than technical, Werasakun and Piriyakrit told This Week in Asia.

“The initiative builds on momentum generated under the previous Pheu Thai-led government, which demonstrated its ability to mobilise investment behind strategic sectors such as data centres. Siam Silica is now being advanced by Deputy Prime Minister and MHESI Minister Yodchanan as a national priority. However, semiconductor ecosystems require sustained policy support over many years,” they said.

“Given Thailand’s changing coalition dynamics, investors will likely pay close attention to whether the initiative remains a consistent cross-government priority or becomes associated with a particular political leadership or ministry.”

The country’s approach to work with Asean could also come up against nationalist ambitions.

“The six Asean countries with a stake in the semiconductor value chain all want to hold on to the highest value-creating segments for themselves. That dynamic may end up making their relationship more competitive than complementary,” Pavida said.

With a bit of patience, though, Thailand could become a leading player in the region, Walker said.

“Thailand has a strong manufacturing ecosystem and pre-existing semiconductor capabilities, with a relatively well-educated workforce. Combined with a competitive wage level, Thailand is well positioned to push a strategy to become a larger semiconductor hub in the region,” he said.

Rather than meeting its competition head on, Thailand could be a helpmeet, Werasakun and Piriyakrit said.

“Thailand’s competitive advantage lies in complementing, rather than replicating, the strengths of other Asean semiconductor hubs,” they said.

Siam Silica was drafted “to attract companies to help Thailand build a semiconductor ecosystem, and not to compete across the entire value chain in this early stage”.

By building on its existing strengths, Thailand could carve out a niche contributing to the broader value chain of the digital economy, Pavida said.

“One bright spot is the country’s dominance in hard disk drives, which are becoming an integral part of the AI ecosystem, as hyperscalers and data centres increasingly need cheap, high-capacity storage at scale,” she said.

“It may not be as glamorous as advanced chipmaking, but it gives Thailand a differentiated path – becoming an essential, if unglamorous, link in the AI supply chain, while building up a more highly skilled ecosystem and workforce over time.”

Ultimately, a more realistic benchmark is whether companies view Thailand’s contributions as indispensable, according to the BowerGroupAsia analysts.

“If Thailand can deepen its strengths in selected segments while continuing to attract strategic investment and develop skilled talent, then it can become an important regional semiconductor node.”

item.title: [SCMP] Climate crisis leaves Malaysia with hot-headed youth
item.description:
Young Malaysians are reporting worsening illnesses, heat-related health problems and disruptions to basic services as climate change intensifies, raising questions over whether the country’s adaptation policies can protect future generations.

Unicef Malaysia’s National Youth Climate Change Survey 2025, released in July, found that climate change was no longer only an environmental challenge but an immediate public health and economic issue.

The survey gathered responses from 1,420 young people aged 15 to 30 across Malaysia between June and October 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Young Malaysians are reporting worsening illnesses, heat-related health problems and disruptions to basic services as climate change intensifies, raising questions over whether the country’s adaptation policies can protect future generations.

Unicef Malaysia’s National Youth Climate Change Survey 2025, released in July, found that climate change was no longer only an environmental challenge but an immediate public health and economic issue.

The survey gathered responses from 1,420 young people aged 15 to 30 across Malaysia between June and October 2025.

Experts warned that policymakers must invest not only in reducing emissions but also in adapting to more frequent heatwaves, floods and other climate-related shocks, or risk deeper disruption to children’s health, education and Malaysia’s future workforce.

Unicef said the survey’s findings showed climate change was affecting young people’s health and well-being, with respondents reporting significant concerns: one in four, or 25.9 per cent, said existing illnesses had worsened, while 19.7 per cent reported skin conditions, 18 per cent cited heat-related illnesses and 14.3 per cent respiratory problems.

More than half said climate-related disasters had affected their access to essential services, including information, education and safe spaces.

Dr Jemilah Mahmood, executive director of the Sunway Centre for Planetary Health, said the Unicef findings showed the issue had evolved from an environmental concern into a public health challenge.

“We are already seeing the classic climate and health picture – direct injury, infectious disease, exacerbation of chronic conditions and psychological burden, all occurring simultaneously in a population aged 15 to 30, at what should be their healthiest years,” she said.

Experts say the findings underscore Malaysia’s need to emphasise adaptation plans, arguing that climate resilience should act as an investment in the country’s future workforce.

“It is no longer an either-or conversation. Malaysia must continue reducing emissions while significantly strengthening adaptation,” said Renard Siew, climate adviser at the Malaysia-based Centre for Governance and Political Studies.

Siew said children and young people were among the most vulnerable to climate change, and the biggest gap remained implementation for adaptation across all sectors.

The cost of inaction would exceed the costs of adaptation, he said, adding that more frequent heat stress, disease outbreaks and climate-related disruptions would affect productivity, increase healthcare expenditure and widen social inequalities.

“Over time, this would weaken our workforce competitiveness and economic resilience,” he said.

Public health experts warn that young children are among the most vulnerable to extreme heat because their bodies regulate temperatures less effectively, leading them to become dehydrated more quickly than adults.

“Their body’s heat-coping mechanism is more easily overwhelmed in these situations, such as getting dehydrated faster and the body’s cooling mechanism being overwhelmed more easily,” Dr Venu Gopalan, a Kuala Lumpur-based private practitioner, told This Week in Asia.

Immediate health risks of extreme heat, he said, included heat cramps, fainting, heat exhaustion and heatstrokes that could even cause death.

Gopalan warned that in the long term, repeated extreme heat exposure could lead to deteriorating kidney function and worsening heart and lung diseases, while increasing the risk of stroke caused by dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

While Malaysia had big ambitions, climate, health and education often operated independently, Siew said.

“We need climate risk assessments embedded in schools, stronger heat-health action plans, better air quality management, and greater investment in climate-resilient public infrastructure where young people learn and live,” he said.

The Malaysian Meteorological Department has repeatedly issued hot weather alerts this year, as temperatures hit between 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) and 40 degrees between March and May in the northern states and some parts of Sabah.

On Monday, data from the department showed that Kuala Krai in Kelantan registered the country’s highest temperature, at 35.7 degrees, followed by Temerloh in Pahang at 35.3 degrees.

The heat was not without consequences, as the Ministry of Health recorded a total of 73 heat-related illnesses from January to July this year.

According to national news agency Bernama, Public Health Medicine Specialist Dr Hazlina Yahaya said the cases involved 59 reports of heat exhaustion, six exertional heatstrokes, four heatstrokes, two cases of post-partum hyperpyrexia (high fever following childbirth), and two heat cramps.

Four deaths have been reported: two adults and two children aged two and four.

Progress but with gaps

In a statement on July 31, the World Meteorological Organization warned that the extreme heat phenomenon El Nino would continue to intensify steadily, dominating global climate patterns between August and October this year.

The agency said this would increase the likelihood of above-normal temperatures, driving significant shifts in rainfall patterns. “The developing El Nino is expected to shape weather patterns across many parts of the world in the months ahead.”

Gopalan said Malaysia’s current public health measures to address heat-related risks were inadequate, arguing that warnings alone were insufficient, especially for those who could not avoid prolonged exposure, such as outdoor workers, the homeless, and students.

“Early signs of heat stress should be recognised early by the community to enable rapid preventive measures to be taken,” he said. “Simply telling people to stay out of the sun is not practical for large segments of the community.”

Jemilah said while Malaysia had taken important steps – including identifying public health as a priority sector under the National Adaptation Plan, introducing heatwave health action plans and advancing climate legislation – implementation was still far behind.

According to Jemilah, the biggest challenge is ensuring national climate ambitions are translated and coordinated across health, education and local government, particularly as more than half of the young people affected by climate-related disasters reported lacking access to at least one essential service.

“The health aspect is lagging behind the exposure,” Jemilah said.

Siew warned that such gaps reflected a broader weakness in Malaysia’s climate adaptation effort where health, education and environmental policies were still often developed in silos despite their overlapping risks from extreme weather.

Climate adaptation, he added, should not be confined to environmental ministries.

“Even if we achieve our climate targets, the impacts of climate change are already here because children and young people are among the most vulnerable,” he said. “Investing in climate resilience today is ultimately an investment in our future human capital.”

item.title: [SCMP] Bangkok branches out: secret to Thai capital’s green revival
item.description:
In recent years, Thailand’s capital has discovered a surprising new attraction to add to its temples, shopping malls and street food: urban greenery. Unlike the others, which took decades to develop, Bangkok’s green credentials are a more recent phenomenon, emerging only during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Despite their novelty, the city’s greening efforts are already bearing fruit. Visitors returning to Bangkok after the pandemic are often surprised by how green and walkable the city has become. It comes as a nice surprise given the city’s long-standing reputation as a concrete jungle with chronic traffic jams and accompanying air pollution.

It is even more unusual considering how Thai politics, in the last two decades, has been highly polarised. Bangkok’s early success in urban greening shows that it is possible, despite contentious politics and a divided and highly unequal society, to build a societal consensus around making the city greener.
item.content:encoded:
In recent years, Thailand’s capital has discovered a surprising new attraction to add to its temples, shopping malls and street food: urban greenery. Unlike the others, which took decades to develop, Bangkok’s green credentials are a more recent phenomenon, emerging only during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Despite their novelty, the city’s greening efforts are already bearing fruit. Visitors returning to Bangkok after the pandemic are often surprised by how green and walkable the city has become. It comes as a nice surprise given the city’s long-standing reputation as a concrete jungle with chronic traffic jams and accompanying air pollution.

It is even more unusual considering how Thai politics, in the last two decades, has been highly polarised. Bangkok’s early success in urban greening shows that it is possible, despite contentious politics and a divided and highly unequal society, to build a societal consensus around making the city greener.

There are three lessons from Bangkok’s urban greenery playbook that other cities, including Hong Kong, should pay heed to.

Clear goals

This first is to set clear, measurable goals. In December 2019, the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) launched the Green Bangkok 2030 initiative that set three ambitious targets:

Increase green spaces in the city to 10 square metres (110 square feet) per person from 7.6–7.8 square metres per person;

Increase the green spaces that people can access within 400 metres – or five minutes’ walk – to at least 50 per cent of Bangkok’s total area; and

Increase the urban tree canopy to 30 per cent of Bangkok’s total area.

In mid-2022, the BMA initiated the Bangkok Million Tree Planting Project to increase urban green spaces, reduce air and dust pollution, and cool the city. Initially, the project sought to plant 1 million trees in the city by 2025. But after that goal was surpassed by mid-2024, it was increased by another 1 million. To date, nearly 1.2 million trees have been planted.

Pocket parks have also been built under transit lines and expressways as well as on under-utilised public or private lands such as abandoned piers, neglected canal paths and even garbage dumps.

The main benefit of setting such goals is to demonstrate the government’s seriousness of intent and its willingness to be held accountable. Governments are seldom short of visions but without committing to measurable goals and coming up with specific implementation plans such as the Million Tree Project, these will just be cheap talk.

A second benefit is to define exactly what is being measured and targeted. For example, much of Bangkok’s urban green spaces is not easily accessible. Actively accessible urban green spaces in Bangkok stand at a low 1.5-1.7 square metres per capita, well below the World Health Organization’s guideline of at least 9 square metres per capita for a healthy city. This is why the second target under the Green Bangkok 2030 blueprint is necessary: to highlight the importance of increasing green spaces that can be easily accessed by residents.

In a similar vein, BMA’s tree-planting initiative has not been sufficient to offset the city’s loss of urban tree canopy due to deforestation. This is why the third Green Bangkok 2030 target matters: to emphasise the protection of existing, mature trees even as new ones are planted.

Public support

The second lesson is to build public support and momentum with politically salient early successes. For Bangkok, this came in the form of the Benjakitti Forest Park, which opened in early 2022.

Situated between the two main commercial areas – Sukhumvit Road and Sathorn Road – the park has already become a popular destination that attracts tens of thousands of users daily. It also connects to the older Lumpini Park via a 1.6km-long treetop bridge that is reminiscent of New York’s High Line.

Sitting on 720,000 square metres of what used to be brownfield land that previously housed tobacco factories and warehouses, Benjakitti has become the city’s main green lung. Equally impressive is the fact that the forest park was planned to be a low-cost, low-maintenance operation through a self-sustaining, “messy nature” design and reliance on native plants to regenerate organically.

Since its opening, Benjakitti has served various environmental and social objectives. For example, its woodlands and constructed wetlands act as sponges to mitigate flooding in the city. It is home to diverse wildlife – including 91 species of birds – and its numerous boardwalks over the wetlands and a canopy skywalk provide visitors with an immersive urban nature experience. The sports centre and museum, both converted from old warehouses, provide residents with much-needed space for leisure activities, while an open-air amphitheatre can host events for 15,000 people.

Besides being aesthetically pleasing, the various functions of the forest park have helped endear it to the public. That it was built for under US$20 per square metre and was completed in about 18 months during the pandemic – a time when everyone could see the need for open public spaces – shows the BMA’s ability to deliver sustainability projects on time and on budget.

It is hardly surprising, therefore, that just four years after it opened, the park is already celebrated as the most vivid showcase of how Green Bangkok 2030 is transforming the city.

Good connections

Urban greening initiatives are also more likely to succeed if they are combined with efforts to make the city more walkable and public transit more accessible. To support the former, the BMA has upgraded more than 1,100km of pavements in recent years, including some along canals in the historic Hua Lamphong district.

While public transit in Bangkok has improved in recent years, the system is still inadequate for a sprawling city of more than 10 million. The sprawl makes public transit less viable financially, as more and longer lines are needed to serve a dispersed population. Reducing it, in turn, requires significant changes to urban and land-use planning.

Harnessing the energies of the private sector and the community is also key to the long-term success of greening efforts. Encouragingly, new commercial developments in Bangkok seem to have embraced the city’s greening push. For instance, Bangkok’s highest office building at the new One City Centre development in Ploenchit incorporates a large and verdant green space, including a rooftop garden.

Bangkok residents can also join tree-growing campaigns and support local groups to monitor and protect urban forests. The BMA engages local networks to come up with better rules for tree trimming and public space management.

Bangkok’s transformation into a green, walkable and sustainable city is far from complete. But already, its achievements in the last few years are a clear demonstration of what setting measurable goals, taking implementation seriously, having highly visible early success stories and synergising with the rest of society can do.

Donald Low is Senior Lecturer and Professor of Practice of Public Policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong aims to be a global tech hub, but can it hold on to its young talent?
item.description:
At just 18, Hong Kong tech enthusiasts Rexan Wong Chak-chi and Ken Mochizuki are both rushing to deliver their business ideas.

However, their choices of launch pad could not be further apart. While Wong is eyeing Silicon Valley in the United States for better support, Mochizuki is keen to stay in the city and contribute to the local community.

Their contrasting approaches highlight Hong Kong’s advantages and challenges as it strives to become a global innovation and talent hub under China’s strategic blueprint, with artificial intelligence (AI) and research transformation listed among the priorities of the city’s first five-year plan, to be released by the government later this year.
item.content:encoded:
At just 18, Hong Kong tech enthusiasts Rexan Wong Chak-chi and Ken Mochizuki are both rushing to deliver their business ideas.

However, their choices of launch pad could not be further apart. While Wong is eyeing Silicon Valley in the United States for better support, Mochizuki is keen to stay in the city and contribute to the local community.

Their contrasting approaches highlight Hong Kong’s advantages and challenges as it strives to become a global innovation and talent hub under China’s strategic blueprint, with artificial intelligence (AI) and research transformation listed among the priorities of the city’s first five-year plan, to be released by the government later this year.

While the city boasts cutting-edge university research, critics have warned that an increasingly risk-averse culture and a lack of early-stage support may push young tech talent towards overseas ecosystems.

California dreaming

Wong developed an interest in AI when he was 15 after joining a class on building mobile applications.

He later connected with many leading tech entrepreneurs through X, formerly known as Twitter, and built an AI-powered app called Text Behind Image in 2024. He said the app allowed its 500,000 users to design images with text behind featured objects.

Despite launching his first product in Hong Kong, Wong is looking to San Francisco and nearby Silicon Valley as the future launch pad for his AI business, believing the US tech hub can offer him better support.

“The main reason was really the access to support for early-stage founders. In Hong Kong, I think there is really a lack of support,” said Wong, a computer science undergraduate at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“In San Francisco, there are a lot of incubators that help young founders go from zero to one.”

In January, he joined a two-month incubation programme with Founders Inc, a major San Francisco-based start-up community, making connections and receiving guidance from those with experience.

The “beauty” of the programme was having founders at different stages under the same roof, allowing them to discuss problems they faced, he said.

Intending to run an AI-powered market analytics company in the future, Wong is busy reaching out to tech start-ups in San Francisco and observing their operations.

Wong also pointed to the United States’ early adoption of advanced AI tools, such as models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, as an advantage, while most Hongkongers used AI “at a very basic level” and some tools were not even available in the city.

“So it is really a lack of talent density, a lack of support and a lack of accessibility to these tools and knowledge on how to use frontier technology that holds Hong Kong back, which is why I picked San Francisco over Hong Kong,” he said.

Silicon Valley has been ranked the top start-up ecosystem in the world, while Hong Kong has come 29th, according to this year’s Global Startup Ecosystem Report, released by consultancy firm Startup Genome.

On a scale of one to 10, Hong Kong scored only two to four for its start-up performance, funding, talent, market reach and the degree to which it encourages AI start-ups. In contrast, Silicon Valley received full marks for each of these indicators.

Hong Kong only scored one for its research and development capacity, compared with Silicon Valley’s score of five.

Other Asian markets, such as Singapore and Seoul, and some major mainland Chinese cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Hangzhou, also outperformed Hong Kong.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said Beijing’s strength lay in its strong research capabilities, supported by top universities and close collaboration among the industrial, education and research sectors.

South Korea excelled because major enterprises devoted resources to research in key sectors such as semiconductors and biotechnology, while Singapore had outperformed Hong Kong because of its high density of venture capital firms and incubators – all of which Hong Kong could learn from, Shui added.

“If we cannot have our own major [tech] companies now, we should think about how to attract some of the largest institutions from other places to operate in Hong Kong,” he said.

According to the government’s investment arm, InvestHK, Hong Kong was home to 5,221 start-ups as of 2025, with 186 of them focusing on core or applied AI.

The San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley, has nearly 200,000 funded start-ups, with 80 per cent of funding going into AI, according to start-up data tracking platform dealroom.co.

‘A-Eye’ funding

But as Mochizuki sees it, Hong Kong’s young tech entrepreneurs are blessed with abundant support, and the only problem is that they are not told about available resources, so more publicity was needed.

Mochizuki, who is studying electrical engineering at City University (CityU), learned coding on his own in 2022, when he was still in secondary school and the Covid-19 pandemic forced pupils to study at home.

Within two years, he built “A-Eye”, an AI shopping assistant designed to help visually impaired people identify products and compare prices.

The project recently received HK$200,000 (US$25,500) in funding from CityU and the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) through the university’s HK Tech 300 project.

CityU’s law school also offered free legal consultation under the programme, he added.

“My goal is to stay in Hong Kong and try to use my skills to contribute to this place and serve people,” Mochizuki said.

“Although other countries like the US or the United Kingdom may have better resources or a better culture for start-ups, the competition is much [fiercer] than in Hong Kong.”

Apart from university-based projects, Hong Kong authorities have made multiple start-up programmes available through the government-backed HKSTP and Cyberport.

HKSTP offers a range of start-up support programmes covering different stages, including ideation, incubation, acceleration and global expansion.

According to its latest annual report, 570 start-ups graduated from its support programme in 2024-25, and it spent more than HK$415 million on incubation and tenant support during the period.

Cyberport had more than 200 start-ups graduate from its entrepreneurship schemes in 2025-26, including an incubation programme offering grants of up to HK$500,000 and rental subsidies of up to HK$200,000, as well as the Creative Micro Fund, which helps early-stage start-ups move towards incubation.

The Home and Youth Affairs Bureau has also launched a funding scheme for young entrepreneurs to start their businesses in Hong Kong, Macau and the nine Guangdong cities under Beijing’s Greater Bay Area blueprint.

Shui said funding for early-stage start-ups remained insufficient as local investors preferred “easier and more certain” options, and investment activity tended to be cautious amid a turbulent economic environment.

“Tech start-ups have a higher chance of failure, but when they succeed, they can bring high returns,” he said, urging the government to step up support for early-stage founders.

A start-up usually goes through multiple rounds of financing, including the pre-seed stage, when founders develop an idea and work towards a minimum viable product (MVP); the seed stage, when they refine the MVP for market fit; and the series A to C stages, when they scale the business, before exiting through an initial public offering or an acquisition.

According to a recent Our Hong Kong Foundation report, only 10 per cent of founders in the city received support from venture capital or angel investors, 30 per cent got funding from the government, and 85 per cent had to tap personal savings.

But the report highlighted a stark imbalance in the government’s funding allocation.

As of 2024, funding was concentrated heavily at the pre-seed stage, at HK$49.5 billion, and in late-stage investment beyond series C, at HK$62 billion, leaving those in between – often described as the “valley of death” – largely underserved, with only HK$3.4 billion in capital support.

Apart from a lack of funding and support, Hong Kong founders have complained on online forums about high office rents, talent costs and the city’s small market size, with some pointing to places such as Bangkok and Shenzhen as better choices.

Headwinds

Alberto Moel, a professor of practice in finance at the University of Hong Kong, said it would be harder for young entrepreneurs such as Wong and Mochizuki to grow businesses built from their own ideas in the city, as the government and universities dominated the local start-up ecosystem.

“We are in a stage in Hong Kong where university research projects are the ones driving the pool of innovation,” he said.

“If your idea is outside that pool, then you are basically up against the usual headwinds in venture capital that have been around for a long time, namely that it is difficult to get capital and difficult to put together a team.”

Moel added that Hong Kong’s risk-averse culture was also reflected in the investment behaviour of venture capitalists, resulting in limited capital for very early stage start-ups or those taking on more risk.

In contrast, funding for such companies in the US was much broader because the culture there was more inclined to “try things and see what happens”, while there was much more capital in the country, he said.

Hong Kong’s young entrepreneurs would stand a better chance of success if they looked at opportunities arising from university research projects, Moel said.

“If the policy is not focused on [independent ideas], you are more likely to fail, and it is going to discourage you,” he said.

“I would recommend young entrepreneurs look at the existing platforms and work within them because you will find much better chances and opportunities to monetise [ideas] into a company.”

The government should do more to publicise and create opportunities for building businesses from research projects by linking tech-minded businesspeople with innovative ideas, he added.

Derek Chim, HKSTP’s head of start-up ecosystem and development, agreed that access to early-stage capital remained important in helping innovative ventures scale up, and said the park had teamed up with the private sector to catalyse start-up growth.

“While different investors naturally have different risk appetites and return expectations, we are seeing growing interest in deep-tech and innovation-driven companies that require longer development horizons,” he said.

The Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau said the government attached importance to encouraging and cultivating a thriving I&T ecosystem for start-ups, and acknowledged that its sustainability relied heavily on private sector participation.

It said the government would launch an HK$10 billion Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund this year to channel more social capital into “emerging and future industries of strategic importance”, benefiting companies at different stages of development.

Despite the growing range of start-up funding options in Hong Kong, Mochizuki and Wong agreed the city’s cautious culture still made it hard for young entrepreneurs to strike out on their own.

“In Hong Kong, the culture drives most people down a very traditional path – primary school, high school, graduating from college, working in a full-time job – and it is very hard to pivot if you want to change your profession based on your interests,” Wong said.

“Everything is laid out for you, and this sense of security is embedded into young Hong Kong people growing up.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why was a US Yale graduate hounded out of his job promoting Chinese culture?
item.description:
In just two months, Yale graduate Edward Kuperman went from being praised by Chinese state media to being bombarded by public accusations that he was a spy.

It began with a June 18 article from state news agency Xinhua, in which he was described as an eager 24-year-old sinophile who made the unconventional choice of spurning China’s eastern metropolises to live in Dunhuang, an oasis in the country’s northwestern Gansu province.

His interest in China started with a Chinese language class in junior high school, as well as books and films about China, Xinhua reported. At 17, he was an exchange student in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After returning to the United States, his parents hired a Chinese tutor for him, it said.
item.content:encoded:
In just two months, Yale graduate Edward Kuperman went from being praised by Chinese state media to being bombarded by public accusations that he was a spy.

It began with a June 18 article from state news agency Xinhua, in which he was described as an eager 24-year-old sinophile who made the unconventional choice of spurning China’s eastern metropolises to live in Dunhuang, an oasis in the country’s northwestern Gansu province.

His interest in China started with a Chinese language class in junior high school, as well as books and films about China, Xinhua reported. At 17, he was an exchange student in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After returning to the United States, his parents hired a Chinese tutor for him, it said.

Kuperman, who also goes by the Chinese name Gu Aihua – “Loving China” – started his first job as an intern live-streamer at the Dunhuang Culture International Communication Centre (DCICC) in April, the article said, adding that he believed the city was a “unique entryway to observing China, understanding China and telling China’s stories”.

Dunhuang was for centuries a stop along the Silk Road and in the article Kuperman’s life there is presented as typically rosy. One anecdote describes how he spent three hours helping a Dutch tourist find their lost backpack. “Kuperman told the relieved tourist, ‘In China, nothing gets lost.’ The tourist nodded in agreement,” the article said.

The DCICC’s Instagram account featured Kuperman in three videos in May and June, interviewing participants at the Third World Conference of Sinologists and introducing the city’s Crescent Lake, one of its main attractions.

Dressed in a buttoned-up waistcoat and trousers, he walked in the sand around the lake, introducing it as a place lovers flocked to. “I don’t know about romance for me, but I will say that I love this place,” he said.

But Kuperman’s problems began in July, when he was hired by the Dunhuang Convergence Media Centre, an outlet run by the local government.

The hiring notice, which was picked up by Chinese media, showed that Kuperman was the only foreigner among three new hires. The other two women, both Chinese, had studied translation and communications at British universities.

Posts questioning Kuperman’s qualifications soon emerged on Chinese social media. Some claimed that he received an annual salary of 900,000 yuan (US$133,000), and questioned the pay. “Aren’t they using taxpayers’ money to pamper foreigners?”

That salary would far exceed what a Western graduate would usually expect to be paid in China. For a fresh Chinese graduate, that wage would be astronomical. According to the Hong Kong-based MyCOS Research Institute, the average starting salary for Chinese bachelor’s graduates in the class of 2025 was 77,220 yuan a year.

Online rage and suspicion were further inflamed by the discovery that Kuperman had studied Chinese at National Taiwan University and had interned at the conservative American Enterprise Institute’s Coalition Defence of Taiwan programme.

Hu Xijin, the former editor-in-chief of state-run tabloid Global Times, which has an English edition, waded into the controversy.

He wrote in a now-deleted online post that most foreigners employed by Chinese organisations had “complex experiences”, such as previously working in American media or think tanks, where they may have written reports viewed as unfavourable by the Chinese.

Hu said netizens wanted to “spoil his job” using spy accusations, because they were unhappy Kuperman was paid so much.

Kuperman has said that his interest in East Asia is cultural, not political. He previously wrote on Yale’s website that he studied the region “because of its unique combination of ancient tradition and dialogue with the West”.

Regardless of netizens’ intentions, their furious posting got results.

By Friday, Kuperman had decided not to take the job, state broadcaster CCTV reported. The local authorities clarified that he was only offered an annual salary of about 330,000 yuan – not 900,000 yuan – with various allowances on top. An investigation had been launched to see if there were any problems with the hiring, it said.

A salary of 330,000 yuan is within the normal range for Western graduates working in China.

Kuperman could not be contacted for comment, while the DCICC and local media centre did not respond to interview requests.

Einar Tangen, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and chairman of Asia Narratives, said that while Dunhuang was a city of just 200,000 people, it had more than 20 million visitors annually, with its Mogao Caves representing shared heritage spanning Buddhist, Persian, Greek, Indian and Chinese civilisations.

Dunhuang has been using this identity to try to tell its story to global audiences through what it calls the “innovative Dunhuang model”. A 2025 article from the city’s propaganda department said the DCICC was an important part of that effort, with 28 global social media accounts, 800,000 fans, 5,100 posts and more than 65 million cumulative views.

“We will make Dunhuang an important window for the world to understand China and feel Chinese civilisation,” it said.

The Chinese authorities are keen to win foreigners’ praise for the country’s heritage and modern technology. In 2025, when American influencer IShowSpeed visited Beijing and Shanghai, the Chinese embassy in the US said he was “bridging cultural gaps” and multiple state media outlets ran glowing pieces praising the trip.

Governments often actively invite foreign influencers to China. In June last year, the Hainan provincial tourism board invited 19 influencers from 12 countries to explore the southern island and produce content.

Despite this, a political scientist who wished to stay anonymous acknowledged that in recent years Chinese public opinion had become increasingly sensitive when it came to any issue involving foreigners. He said the resolution of any controversy depended on the style of the decision-maker.

“If you have an open mind or do not think [such backlash] matters, then this will boost cross-cultural exchanges,” he said.

Tangen added that he was worried by the instinct to build walls rather than bridges.

“Dunhuang’s entire model is built on openness. It processes visa-on-arrival for international tourists, has established sister-city ties with cities abroad and hosted over 600 global events in 2025,” he said.

“China is extending visas and inviting the world to see the country as it is, not as hostile or ignorant media portray it. If Kuperman had genuine issues in his background, then they should be addressed – through proper channels.”

item.title: [SCMP] China hits back at US with barrage of sanctions, drone industry curbs
item.description:
China has hit back against a round of US sanctions with a barrage of counter-sanctions targeting a group of American entities and a tightening of export restrictions on the drone supply chain, the Ministry of Commerce announced on Wednesday.

The export controls will subject any shipments of “drones, their key components and related technologies” to the US to “strict case-by-case scrutiny”, with the measures set to take effect immediately, the ministry said in a statement, citing the need to “safeguard national security and meet China’s international commitments on non-proliferation”.

On the same day, the commerce ministry also added six US entities to its countermeasures list – banning Chinese entities and individuals from cooperating with them – over allegations that they had assisted US sanctions related to China’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, describing their conduct as “egregious”.
item.content:encoded:
China has hit back against a round of US sanctions with a barrage of counter-sanctions targeting a group of American entities and a tightening of export restrictions on the drone supply chain, the Ministry of Commerce announced on Wednesday.

The export controls will subject any shipments of “drones, their key components and related technologies” to the US to “strict case-by-case scrutiny”, with the measures set to take effect immediately, the ministry said in a statement, citing the need to “safeguard national security and meet China’s international commitments on non-proliferation”.

On the same day, the commerce ministry also added six US entities to its countermeasures list – banning Chinese entities and individuals from cooperating with them – over allegations that they had assisted US sanctions related to China’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, describing their conduct as “egregious”.

A seventh US company, Compliance Testing LLC, was added to the countermeasures list for assisting the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in introducing measures that “endanger China’s sovereignty, security and development interests”.

Separately, the commerce ministry launched a national security investigation regarding imported printing and copying office equipment with foreign-made software. US tech firms – such as Microsoft and HP – are seen as major players in the printing software sector.

The inquiry is the first to be launched using the new national security provisions laid out in China’s revised foreign trade law, according to the commerce ministry, adding the investigation would cover the effect of foreign government policies on China’s security interests.

The measures are a response to a string of recent actions by US authorities.

Last week, Washington added 43 Chinese companies to its own entity list under the Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act, covering sectors ranging from food and cotton to pharmaceuticals, metals and lithium production. Beijing has repeatedly denied allegations of forced labour in Xinjiang.

Meanwhile, the FCC banned the import and sale of new foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters, two sectors where China is a leading global player.

Beijing is extending the rare-earths playbook up the value chain, from raw inputs like germanium to finished-goods components

Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis

“China’s countermeasures have been restrained overall. China values the hard-won stability of China-US economic and trade relations. We hope the US side can work with China in the same direction,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.

But the ministry demanded that Washington immediately rescind its measures, warning that China would retaliate further if the US pressed ahead with new restrictions.

In response, a senior US administration official said Washington was “deeply disappointed” that China “has chosen to announce another round of escalatory measures”.

“While our leaders have a close relationship, expanding the cycle of retaliation will not produce a durable solution,” the person said.

Analysts said Beijing’s response marked a “calibrated escalation” in the US and China’s ongoing trade and technology dispute, which has seen both sides attempt to gain strategic leverage by threatening to cut off access to key resources and technologies.

For some, the drone industry restrictions build on the tactics Beijing used during its trade war with Washington last year, when it tightened export controls over rare earth minerals – a vital industry where it controls most global supplies.

“Beijing is extending the rare-earths playbook up the value chain, from raw inputs like gallium and germanium to finished-goods components in a sector it dominates,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis.

Drones were already a point of friction in US-China relations. Chinese companies are the undisputed leaders in the industry, dominating the global supply chain. In December, the FCC banned the import of all new models of foreign-made drones and related components, citing national security risks.

Beijing appears to have taken particular issue with the timing of Washington’s latest actions. The US sanctions were announced on July 31, a day after Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng held a video call with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

During the call, China expressed serious concern over the US’ recent economic and trade moves, Xinhua reported. But Washington had pressed ahead with its measures “in complete disregard” of China’s repeated representations, the commerce ministry said.

The decision “seriously contravenes” the consensus reached by Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump during their recent meetings and seriously harms China’s “legitimate rights and interests”, according to the statement.

The contest is shifting from tariffs towards control over critical technologies, supply chains, and dual-use goods

Matteo Giovannini, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China

For Garcia-Herrero, Beijing was trying to signal it was “keeping its powder dry” as both sides race to “de-risk” their economies – plugging holes in their supply chains before the other side can weaponise the vulnerability.

Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said Beijing’s move was a reciprocal response rather than an escalation, pointing to Xi’s expected visit to Washington in September.

Xi and Trump last met during the US president’s visit to Beijing in May. At the time, Trump said Xi would visit America “on September 24, or thereabouts”, with subsequent meetings likely to take place on the sidelines of major international summits in November and December.

“Xi’s visit is an important event. Following China’s countermeasures and continued communication between the two sides, tensions are expected to ease,” Xu said, though he added that the possibility of engagement being derailed by further unilateral US actions could not be ruled out.

Matteo Giovannini, a senior finance manager at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, said the key signal was that “export controls are no longer exceptional policy tools, as they have become a normal feature of strategic competition”.

“The contest is shifting from tariffs towards control over critical technologies, supply chains, and dual-use goods, where both Washington and Beijing believe they possess meaningful leverage.”

item.title: [SCMP] Wok with Yan’s return: Hong Kong-Canadian TV chef Stephen Yan resurfaces decades after disappearing
item.description:
“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.
item.content:encoded:
