“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.

“When [Polo] went back to Italy, he learned how to make it all right,” says Yan to the camera, in his Cantonese-inflected English, “but he changed the name chow mein to spaghetti and changed wonton to ravioli. Wok the heck, I’m going to make one thing perfectly clear: I want to make this thing right and correct. I don’t want to make it the wrong way. I want to make it the Yan way.”

Once Yan had plated a dish, he’d invite someone from the audience to dine with him, and, this being Canada in the 1980s, they would not all be proficient with chopsticks. Yan would open a fortune cookie, translate the Chinese message inside and then, as the credits rolled, the rest of the studio audience would make sure no food went to waste.

With the coast-to-coast-to-coast reach of the CBC, Yan became a national figure and arguably the first Asian celebrity television chef in the West.

“I watched [Yan] with my grandparents because, back then, your house had one TV,” says Karon Liu, who was only a few months old when his family moved to Toronto in 1987, one of more than 355,600 Hongkongers who moved to Canada in the late 80s, according to the Canadian International Council. “So, what they watched, you had to watch,” says Liu, who is now a food reporter with the Toronto Star newspaper. He remembers his grandmother hollowing out a cucumber and filling it with stir-fried beef, making it look like a boat, because that’s what Stephen Yan did in one episode.

“He was the Chinese Julia Child. He wasn’t some snooty Michelin French chef; he cooked the way my grandmother would cook at home,” says Liu. “He explained a lot of ingredients that weren’t as well known outside of a Chinese audience at that time.”

While Chinese-Canadians delighted in Yan’s familiarity, other Canadians were learning that Chinese food was not just egg foo yung or sweet and sour chicken balls, a step towards the multiculturalism the country would more fully embrace. But then one day in 1995, after more than 500 episodes, Wok with Yan ended, and the chef was not seen on television or in other media again – well, until he briefly surfaced the year before last.

Born and raised in the Toronto, Ontario suburb of Scarborough in the 80s, one of Yan’s biggest fans was Steve Gaskin. Before he was old enough to go to school, Gaskin’s Guyanese father and Chinese mother would drop him off at his grandparents’ home at 7am before going to work, and pick him up 12 hours later.

“I found it very hard to connect with my gung-gung [maternal grandfather] because my parents never spoke Cantonese, and he didn’t speak much English. I took Cantonese lessons, but I didn’t retain any of it,” says Gaskin. His grandfather, who ran a laundromat business in his adopted home, brought his family from Hong Kong to Canada via Guyana more than 50 years ago.

“My gung-gung only communicated in Chinese,” says Gaskin, “but just from grunts and facial cues, I knew what he was saying.”

The pair managed to bond over Wok with Yan. “I would sit next to him on the La-Z-Boy and just without even talking, we would laugh at the jokes and he would just kind of nudge me when something funny came on, or he wanted me to watch the technique.

“In the 80s, Stephen Yan was probably the only Chinese-Canadian celebrity. I was probably six years old, and the only Asian person on the big screen was Bruce Lee or Jackie Chan, so to see somebody like Stephen Yan, who’s in Canada, who was so approachable, was really important.”

In 2018, Gaskin and a friend launched Retrokid, a company that, through T-shirts and accessories, recalls childhood memories for Gen Xers who grew up watching Canadian television shows such as Mr Dressup, Polka Dot Door and Degrassi. Gaskin was determined to track down his hero.

After years of dead ends, in 2022, he finally got a response. But it wasn’t until a year later that Yan agreed to meet him.

Gaskin is coy about how he finally got in contact with Yan, divulging only that the former chef wanted “to work with a company that understands everything he’s done”. And with the success of Retrokid and the wider appetites for online nostalgia spun into products, Yan the savvy businessman must have seen that the time was ripe for a revival.

“Stephen Yan always said that he appreciated that there was this personal connection I had with my gung-gung as to why he wanted to do this with us.”

Together, they turned out “Wok with Yan” T-shirts, hoodies, tote bags, badges and fridge magnets, bearing the chef’s likeness from his television days. And, of course, a range of aprons with witty Yan-isms has proved to be the bestseller.

To help launch the collection, Yan agreed to fly from Vancouver to Toronto in August 2024 for a meet-and-greet with fans.

“It was pretty shocking to see him just come out of the arrivals gate,” says Gaskin, who picked Yan up at the airport. “Like, oh my God, it’s Stephen Yan. I didn’t know if he was going to come off a plane in a wheelchair or on crutches, right? But no, he’s super strong and mentally healthy for 85.”

While Yan was in Toronto, Retrokid gave Liu a chance to interview the chef for the Star, and, like Gaskin, the reporter was transported back to his childhood.

“It was really surreal,” says Liu. “He was still making jokes, he was just like a grandpa, where you ask one question and then his answer is, like, 10 minutes long because he’s lived such a full life.”

According to what he said in the interview, it was Yan who decided to pull the plug on his show in 1995.

“One day, I asked my accountant how much money I needed to survive,” Yan told Liu. “He said I already had a house and I didn’t need a dollar more. I wanted to contribute my time to those less fortunate, so I helped out with orphanages and schools in places like Thailand and China. I had enough earthly belongings.

“Back then, I had three restaurants [in Vancouver] and I had three disciples, including Martin Yan [no relation; a Hong Kong-American who worked with Yan in the 70s],” he explained. His protégé’s own television show, Yan Can Cook, also first aired on Canadian television in 1978 (initially as Yan Can), before having a highly successful run in the US, on PBS.

Stephen Yan also told Liu that, after quitting the show, he spent more time with his family and became much more active. “I ran 11 marathons, four times at the Boston Marathon and won the masters division. I also climbed Mount Everest.”

For someone so beloved, there isn’t a lot of biographical information available online about Yan, and he guards his private life closely. His birth date, for example, is not widely known, only that he was born in Hong Kong in 1939.

Not long after, in December 1941, the Japanese occupation of the city began and basic ingredients such as rice, flour and oil were rationed.

“[As a child,] I was poor and went to people’s stores where they would give me leftover food,” Yan told Liu.

“I was spending my time on the streets next to a theatre that was starring a Chinese actor, who was Bruce Lee’s father. Bruce and I became friends, and we used to play in a nearby warehouse, but I needed a job.”

When Yan was nine years old, a restaurant cook gave him work in exchange for food. One of his most laborious tasks was to take thousands of lotus seeds from a pot of boiling water, without gloves, and use a toothpick to push out their bitter cores. After three months, Yan was allowed into the kitchen, to learn from the cook, who taught him how to kill and pluck chickens, and use every part of the bird, as well as shop for the best ingredients.

Yan claimed to have been the fastest dishwasher at the restaurant. “Humans are adaptable and can do anything if they have the opportunity,” he told Liu.

He became a fully-fledged cook, and when he was around 15 years old, the chief cook of the restaurant arranged for him to go to school. Later, Yan said, he was one of two students chosen by an American senator to study business administration in the US, to which he sailed on an 18-day voyage to San Francisco.

Fearing being called up to the military as the US fought in Vietnam, Yan crossed the border to Canada in the late 50s or early 60s, he told Liu, one of 20,000 to 30,000 draft dodgers to have done so, according to Canadian immigration statistics.

By the late 70s, Yan was already managing his own restaurants when he was noticed by a television talent scout while leading cooking demonstrations in a shopping mall in the run-up to Chinese New Year.

The weekly Yan’s Woking debuted on Vancouver station BCTV in 1978. Two years later, national broadcaster CBC bought the show, rebranded it as Wok with Yan and shifted formats to present a daily afternoon cooking series.

Gaskin says some 230 people showed up at Toronto’s storied Royal Theatre for 2024’s meet-and-greet.

“It was great to give [Yan] a platform where he could just say thank you to all of his fans and the fans showed up,” says Gaskin. “Obviously, we could have packed that theatre to 500 people, but we also wanted to give the fans a chance to meet him, to actually go up and take a photo, and they loved it.”

Since then, Yan has remained elusive. All attempts to contact him by this author have been fruitless. The Retrokid team has been sworn to secrecy; Liu says he never got direct contact. And even now, almost two years after Yan’s rarest of public appearances, he shows no signs of emerging into the spotlight again, even to contribute to this article, to connect with his hometown, Hong Kong.

Vancouverite Billy Snaychuk wasn’t at the meet-up but considers himself a fan. “My most favourite part about Stephen Yan would have to be his aprons, and the way he always made the audience laugh,” he says. “He just captured the audience right away from the get-go. He definitely caught me as a kid, because I just loved watching him.”

Snaychuk’s father, a fisherman and entrepreneur, got to know Yan through Chinese friends who caught fish for the chef, delivering them to his restaurant, Yan’s Garden. From the age of six, Snaychuk watched Wok with Yan with his mother every day after school.

“My parents had the largest collection of Stephen Yan books, and I remember sneaking out of my room in the middle of the night and grabbing his books on the bookshelf and bringing them back. And I would just look at all the pictures and read the recipes,” he recalls, with a chuckle.

Once a month, his parents invited friends over and cooked dishes from Yan’s cookbooks, including Snaychuk’s favourite, gold coin beef.

“The flavour profile in it is just next level. And the texture of the beef, you can almost chew it with the roof of your mouth and your tongue, it’s just that tender,” says Snaychuk, who would follow in his hero’s footsteps and become a chef himself. He was promoted to executive chef at the age of 28 and went into restaurant consulting and even competed in the Food Network Canada cooking reality TV show Wall of Chefs.

As he got older, Snaychuk paid attention to Yan’s technique, particularly how he created flavour profiles by adding ingredients to the wok at different times.

“A lot of people, when they cook, they just kind of throw everything in there. If you do that, the whole dish is basically going to taste the same. But if you add things at different times and take them out and put them back in, you layer the flavours. And that’s something I really noticed – he layered his flavours with his cooking.”

While watching Yan was a joy for so many, working for him was not always so pleasurable, says former assistant Brenda Gonneville, who also has no idea where Yan lives now. “He’s not the face you see on TV.”

In 1981, Yan hired a 26-year-old Gonneville to help him in his office, which was above Yan’s Chinese restaurant, in Port Coquitlam, British Columbia. She had worked as an assistant to high-powered executives in the steel industry, says Gonneville, so was “well versed in dealing with high-powered, difficult people”.

Her job, as a native English speaker, was to look after Yan’s public relations, devise witty lines for the aprons and procure props and have them shipped to Ottawa, where his show was taped for two seasons before moving back to Vancouver. She recalls being the only Caucasian in an office full of Cantonese-speaking people but says she got on well with all the other staff. Gonneville was aiming to forge a career in entertainment, so worked for a low wage. After paying rent, she says, she was left with enough money only for a diet of white rice and boiled eggs.

“After three months, I’d had enough,” she says, “because he is a perfectionist, and nothing pleases him. He’s a hard worker. He expects more than 100 per cent from his employees.”

One day, she says, he was dictating content for a show and Gonneville was struggling to write it all down in shorthand, because he was speaking quickly.

“He had me read it back and I said, ‘I’m sorry, I didn’t get most of that.’ I decided then and there, and so did he, that we’d come to the end of the road.”

Fortunately, her brief stint with Yan led to a 20-year career in film and television.

When she returned to pack up her things, the office manager “took my hand and said, ‘Don’t you worry, you lasted longer than anybody’”, she recalls with a laugh.

“[Yan’s] an A-type personality, he’s driven. He expected everybody to put in the same effort as him, and if you failed, he wouldn’t put up with it.”

Difficult he may have been for those he employed, but, given the delight he’s brought to television viewers, one cannot begrudge his telling the hosts of Toronto daytime talk show The Social, in August 2024, that, “I was hiding; I want a simple life.

“I […] cannot believe that people remember me after 30 years,” he said on The Social. “And they want to know, am I alive? I am! I’m alive!”

And maybe that’s enough, to know that he’s alive. With Yan now well into his 80s, a quiet, simple life is perhaps just wok he needs.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Surprising’ how quickly China’s military is closing gap with US: analyst Lyle Goldstein
item.description:
Lyle Goldstein is a senior fellow at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs at Brown University, and director of Asia engagement at the Washington think tank Defence Priorities.

How do you assess the progress of the People’s Liberation Army’s modernisation drive in the past 10 years and its significance in modern military history? How do you forecast the PLA’s position in 2027, which it set forth as one of three vaguely defined modernisation benchmark years?

My view is that China’s military has made tremendous progress in the process of modernisation over the last 10 years. It’s almost like an aircraft going full throttle or a car that’s going into fourth gear. It really is the pace that has picked up a lot. We had an inkling that this was under way and that major results were going to be forthcoming. But here they are. I have to say, as a military analyst, it’s very impressive. I might even go as far as to say that it could even be unprecedented in its scale and dimensions, and also implications.
item.content:encoded:
Lyle Goldstein is a senior fellow at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs at Brown University, and director of Asia engagement at the Washington think tank Defence Priorities.

How do you assess the progress of the People’s Liberation Army’s modernisation drive in the past 10 years and its significance in modern military history? How do you forecast the PLA’s position in 2027, which it set forth as one of three vaguely defined modernisation benchmark years?

My view is that China’s military has made tremendous progress in the process of modernisation over the last 10 years. It’s almost like an aircraft going full throttle or a car that’s going into fourth gear. It really is the pace that has picked up a lot. We had an inkling that this was under way and that major results were going to be forthcoming. But here they are. I have to say, as a military analyst, it’s very impressive. I might even go as far as to say that it could even be unprecedented in its scale and dimensions, and also implications.

If we talk about history, what does it mean in modern military history? This is a very big moment. China has said for a long time it wants to be a world-leading military, a world-class military. Clearly, China is there. The areas where it has achieved that status seem to be increasing every day. In a sense, they have achieved what they’ve set out to do.

I know that a lot of people are very anxious about 2027, what it would mean and so forth. But I don’t think that’s the way to think about it. It goes without saying that, [10 years on] in 2037, China will be much, much stronger. Even so, this is part of a process. There clearly are programmes that are not really mature yet. Most obviously the aircraft carrier programme, but from what I can see, China has indeed a very formidable military.

There are areas where there’s now emerged a big discrepancy between China and other countries, and ultimately that does hurt China because there is fear. You can sense it in the region. There’s quite a palpable anxiety about where the region is going in a world where clearly the United States is playing less of a role and China is playing much more of a role.

If China was more transparent, people would begin to feel less anxious. Although it’s quite reasonable why China has in the past not been so transparent. Chinese military leaders would say, “we’re hiding our weakness” and that transparency is a luxury for the strong. Well, now China is strong, so it pays for China to gradually become more transparent.

Based on its latest modernisation, do you think the PLA is expediting its own pathway for military advancement or is it merely copying the history of other countries’ military development, such as that of the US? What are the major signs that suggest the former or latter?

Unquestionably, there’s been a lot of copying. Obviously, China is very proficient at that, but that is just normal. That’s how militaries improve, by mimicry, by taking the best practices of other militaries. It is an American cultural habit of disdaining the PLA because they say, “they took this, they took that”. And I’ll tell you, a lot of China’s most impressive platforms, the Y-20 military transport aircraft, for example, or the new naval and general utility helicopter Z-20, they look a lot like leading American platforms. No question about it. So, people kind of have a good laugh about that.

But my response is it’s quite plausible that the Chinese platform is actually superior. Just because the exterior looks similar does not mean they’re equivalent. And I do think that they have innovated. And by the way, so many standard Chinese PLA platforms are based off of Russian designs. China doesn’t deny that. They understand that to get ahead, you do whatever you have to do. It has pushed China to the forefront, and it would be foolish to dismiss Chinese development that way.

About five or eight years ago, we started to see some new developments. You could even put it down to the J-20 fifth-generation fighter jets, for example, as a first plunge into a very distinctive Chinese design for a major combat platform. We’re starting to see these things more across the board. It’s pretty clear that China now has the confidence to begin to have distinctive designs, and probably the biggest example is this new set of sixth-generation fighters. They have very different designs, where China begins to be the leader and the other countries are following. That’s a very important historical moment.

When I saw the first headlines about [China’s] September 2025 [military] parade, I remember thinking, “wow, that’s pretty remarkable”. But as I went over the details of what exactly was revealed there – and I thought I’d seen everything in this field – it was a moment of shock, just how many new types of platforms [there were].

I have said for years that it was rather stunning to me that the Chinese navy deploys a supersonic missile aboard its submarines. This was the YJ-18, and it’s pretty shocking. For the last decade, basically, China has had this very impressive anti-ship capability on board its submarines, and the US has no equivalent to that. But now that turns out to be a very dated assessment because now we have this new missile that was unveiled at the parade, the YJ-19, and it has a very distinctive shape, and indeed, Chinese sources confirm it’s a hypersonic missile.

So now China’s submarines are firing hypersonic anti-ship missiles, and the United States is still firing subsonic missiles from its submarines. It suggests that at least in this one realm of undersea warfare, that China is not just ahead but far ahead. That is a new reality. I don’t mean this trend holds for undersea warfare as a whole. Rather, I mean that one narrow domain of submarines firing anti-ship cruise missiles. But that’s an important issue. So, what we’re seeing is something quite momentous.

There has been a lot of talk about the narrowing gap between the US and China in their military capabilities. If the PLA modernisation drive continues, what do you think are the major areas where the PLA may gain an edge over the US?

That is a very tough question, to look into a crystal ball. The good news is the Chinese military has not been tested in combat. The point is that a lot of this is unknown. Now, US weapons have been tested more regularly. But again, that even is not a perfect crystal ball at all because a lot of these wars that the US has been fighting have been against much weaker opponents. So there has been no peer-to-peer engagement, thankfully.

We have seen a very gradual but steady increase in China’s capabilities. I think it started in air defence; we can imagine why Chinese air defence got serious before these other areas. Partly it was the lessons of the Korean war, but it was also that they were able to grasp the Russian technologies pretty quickly and move up several levels.

But what has been surprising now is how quickly they’ve closed the gap. I would even say at this point it’s hard to think of an area where they’re not either closing the gap or pushing ahead. In terms of the navy, sinking ships is pretty important. China seems to take that with utmost seriousness. I’m extremely impressed by this new array of anti-ship cruise missiles that we’ve seen. Basically, China’s done a lot of things in the realm of anti-ship weaponry that suggests that it’s ahead and not just ahead but far ahead.

What do you think are the usual misunderstandings about the PLA in the West? What do you think the US or other regional US allies are overestimating or underestimating about Chinese military capabilities?

I do believe the West engages in a vast tendency towards threat inflation, and I see it literally in almost every media article. You can see that there’s a natural anxiety at a period of major change. This rather pervasive hinting that China has very expansive military goals, whether it’s conquest of the western Pacific or Africa or the Middle East, is not warranted and constitutes analytical malpractice, to my estimate. I hasten to remind people all the time that there’s just no record at all of Chinese military aggression, certainly not in the modern era, and that should give us substantial confidence that we are not confronting some kind of enormous threat.

A lot of people in Washington are fond of saying, “China is much more powerful than the Soviet Union ever was. So we need to not just do what we did in the Cold War, but do two or three times what we did in the Cold War” in terms of gathering up alliances and preparing for war, basically. I think this is very foolish. It is true that China is very powerful and formidable, but I maintain that national security calculations have to take intentions into account, and there is this tendency to try to act like China has very aggressive intentions, which I just don’t see any evidence for.

It’s also interesting and quite dangerous that Westerners tend to underestimate China’s strength, including its military power. One of the things that has to be realised is that China’s industrial strength stands behind its military strength. I tell people, for example, what if the US and Chinese navies go head-to-head and they both experience huge losses, which is quite likely in a naval war, both losing dozens of ships. Tell me which navy can reconstitute faster? The answer is obvious. China has much greater shipbuilding capability, so that could be a huge difference maker.

But overall, people have not come to grips with what it means that China has more than 200 times the shipbuilding capacity of the United States. That is a force multiplier and of great significance. Generally, I would say the US and its allies, in my view, underestimate China’s capabilities and there are many reasons for that. But some of it could be somewhat legitimate in the sense that China’s military in the modern era is untested. We don’t have a single case of China fighting a large-scale naval battle. That is an issue. But I don’t regard that as much of a problem for China’s military.

How successful do you think the civil-military fusion strategy in the Chinese defence industry has been?

China’s military industry is very impressive – it’s both broad and deep. I cannot think of a single area where China has neglected or where we see pockets of weakness at all.

China understands just how crucial this is in conflict. It doesn’t have any illusions about short wars or cost-free wars or wars that don’t impact the homeland. China is well aware that wars are bloody and costly, and the homeland is badly affected and that it often comes down to who is willing to pay the heavier price and who can outproduce the opponent.

As for the civil-military fusion, part of this is just in the DNA of the PLA – the “people’s war” doctrine – looking for that kind of deep integration between society and the military, and that seems to make sense intuitively to many Chinese.

In some respects, however, they’re also reading off the US script, and they’ve studied our military-industrial complex very thoroughly. They know where much of the innovation happens in the US military: it’s places like Caltech and MIT. The Chinese know that very well, and so you can see a real determination to have their leading universities, their leading research centres and their leading companies tied in with the military.

The number of engineers in related fields that are produced, like naval architects, for example, is astounding. If you put China versus the West or China versus the United States, it’s not even close. That’s a very important asymmetry that has served China’s military very well.

The lack of combat experience is a much-talked-about weakness of the PLA. How important is it in your mind?

It does have some importance. Looking on the naval side, it is very striking that in the modern era, China has not fought any major naval battles. It’s not only the practical issues related to that in terms of training, institutional learning and culture, but also there’s a bit of a self-confidence issue, which is natural.

But I do in general think people make too much of this issue. If you want to say that the US military is more combat experienced, well, in what respect? The United States has been fighting wars, say, in Afghanistan or against the Houthis in the Red Sea or in Iraq. I would argue that yes, that is a kind of combat experience, but is it really? Are you learning the right lessons from this combat experience? The Houthis, for example, have almost no air defence. So, what are your pilots actually learning from that experience? All the wrong lessons, it turns out.

Indeed, we’re seeing in the current war with Iran that one reason why US bases have been hit rather severely and US operations have been quite badly disrupted by Iranian missile strikes is that we’re not used to fighting against a country that can deliver some major blows.

I just don’t think the United States has faced a peer military in combat since 1945, and I can’t underline that strongly enough. So, therefore, I don’t think that China is at a major disadvantage due to lacking combat experience.

Unprecedented numbers of top PLA generals have been sacked in the country’s anti-corruption drive over the last few years. How big do you think the impact is on the PLA’s combat readiness in the short term and in the long run?

Here as usual, I’m departing from conventional wisdom. I don’t see any major impact. It may be the opposite. It’s just common sense that you want a military run by younger folks. And having a military run by people in their 40s and 50s is going to be much better for a lot of obvious reasons than by a bunch of elderly gentlemen. Is there corruption in the PLA? Absolutely, but there’s corruption in every military, and therefore, I do not think the PLA is any kind of outlier here.

Every PLA expert has their theory about what is actually going on. My leading candidate theory is that militaries in an authoritarian system like China’s have a big role in succession. So, the most obvious explanation would be that this is related to the succession, and that probably Chinese President Xi Jinping wants to choose the next leader of China and doesn’t want very senior generals “playing in the sandbox”, so to speak.

Another theory I have though – and this is one that keeps me up at night as I hope this is not true – we cannot rule out the idea that there is a real possibility of a Taiwan contingency and that Xi and the people around him are very systematically picking the people that they want – new faces with fresh ideas and fighting spirit, people whose heart is in this and who are ready to command.

I hope that’s not true. I hope I’m wrong here, but we have to consider that as a possibility that the PLA is being radically restructured for war. Unfortunately, that might be true. I hope it’s not.

In the first half of 2026, the number of PLA fighter jet sorties near Taiwan was at its lowest since 2022, when then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan. What do you think this signals about Beijing’s intentions about Taiwan?

Well, if my last answer sounded somewhat pessimistic, I’m generally pretty optimistic about the situation. I think there is a peaceful solution here, and it’s pretty obvious what needs to happen in terms of cross-strait relations and pacifying the situation. It takes goodwill on both sides, which we’re beginning to see.

I’m rather hopeful that both sides will step back from the brink. Both sides will realise that if they accommodate a little bit, there is a solution space here because this war just would be so devastating for everyone. So, I do think common sense will prevail.

The Donald Trump administration has ushered in a more realistic policy in the Asia-Pacific. The summit [with Xi in May], I think, was very good. Both sides are looking for off-ramps. I’m reasonably optimistic that all sides of this equation here – Washington, Beijing and Taipei – all understand this.

China recently conducted a missile test from a nuclear-powered submarine for the first time. What does it say about the readiness of the PLA’s nuclear force and Beijing’s strategic intentions? What is the message of Beijing’s call to speed up building its nuclear arsenal?

That’s a big issue. First of all, the launch that we just saw was quite momentous because it shows China’s rising confidence. The naval part of the triad was previously seen as a much weaker part. So, this demonstrates the filling out of the PLA nuclear triad.

But speaking specifically to China’s submarine-based nuclear missiles, this was a big step because we had seen reports that China likely could now fire these missiles from locations near China. So that’s a very different situation. Five or 10 years ago, Chinese submarines would need to sortie out into the mid-Pacific, or at least into the Philippine Sea and beyond, to get into firing position. But now that doesn’t seem to be the case, and that does change the equation.

The truth is China’s nuclear deterrent is very formidable, and I don’t doubt that in a nuclear exchange China could destroy the United States. Of course, China would also be destroyed. So, I think we are firmly in a condition of mutually assured destruction. While many Americans are wringing their hands about this, I think this is good because both sides will be more cautious. It means that we are coming into a situation of greater balance. That balance implies greater stability in the future.

However, I will say I found the first evidence that I’ve seen of Chinese commentators connecting the nuclear build-up directly to the Taiwan issue, and that is a little bit troubling. Of course, there’s a hypothesis that this could make a Taiwan scenario more likely, and that’s concerning.

Unfortunately, the way I understand nuclear strategy, a lot of it comes down to what we call not just the balance of power but the balance of fervour. In other words, which side cares more? Which side is more willing to take risks and take losses? And unfortunately, in this case, it’s absolutely clear to me that China would win the balance of fervour and would have more credibility to take risks in that scenario. So, it’s just another reason why the United States and China should be extremely cautious and even wary of a Taiwan scenario.

How do you forecast the PLA’s future development after 2027? What role does the PLA have in global geopolitics in the future? Will it have its own sphere of influence?

I’m quite optimistic. I’m very impressed that China has built up its strong military without resorting to the use of major force. It is remarkable that China has not used force on a large scale since 1979. That’s an extremely impressive level of restraint – very admirable. I wish I could say that about my country. Can a great power exercise that kind of restraint? We have a saying in the United States: “If you have a really nice hammer, then everything starts to look like a nail.” So, in other words, if you have very large, robust powerful armed forces, which are almost unmatched, maybe you are tempted to deploy them to solve every problem.

I do think, unfortunately, the United States has fallen into that trap. Arguably, we’ve been in this trap for a very long time. Now I do think China has learned some lessons from that experience and is determined not to become the USSR or the United States. And of course, they say this again and again: “we do not seek hegemony”. China also says they don’t seek a sphere of influence.

I actually think China does have a sphere of influence, but here they are using slightly different terminology. What I think it means for Chinese leaders is that it just simply implies China has a set of core interests logically along its periphery. China will expect that its voice is heard very clearly and will have a veto on what goes on there. But I don’t think China is seeking a sphere of influence to control everything that goes on in Vietnam or Cambodia. That’s not China’s aim. Nevertheless, China will quite reasonably insist that it not be threatened from its peripheral areas.

So that is what we’re seeing in the region, and that is a hard transition to that new era of geopolitics, where China is very strong, and China is going to demand that its core interests are respected. There is a possibility that as a country gets more powerful, its core interests grow and expand. That will be the difficult challenge for Beijing, to resist the temptation or trap, wherein its leaders become that “hammer looking for a nail”.

item.title: [SCMP] CJ Hendry brings Juju World to Hong Kong with exclusive collectibles
item.description:
The Australian artist Catherine Jenna Hendry, best known to the world as CJ Hendry, first entered the public consciousness through social media, by sharing her hyperrealistic interpretations of luxury items on Instagram. The ink drawings gained Hendry a following of almost a million, and celebrity collectors of her works include Kanye West, Vera Wang, Floyd Mayweather and Pharrell Williams – an impressive feat for someone without formal training or gallery representation.

The New York-based artist has expanded her drawing practice from black and white to colour. But not one to stay confined to a single medium, Hendry has also made waves with her viral plush “flower markets”.

She has also created Juju, a kawaii collectible with floppy ears and a flower for an eye. Running until August 16, Pacific Place is hosting “Juju World”, a fluffy and fun exhibition inspired by the character. Giant Jujus, swings and a chamber filled with 400 plushies await.
item.content:encoded:
The Australian artist Catherine Jenna Hendry, best known to the world as CJ Hendry, first entered the public consciousness through social media, by sharing her hyperrealistic interpretations of luxury items on Instagram. The ink drawings gained Hendry a following of almost a million, and celebrity collectors of her works include Kanye West, Vera Wang, Floyd Mayweather and Pharrell Williams – an impressive feat for someone without formal training or gallery representation.

The New York-based artist has expanded her drawing practice from black and white to colour. But not one to stay confined to a single medium, Hendry has also made waves with her viral plush “flower markets”.

She has also created Juju, a kawaii collectible with floppy ears and a flower for an eye. Running until August 16, Pacific Place is hosting “Juju World”, a fluffy and fun exhibition inspired by the character. Giant Jujus, swings and a chamber filled with 400 plushies await.

There’s also a pop-up store selling iridescent Jujus, created exclusively for Pacific Place. In this line, there are nine standard versions and five additional “secret” versions, which come in limited-edition blind boxes. Visitors can also unlock surprise accessories at the Capsule Toy Station and customise their Juju with interchangeable flower eyes, outfits and more.

At the launch of “Juju World”, we meet an energetic Hendry for a conversation about art, artificial intelligence and what it takes to make it in the industry today.

Describe your routine.

I have studios in Hong Kong and New York, so we’re here every other month. In the studio, every day is different. With three children aged between one and five, it’s mostly chaos. We are just piecing it together and there’s a lot we want to create and achieve, and that comes a little bit chaotically sometimes.

How has that influenced your art?

A lot of my artistic concepts are childlike and have a lot of whimsy. I’m not sure if that’s because I have children and I’m surrounded by childlike wonder, but creating ideas that appeal to both adults and kids is what I want to do. Sometimes, there’s no rhyme or reason to it.

You’ve tackled various mediums. Is there a thread that ties them all together?

Over the past three years, I have started to use this very feminine flower shape. Because I had so many unusual, different concepts, the flower shape allowed me to connect them all together. That has become a branding moment for everything. Even with the Juju logo, there’s a flower on top of the letter J.

Why the pivot from ink drawings to the kawaii collectibles realm?

My drawing practice is very labour-intensive, focused and intimate. I was finding it frustrating because those works are only available to a few people, as they are expensive and hard to come by. I was uncomfortable with that. I still draw, but maybe one-tenth of the time I used to. It has allowed me to spend time creating these other, kooky concepts, such as Juju and the flower markets.

I’ve created these concepts so that more people can appreciate and experience them. You don’t need money to appreciate the flower market: people can access it for free and even their first flower is free. Juju is not necessarily the same, but this fun, friendly character is appealing to many.

How would you explain Juju?

Juju is a fun character with a flower over their eye and no mouth, so they can’t talk back. They are a character that can take you through the happiest of times and the darkest of times, one who is with you no matter what.

How did Juju come about?

Juju’s name comes from my mother. Her name is Judy and my kids call her Juju. My mum is a very elegant lady who wears all white. So the rarest Jujus are always white.

I used AI to help design Juju in early 2025. AI is interesting because everyone kind of belittles it. But as an artist, it’s important to use different tools. I used AI for a very small portion of the design process.

AI is controversial, especially in art because it draws from existing works. Tell us more about your position on it

AI can be used very cleverly, and it can be used very poorly. It depends on what you want to do and the story you want to tell. Anyone can design anything in AI in seconds, but designing something and then making it a reality is a totally different skill set. My artistic process is more in bringing it to life and rolling it out.

I’ve been an artist for 15 years and I’ve been plagiarised for much of that time. So, I’ve become confident enough in my practice to know that no ideas are original, even before AI. Everyone’s referencing everyone else. AI is just speeding that up.

Art is all about collaboration and moving forward. If your entire practice is based on AI, I don’t think you’ll get very far. Mine is based pretty much entirely on design and creativity and using AI only for very small parts.

So, in the age of AI, do you see the role of an artist as more of a curator of sorts?

Yes, absolutely. It’s important to have your own voice. You can use AI to perhaps start a concept, but to build and develop that takes a lot of energy and thought.

Because I’ve been doing this for so long, I feel very comfortable talking about AI. People want to pretend it’s not there. But I’m like, “It’s here, you’ve got to go with it.” I’ve used AI and I will continue to use AI.

Building real-life experiences is so important to me. Like with “Juju World” in Pacific Place, for example, you can only buy these Jujus in person. I’ve purposely taken this offline. Also, we haven’t made many of them. So, when they sell out, they sell out. They’ll never be made again. We never revisit it and we never will.

Like Takashi Murakami, Kaws and others, you seem instinctively aware of how social media, branding and merchandising works. How important is that for an artist today?

It’s hard to be an artist nowadays. Everyone pines over the old days, but they are not coming back. Technology is a beautiful tool, if you can use it in a clever way. But because everyone has social media, it has become oversaturated. I’m interested in in-person experiences. When I build concepts and installations, it’s important to create something unique for people to experience.

That said, I also think there are so many ways to be an artist. I see my job as creating and starting discussions. I’m a commercially successful artist, but that’s not for everyone. Not everyone wants to have merch at their art exhibition. Some people just want to have one extraordinary painting that they’ve taken two years to make. That’s special and important. It depends on the artist you want to be. I’m just one type of artist. Art comes in so many ways, in so many voices.

Who inspires you?

I don’t think, for me, there are people who are inspirations. Like I said before, nothing is original any more. Everything’s being built on something else.

I’ve always interpreted my concepts off other things, blended them, meshed them, reinterpreted them in my own voice, in my own way. Actually, a lot of my ideas come from runway shows, which are extraordinarily inspiring in the way they bring together worlds to showcase concepts and clothing.

When we launched Juju at Phillips West Kowloon (in late 2025), a lot of that inspiration came from the Chanel runway show at the Grand Palais, in Paris, where they did it like a Chanel supermarket.

What do you want people to take away from this particular exhibition?

I’ve always been pretty open with the fact that when I build ideas and exhibitions, I don’t expect anything from anyone. That’s not my job. I believe, as an artist, you’re meant to build something and what people experience is none of my business. A lot of artists might put a plaque on the wall explaining the idea, but I’ve never done that and I never will. I build the idea and people can come and experience it however they want.

What’s next for you?

Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. It’s too hard to predict the future. My art could crash and burn, or I could reach the stars. You never know.

What I do know is that I’m relatively creative. I have a lot of energy, a lot of excitement and a lot of really kooky ideas. I love executing, building and creating. There’s no shortage of ideas. I just love working with my team to come up with stupid stuff all the time.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] China’s military goal is to stand neck and neck with the US: ex-PLA colonel Zhou Bo
item.description:
Zhou Bo is a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, and the author of the book Should the World Fear China? This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is approaching its 2027 centenary, a major benchmark set by Beijing to achieve military modernisation. What is that goal actually about?

China has set two major military goals: one [is for the] centenary of the PLA in 2027 and another [is for the centenary] of the People’s Republic of China in 2049.
item.content:encoded:
Zhou Bo is a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, and the author of the book Should the World Fear China? This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is approaching its 2027 centenary, a major benchmark set by Beijing to achieve military modernisation. What is that goal actually about?

China has set two major military goals: one [is for the] centenary of the PLA in 2027 and another [is for the centenary] of the People’s Republic of China in 2049.

Between those two milestones, China aims to basically achieve the modernisation of its national defence and armed forces by 2035. That means the PLA would not yet be fully modernised by 2027 by China’s own high standard.

The stated highest objective is to build a world-class military by 2049. However, we first need to consider how many countries are considered to have world-class militaries. The Chinese government has not specified this.

If there is only one, then it is obviously the United States. But if there can be more than one, then is China not already the second-strongest military power in the world?

That naturally leads to a comparison with Russia. I do not want to belittle Russia, but it clearly did not perform well at the beginning of the Ukraine war. It lacked effective centralised battlefield command, encrypted communications and adequate logistical support. The conflict has since become a war of attrition.

What about the PLA? Its budget is roughly one quarter that of the United States, but about 1.8 times Russia’s. It has the world’s largest armed forces and the largest number of naval vessels. Its state-of-the-art fighter jets outnumber Russia’s by a big margin. China and the United States are also the two dominant powers in applying advanced military technologies.

So, it depends on how we define a world-class military. If there can be more than one, China is arguably already among them. If there can be only one, then the 2049 objective is clear: to stand neck and neck with the United States.

Would it even be possible for China to surpass the United States? Well, it is difficult to verify whether China will actually overtake the United States. The United States has fought many wars, while China has continued to develop peacefully, and I hope that will continue.

Are there any visible indicators of the PLA’s progress towards its 2027 goal, including developments in areas such as its aircraft carrier fleet and defence budget?

There are two sides to this question.

Some developments are very visible. For example, outside observers can easily determine whether China has commissioned another aircraft carrier or whether a carrier is equipped with the so-called electromagnetic launch system.

However, other factors are much more difficult to assess.

For example, we do not know how effectively soldiers would perform in actual combat. Factors such as combat effectiveness, morale and the ability of personnel to operate under wartime conditions cannot be easily assessed unless a war actually occurs.

What China can do, in my view, is to maintain a clear long-term objective, ever sophisticated training and sustain its investment in defence. By sustained investment, I mean steady investment rather than a drastic or sudden increase.

What is valuable about China’s approach to defence spending is that, from the late 1970s, Deng Xiaoping made it clear that military development had to remain consistent with China’s economic development.

You mentioned that some capabilities cannot be assessed in a peacetime context. Does the PLA face challenges in validating systems such as AI without the combat experience the United States has gained from recent conflicts?

The United States has the advantage of being able to verify its systems in ongoing wars.

China therefore faces a dilemma because it has been at peace and consequently has had no opportunity to verify its weapons in actual warfare.

At the same time, we should not forget that peace itself has been the greatest dividend of China’s peaceful rise. It has provided China with decades of a peaceful environment, allowing the country as a whole to rise to its present level.

Sometimes you want to know how sharp your sword is. If you do not use the sword, how can you know how sharp it is? But you cannot simply cut off someone’s head to find out. This is the dilemma facing China.

Nevertheless, even with this dilemma, people should not draw the mistaken conclusion that the People’s Liberation Army cannot fight.

This is something that is often discussed in the West: the PLA may be unable to fight because China has been at peace. I think this question can be clarified quite easily.

For example, among China’s various missile launches, whether submarine-launched or land-based launches into the South Pacific, has any one of them failed? No, they have not failed. The combat capability of Chinese air power has also been demonstrated by Pakistan in its aerial combat with India using Chinese fighters.

People shouldn’t have doubts about China’s military capabilities. They are supported by a defence industry that is second to none, as well as by ambition, careful planning, and stable and sustained investment. I think the goal is totally achievable.

Do you think the anti-corruption efforts in the PLA will ultimately strengthen or weaken the PLA’s capabilities?

The Chinese government’s approach towards corruption is essentially one of zero tolerance. That is why cases of this kind are exposed from time to time.

We do not live in a vacuum, and the PLA is likewise not immune from the wider environment. It is regrettable that such matters can occur within the military.

However, the exposure of corruption and the decision to bring those responsible to justice can also be understood in another way: they demonstrate that we are trying to cleanse the organisation.

As a result, the PLA could become more effective. Developments have also demonstrated that it has not necessarily been weakened by these cases. As I mentioned earlier, we have seen Chinese missile launches in different locations, as well as the effective use of Chinese weapons systems by the Pakistan Air Force, among other examples.

I therefore believe that these anti-corruption efforts are healthy for the PLA.

Some assessments have linked the PLA’s 2027 centenary goal to Taiwan. How credible is this view, and has the risk of conflict in the Taiwan Strait declined since Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump met in May?

I think the Chinese government still sincerely hopes for peaceful reunification.

This has been demonstrated not only in remarks made by the Chinese leadership, but also, for example, during the visit of the chairwoman of [Taiwan’s main opposition party] the Kuomintang to Beijing. The visit involved not only warm handshakes, but also 10 preferential measures. These measures were, of course, intended for the benefit of the Taiwanese people, and they must have been carefully prepared. This means that they were not simply ideas developed overnight.

People always mention the “stick” element of mainland China without discussing the “carrot” element of its policy towards the Taiwanese people.

The reality is that we want normal cross-strait exchanges. However, the Taiwanese authorities are afraid of such exchanges. It is they who have stopped this kind of cross-strait interaction, including even academic exchanges.

Regarding the discussion of 2027, it is worth noting that, over the past 10 years or so, many American generals and admirals have made conflicting predictions. Has any one of them ultimately been proved correct?

I think this is entirely irresponsible. There is also disagreement at the highest levels of the US government regarding the 2027 claim about Taiwan. For example, the remarks of US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on the situation in the Taiwan Strait are almost the opposite of those of his predecessor Lloyd Austin at the Shangri-La Dialogue.

I believe that China still hopes for peaceful reunification, which is why it has not established a specific timeline. Because China still has hope, it will not provide such a timeline. The absence of a timeline leaves all these people continually guessing, though.

We have not renounced scenarios in which force may have to be used. These circumstances are clearly set out in Chinese law. Nevertheless, I believe that peaceful reunification remains the objective.

Editor’s note: Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

What is your assessment of US arms sales to Taiwan after the Xi-Trump meeting in May?

I believe that the United States’ arms sales to Taiwan will be more and more difficult in the future, right from now.

If the United States continues to sell arms to Taiwan, China could take three types of action.

First, China could also choose not to honour certain commitments it has made to the United States, including commercial agreements, if it believes that the United States has violated the one-China principle. This could involve products such as Boeing, beef and soybeans. None of these products is indispensable to China.

Second, China could adopt a broader range of countermeasures.

Finally, China could conduct increasingly frequent and sophisticated military exercises around the island to wear down the other side’s nerves.

Eventually, I believe the time will come sooner than the United States expects when it will have to ask itself the ultimate question: what are the actual benefits of selling arms to Taiwan, even if those sales are lucrative, when they create more risks than benefits?

Xi and Trump agreed during their meeting in May to pursue a bilateral relationship of constructive strategic stability. How stable, or fragile, is that relationship?

This concept is significant because this is the first time that China and the United States have agreed upon such a concept. It essentially refers to a form of equilibrium of strength between the United States and China.

I would say that this is more significant for China. Many Chinese people may believe that the United States has bullied China and looked down upon China.

As to whether this stability can be sustained, I believe that the word “constructive” means a great deal. It reflects good wishes for the future, but the question is how the relationship can become constructive rather than destructive.

Given the Taiwan issue, there is no guarantee that this objective can always be maintained. The United States maintains a policy of strategic ambiguity over the Taiwan issue. It is not guaranteed that it would become directly or fully involved in a conflict.

Moreover, the China-US relationship is fundamentally a competitive relationship, although this does not rule out areas of cooperation. The question is which aspect is predominant, and the answer is competition.

There will certainly be many challenges to this form of stability. The Americans may emphasise fairness and equality while China talks about mutual respect. Basically, they are talking about the same thing. But stability most certainly rules out the potential for conflict in the South China Sea and Taiwan.

Regarding Taiwan, do you think the Trump administration – or at least Trump himself – is moving away from the United States’ long-standing policy?

First, he said American soldiers should not fight a war 9,500 miles away. Second, he said that he had not made a decision regarding arms sales to Taiwan.

I think he is inclined to make such a decision, but he may find it very difficult. He didn’t say much on the Taiwan issue in Beijing, but there could be another three opportunities for the two leaders to meet. What would he have to say on the Taiwan issue and the arms sales during those meetings, and how might Beijing react? He has to consider all these matters.

Perhaps this indicates a possible adjustment, although this is only my own speculation. Trump’s proposed arms sale would be the largest in history.

This may mean that the United States intends to sell a larger quantity of weapons on fewer occasions. In terms of frequency, it could make each package larger while reducing the number of individual sales.

If you look at the record, arms sales have become increasingly difficult. Therefore, each time the United States decides to proceed, it may sell a large volume. China would then protest only once, rather than making three separate protests against three different sales.

Militarily speaking, the strength of the Chinese mainland is simply overwhelming in comparison with that of Taiwan. Therefore, it does not really matter what Taiwan buys. Nevertheless, the Taiwanese authorities feel that they have to purchase this insurance no matter how expensive it is.

Does the US effort to rebuild its shipbuilding and defence-industrial base signal a deeper industrial competition with China? How could this affect the long-term military balance and both sides’ ability to sustain a conflict?

From a military perspective, the United States is no longer as capable as it once was of projecting power globally.

Its growing focus on the western hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific reflects the fact that it no longer has sufficient resources to maintain an equally strong presence everywhere.

The US’ shipbuilding industry lags far behind China’s. This impact on its navy is already seen. Some estimates suggest that China’s shipbuilding capacity is over 230 times larger. I understand why Washington wants to rebuild its capacity, including through cooperation with Japan and South Korea, but I doubt this can be achieved quickly.

The picture varies by sector. The United States remains dominant in areas such as AI, but the gap is said to be a matter of months; its broader industrial and manufacturing capacity has clearly weakened.

This raises two questions: has the United States declined, and can it recover?

I describe Donald Trump as “Trump the Declinist”. His promise to “make America great again” implies that America has declined. In his own words, it is “carnage” that helped him to win his first presidency because many voters clearly accepted that argument.

The United States has recovered from periods of perceived decline before, including after the Vietnam war. Some believe it will do so again.

However, I think the situation may be fundamentally different this time. Even during the Vietnam war, the United States still had the world’s strongest industrial base.

Today, that foundation has weakened, suggesting that something more fundamental may have changed.

China conducted a missile test from a nuclear-powered submarine this month and subsequently disclosed information about it. What is your assessment of the test and US reactions?

I think people are somewhat curious about Chinese launches, in part because China actually didn’t have a lot of launches in the past.

A launch of this kind clearly carries strategic implications, although different countries may interpret it differently.

From a military and technical perspective, missile testing is necessary. Even after deployment, periodic tests remain necessary to verify that the system continues to function effectively and that the relevant operational capabilities are being maintained.

However, regarding what US officials reportedly said about China providing only a few hours’ notice before the launch, falling short of the practice of other nuclear powers, I don’t think there is any international standard specifying how far in advance such notifications should be given.

I believe an institutionalised mutual notification mechanism would be desirable, but it is unlikely while the United States continues with the Golden Dome project [a proposed missile defence system integrating land-, sea- and space-based sensors and interceptors].

Golden Dome represents an arms race at the highest level and would [threaten] China-US and Russia-US strategic stability. Although such a concept is broader than military affairs, it is primarily about military stability. During the Cold War, US-Soviet strategic stability was based on an equilibrium between their nuclear arsenals.

However, in my personal view, China-US strategic stability will never be based on numerical nuclear parity. I do not believe China would seek more than 5,000 nuclear warheads to match the American nuclear stockpile.

I have always argued that China should possess enough to ensure that the United States would never consider using nuclear weapons against it first.

If China’s objective is to deter the United States from using nuclear weapons against it, how many warheads would China need?

Even according to the Pentagon’s highest estimate – that China may possess 1,500 [nuclear] warheads by 2035 – the number would still remain far below that of the United States, assuming the estimate is accurate.

My argument is that China should possess enough nuclear weapons to deter any nuclear adventurism by the United States. The required number would depend on two factors: how the US nuclear arsenal develops and how China would need to respond to those developments.

In the worst-case scenario of a conflict across the Taiwan Strait, China would not want to be subjected to nuclear blackmail.

The second concerns the broader global strategic level, where the objective is to maintain strategic stability. This was also mentioned in [China’s] 15th five-year plan. We should preserve global nuclear stability. However, the question is how such stability could be maintained if China possessed only a few hundred nuclear weapons.

People should not be excessively concerned about China’s nuclear weapons because China’s no-first-use policy is one of its longest-standing defence policies.

How will AI capabilities affect the long-term military balance between China and the United States?

American dominance in AI is not a sure thing.

Even where one side may possess an advantage in certain areas, China may be stronger in the large-scale application of AI. This therefore makes the overall situation more complicated.

I think both countries are working very hard on the military application of AI.

The character of warfare has already changed, and military forces must become adaptable. If you observed the military parade last year, you would have seen that the PLA has not merely been watching these developments. It has already taken steps to respond to the emerging challenges.

A challenge is that we are not fully aware of how rapidly artificial intelligence can develop or in which particular fields it will advance most quickly.

During wartime, not only people but also artificial intelligence may learn and develop at the fastest pace. We have seen how rapidly AI has changed the battlefield in Ukraine and in the American war against Iran. This shows us how quickly the entire battlefield is being transformed.

I definitely believe that rules limiting AI’s role, such as in military decision-making, should be established. But sadly, as we saw in many cases, sometimes rules are only made after an incident. During the Cold War, there were quite a few false alarms of nuclear attack. Hopefully we shall never have false alarms triggered by AI.

The US military has continued to strengthen its posture along the first island chain. At the same time, the PLA has increasingly conducted operations beyond the chain. In your view, does the first island chain still carry the same strategic significance that it did during the Cold War?

Regarding the first island chain, I do not believe that it matters as much to the PLA as it once did, because the PLA is much stronger today and the overall US military presence at bases in these countries is not particularly large.

Second, I have serious doubts about whether these US allies could provide effective assistance to the United States in an actual conflict. I think all these countries would seek to hedge against such a possibility.

Japan might be an exception, in the sense that it is legally obliged to provide military bases to the United States. However, whether Japan would go further and fight shoulder to shoulder with the United States is not guaranteed, unless it believed that it faced an existential threat.

That is why, when [Japanese Prime Minister Sanae] Takaichi described such a scenario as an existential threat, she was strongly criticised within Japan itself. There is therefore no guarantee that what she described would actually happen in such a scenario.

There has been stronger military cooperation between Japan and the Philippines recently. How does this development challenge China’s strategic interests?

For military planners, any change in the surrounding security environment is naturally a concern because it adds new factors to their calculations. These are trends that China must watch, but I do not see them as game changers.

In the South China Sea, Japan’s role remains largely symbolic. Despite its assistance to the Philippines, there has not been a Japanese naval presence. I would describe it mainly as a political gesture with limited military implications.

In the Taiwan Strait, we should first remember that even US involvement is not guaranteed. The stronger China becomes, the more reluctant other countries will be to intervene. Japan’s role would therefore be secondary, apart from providing bases under its legal obligations.

Japan would have concerns even about providing bases because it would have to consider its own security. Japan could not simply say, “We are only providing bases and are not involved.”

If US aircraft took off from Japanese bases to take part in combat in the Taiwan Strait, China would regard Japan as involved. Japanese leaders would probably make such a decision only at the last moment.

I believe the Philippines is also aware of the risks. It wants to make use of the United States, but not to the extent that it becomes a target itself. That is why it has imposed conditions on US access to its bases, including limitations on their use for attacks during wartime.

Against the backdrop of strained China-Japan relations, could military encounters between the two increase the risks of a military incident?

Chinese and Japanese naval vessels seldom encounter one another. So, the risk is low. But Chinese and American naval vessels often encounter one another. China, the US and Japan are all members of the Code for Unplanned Encounters at Sea, or Cues, and they also have an air and maritime communication mechanism. These arrangements provide technical rules intended to prevent accidents, although they are not legally binding.

All these rules are technical rules, but politics always exists behind them.

There has therefore long been a tension between safety and security. Technical rules address safety, but security involves broader implications, on which the two sides may never agree.

Returning to this particular case, it would of course be safer if the Chinese and American navies could deconflict at sea. However, even if they maintain a so-called safe distance, the question remains: what constitutes a safe distance?

Unfortunately, there is no regulation or agreement that precisely defines a safe distance.

Safe conduct therefore ultimately relies on three abstract concepts: good airmanship, good seamanship and voluntary judgment – and that judgment is inevitably influenced by politics.

The rules were made because both sides have the bottom line, that is, none of us wants an accident. So, this is contradictory.

item.title: [SCMP] Will new batteries give China’s EVs the jolt they need to charge past their rivals?
item.description:
On a cloudy evening in late April, a tech event hosted at Beijing’s National Convention Centre by Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) drew nearly 1,000 people eager for a glimpse of next-generation electric vehicle (EV) batteries that could reshape the global automotive landscape.

Gao Huan, chief technology officer for the auto business at CATL, the world’s largest producer of EV batteries, exuded confidence while promoting the new Shenxing product series.

According to the company, its new, third-generation battery can charge from 10 to 98 per cent in under six and a half minutes. BYD’s second-generation Blade battery, by contrast, takes nine minutes to charge from 10 to 97 per cent.
item.content:encoded:
On a cloudy evening in late April, a tech event hosted at Beijing’s National Convention Centre by Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) drew nearly 1,000 people eager for a glimpse of next-generation electric vehicle (EV) batteries that could reshape the global automotive landscape.

Gao Huan, chief technology officer for the auto business at CATL, the world’s largest producer of EV batteries, exuded confidence while promoting the new Shenxing product series.

According to the company, its new, third-generation battery can charge from 10 to 98 per cent in under six and a half minutes. BYD’s second-generation Blade battery, by contrast, takes nine minutes to charge from 10 to 97 per cent.

With formations of electric current and heating effects projected on a giant screen, Gao sought to reassure his audience about how CATL designs and arranges cells to keep its battery packs safe and efficient.

Though more convenient, fast charging generates heat that can accelerate degradation in lithium-ion batteries, shortening their lifespan.

Gao explained how CATL’s technology isolated individual cells to prevent heat from spreading, saying the Shenxing series used independent sealed exhaust channels, allowing heat and electricity to exit the battery pack through separate paths.

“To accomplish product reliability, we have developed industry-leading testing methods and created a world-leading testing and verification centre,” Gao said. “In manufacturing, we make sure every single battery cell is made under extreme conditions in line with a stringent quality control system, with 7,000 quality checkpoints deployed along [each] product line.”

The battery pack, which accounts for about one-fourth of an electric car’s cost according to industry averages, is among the most important components of an EV and plays a decisive role in the global automotive industry’s shift to electrification, as technological advances are key to easing concerns over production costs, range and vehicle safety.

Higher-performance and lower-priced batteries will further drive electrification of the global automotive industry

Davis Zhang, Suzhou Hazardtex

CATL’s views on the sector carry particular weight.

The company, based in Ningde, in southeastern China’s Fujian province, led the global EV battery market with a 40.2 per cent share in the first five months of 2026, according to South Korea-based SNE Research.

Total global EV battery usage climbed 16.3 per cent from a year earlier to 469.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh), per SNE data. One GWh is enough to power about 20,000 EVs with a range of 500km (311 miles).

The Shenxing batteries’ greatly shortened charging time “materially alleviates consumer range and charging anxiety”, Morgan Stanley said in a research note a week after the CATL tech event. “On the flipside, debates about the safety and durability of ultra-fast charging continue.”

Over the past decade, improvements in manufacturing and rising sales volumes have helped drive down EV battery production costs, bringing some electric cars closer to cost parity with their petrol-powered counterparts.

Attention is now turning to technologies such as solid-state batteries, sodium-ion batteries, faster charging systems, and battery pack designs that enhance thermal management, as more car owners switch from petrol vehicles to electric cars.

In mainland China, the world’s largest automotive and EV market, pure electric and plug-in hybrid cars accounted for 57.4 per cent of the country’s new vehicle deliveries in the first half of 2026, according to the China Passenger Car Association.

The cost of EV batteries was as high as US$1,474 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in 2010. By 2025, global lithium-ion battery pack prices had fallen to about US$108 per kWh, according to BloombergNEF’s annual price survey.

A price of US$100 per kWh is seen by industry officials and analysts as a threshold for making unsubsidised EVs cost-competitive with their oil-guzzling peers.

China’s manufacturing heft has given its battery makers a cost advantage, with average prices in the country falling 13 per cent year on year to US$84 per kWh in 2025, BloombergNEF added, forecasting an average global battery pack price of US$62 by 2030.

Chinese EV battery makers also continued to dominate the global market as seven companies – including CATL, BYD and Gotion High-Tech – were among the world’s top 10 players, according to SNE Research.

Between January and May, the Chinese companies commanded a 72.6 per cent share of the global EV battery market, SNE data showed.

“Higher-performance and lower-priced batteries will further drive electrification of the global automotive industry,” said Davis Zhang, a senior executive at Suzhou Hazardtex, a supplier of specialised batteries. “Apparently, potential technological breakthroughs in solid-state battery could become a game-changer.”

Compared with existing liquid-based batteries, solid-state variants promise higher energy storage, longer driving ranges and improved safety, with a lower risk of overheating or fire. Beijing has been backing efforts to commercialise all-solid-state batteries, which, unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, do not rely on flammable liquid electrolytes.

In late June, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said China would intensify its research and development into key next-generation battery materials, including solid-state electrolytes, to support the growth of its EV sector.

Several companies have already begun those efforts. Chinese battery maker WeLion’s semi-solid-state batteries, for example, power some of the premium EVs assembled by Shanghai-based Nio.

And in March, the state-owned Chery Automobile, based in central China’s Anhui province, unveiled an all-solid-state battery capable of powering a vehicle for more than 1,500km of driving distance on a single charge.

Chinese battery makers and their supply chain vendors are also striving to extend the lifespan of lithium-ion batteries.

Ganfeng Lithium, the world’s largest producer of lithium metal, aimed to raise the lifetime capacity of its energy-storage battery to 18,000 charges by the end of the year, which would allow it to last as long as solar panels, the company’s president, Wang Xiaoshen, told the South China Morning Post in May.

Gotion High-Tech, the world’s fifth-largest EV battery maker by delivery volume, also launched a new product in May that it said could be fully recharged over 15,000 times.

A solar panel is typically estimated to be able to work 25 years or more, while lithium-ion batteries could last up to 10 years, according to analysts.

In China, there is no industry that is not competitive. That’s why China’s products could evolve so rapidly

Wang Xiaoshen, Ganfeng Lithium

Both Ganfeng and Gotion said they had managed to produce batteries with a capacity of more than 580 ampere-hours (Ah) and were planning to boost it to over 600 Ah.

An Ah is a unit of measurement to reflect the electrical charge a battery can hold and deliver over time.

Such advancements in battery technologies, as well as the reduction of costs, partly resulted from the fierce competition within the sector in China, according to Ganfeng’s Wang.

“In China, there is no industry that is not competitive,” Wang said. “That’s why China’s products could evolve so rapidly.”

Even if battery firms from other countries were able to claim achievements in cutting-edge technologies, China’s prowess in manufacturing and supply chains would support the country in retaining its competitive advantage when it came to mass production, said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings.

Chinese battery makers are also moving downstream to enhance profitability and deepen their ties with EV assemblers in fine-tuning thermal designs and battery management.
