Also, when Trump says “I like to talk to my good friend Xi Jinping. We can talk about things” – what does he want to talk about? Not clear.

Compared with other presidents, Trump seems to really like personal diplomacy. In other words, he believes that his personal relationships with leaders are the important thing.

Speaking of leadership diplomacy, what conditions do you think will be needed for Trump and Xi to meet?

I think a meeting between the two leaders is quite likely. Trump is announcing that the deal has been done with China. He would only want to go to China if the deal is kind of there, so he can mark it in a big ceremony and have a prominent meeting with Xi.

I don’t think he would want to go to China to negotiate. We’re moving into a phase where the US wants to get most of its tariff deals done within the next couple of months.

During his first term, Trump had a very grand welcoming ceremony provided by Xi in Beijing. I think he would like to do that again – a big, grand meeting that Trump will think of as a historic event, that showcases he’s able to do negotiations and deals with China in a way that other presidents haven’t been able to do. I think he would want to push quite hard in that direction. That’s my guess.

Are the two presidents likely to get along?

I think that’s perfectly possible. You might remember that when Trump invited Xi to Mar-a-Lago, he said that he gave Xi a big piece of chocolate cake. He never talked about giving chocolate cake to German chancellor Angela Merkel.

That’s a sign that he feels there’s some sort of ability to speak leader to leader in that sense. Xi has said less about Trump, but he hasn’t said any very publicly hostile things personally about him.

Will it stop competition? No. Will it stop conflict? Maybe. In some areas – I would single out technology – I think the US and China are going to be increasingly in competition and there will be less sharing of intellectual property or scientific development.

That would mean other countries could benefit from both, or they may have to choose a side. This will not change because of a meeting.

But can the two leaders talk about lowering the temperature and avoiding misunderstandings that could lead to military confrontation? That might be more possible.

Turning to China’s security environment, how might Beijing’s relations with its neighbours change, given the uncertainties of Washington’s policies during the Trump administration?

My guess is that China will be assessing how solid and secure American security guarantees are in Asia. There’s some evidence that the United States might want to maintain and maybe deepen its relationship with standing allies Japan, Australia and South Korea.

We know that Trump is interested in the Korean peninsula. In his first term, he wanted to do personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. But even when South Korea is going through political change and a lot of turmoil, there’s no sense that I’ve seen that the United States is stepping back from its relationship.

I would say that if you are looking from Beijing, the conclusion to draw at the moment is that things will change much less in Asia than in Europe.

Supposing American security guarantees, naval presence and alliances were withdrawn from Asia – the first thing that would be likely to happen is that Japan and South Korea would think hard about getting their own nuclear weapons. They have the capacity, science and the technology. They could do it, but they won’t do it at the moment.

in a strange way, Beijing’s best bet for keeping the region relatively nuclear-free is to encourage the Americans to stay. And most of its neighbours would share that analysis.

They want the Chinese market, but they also want American security. They don’t want either one to disappear. I think that’s what makes the calculation different in Asia and that will affect the way that China and the US deal with other countries in the region.

What about the South China Sea?

The South China Sea is probably one of the most potentially dangerous flashpoints, along with Taiwan.

The South China Sea has more of a chance of running out of control because it’s not just between two or three entities – seven or eight are involved. The US is not so directly involved in that.

But I would say that China is missing a big soft power opportunity, which it could take up at a time of uncertainty about American security intentions, of being able to provide reassurance to regional neighbours like the Philippines.

If China is not looking to increase its maritime and territorial claims, it could create a much better basis of trust in the region. But right now there’s much more military activity from China, not just near the Philippines but also off the coast of Australia, and that’s heightening tensions in the region.

How is the importance of Taiwan to Beijing shaping the security environment?

One of the most interesting things is that after repeatedly trying to take the island, Mao Zedong basically said to then-US president Richard Nixon, when they met in Beijing in 1972, that the Taiwan problem could be left to the side for 100 years.

That’s a reminder that actually the Taiwan question has not been a constant one at the forefront of China’s relationship with the world.

Right now, there are a whole variety of reasons that China needs to think about its changing place in the world. It has an opportunity to influence the world order at a time when the United States is changing its role.

It also has significant economic problems at home, in terms of creating new forms of employment, dealing with the way technology has changed labour markets, and stimulating domestic consumption, which the party has repeatedly said is a really important domestic priority.

In that context, you could say that with all those important problems, Taiwan doesn’t appear as a major solution or issue that will help to resolve any of them.

If you look at Chinese policy priorities, it’s very clear that the single most important task for the government is the economy.

China needs the Asia-Pacific region to be economically productive to get its economy going again. That means the attention has to be on the domestic economy and how it relates to a peaceful, calm Asia that does not have any sort of confrontation.

In five to 10 years, if current trends continue, the Asia-Pacific region could be even more of a driver of the global economy than it is now. It can become the most economically dynamic region in the world, with lots of foreign direct investment and expansion.

However, for that vision of Asia to emerge, the region needs to stay peaceful and stable and absolutely avoid wars. Any regional confrontations could put that economic future in danger and that would be very bad for China and its neighbours.

Alongside the nationalism that comes with the promise of building a powerful China, there is also a revival of traditional Chinese culture in both society and the official narrative. How do you think this will shape China’s governance and foreign policy?

This is one of the most interesting and important elements of what’s going on in thought and ideology in China today.

First of all, there is a real interest in what some people call traditional thought, or pre-modern thought, which includes the Confucian tradition but also lots of other areas, such as Taoism.

The Chinese government has been sponsoring publication of China’s canon of official writings, with the parts that suit contemporary politics tending to be stressed.

For instance, Confucian thinking does have an interest in proper hierarchy and this is something that is obviously very attractive to the Communist Party, because it wants people, essentially, to be stable and ordered.

But there are other ideas – such as individual self-development or self-cultivation, which could lead more to the idea that people should have individual rights – that are less popular with the party.

China’s political culture since 1949 has been heavily shaped by the Marxism and Leninism that underpins the Chinese Communist Party.

Many of the ideas are still there and you can hear them in the language of Xi and other top leaders. Even while they are praising traditional Chinese culture and wisdom, they are also pointing out that Marxism and Leninism still have significance.

How are these two things compatible? Actually, it’s not easy.

There was a TV show broadcast in Hunan province that got a lot of criticism on Chinese social media. It was called When Marx Met Confucius and was a way of trying to talk about the difficulties in combining these ideas.

There is actually quite an interesting and difficult tension in the way that these two thought systems operate in China today, but I think that they are both very much part of the debate.

How has the Chinese intellectual landscape changed in the past 10 years? Do you share the view that it can be summarised as a rise in nationalism, Sinification of ideas and declining critical voices? What other trends are you seeing and what are their effects?

In some ways, China’s intellectual sphere has narrowed, at least in public, but in other important ways, it has expanded.

The narrowing is real, and probably the biggest obstacle that China places in its own path to developing new ideas at home and being able to exert influence abroad. It’s difficult to persuade the wider world that you’re a force for new thinking if new thinking at home is heavily restricted.

In terms of subjects, including history, most people would say that the room for publication and discussion is much more limited than it was 10, 15 or 20 years ago. Many aspects of modern history are harder to research and write about in China today than in the past.

The most productive recent time intellectually in China was the late 1990s and early 2000s, when there was the most capacity to be able to speak more freely. That time will need to come again as China comes to grips with its new role in the world. It’s not possible to have a very narrowed intellectual sphere and a very wide influence.

But there are some areas where I think things are broader, and I’m particularly thinking about social media and the way it has expanded and grown so significantly in China in the past decade.

Lots of ideas actually are discussed at a popular level, even when there’s censorship a lot of ideas still get out there – not about top-level politics as that’s too sensitive to permit – but if you think about things like concerns about economic change, people’s concerns about their own financial situation, ideas about the position of women, society, feminism, those are quite visible in Chinese social media.

That is not the same thing as two or three scholars sitting in a think tank writing some big paper, but in terms of understanding social trends and how they are shaping China today, social media has been very valuable to reflect those changes.

How has the China studies community been affected by the changes of recent years? What will the subject look like, with a growing percentage of scholars outside the country unable to conduct interviews and on-the-ground research in China?

You have put your finger on one of the most problematic issues – the number of students studying Chinese languages and doing higher-level research in the West on China is going down significantly. It was never very high, but it was going up, and now the numbers are shrinking.

One reason is the sense that doing serious research in China – particularly for social scientists but also for researchers who need to use archives and libraries – is much more difficult than it used to be.

What real China researchers need is to be able to travel and set up their own agendas, to be able to do interviews at the local level that enable them to understand how local government works, or to collect large amounts of data that enables them to see how effective or ineffective particular policies are.

This is the work of real social science, and it involves transparency and openness on data and a willingness to welcome the gathering of data, rather than assuming that it has to be banned for security reasons.

So, although more scholars are coming back to China, opening up more capacity to be able to do real research in China is the next barrier that needs to be overcome.

There are a lot of brilliant Chinese students in many countries in the West who are doing significant social science and humanities research. But their Western equivalents who study China can’t do that kind of work in China, so it becomes very unbalanced.

What about your own experience with the Asia studies and Chinese history students you taught at Oxford and now Harvard?

When it comes to postgraduate students doing PhDs, a significant number are Chinese. We do still have some Westerners, but the problem is that they have to be enthusiastic about China, willing to learn its language and culture, and then be able to find a meaningful project to research.

It’s harder now to assure students that they can find a pathway to doing really good social science research inside China, so a lot of students just leave China out. If people say China is a very difficult place to do research and South Korea is easy, maybe people just decide they want to learn Korean instead.

The sense among Western researchers that it’s hard to do serious research in China has transmitted to students finding it difficult to find a career path if they do study China. I think that’s a great shame.

item.title: [SCMP] US judge blocks Pentagon’s ‘Chinese military’ label for WuXi AppTec
item.description:
A US federal judge on Friday temporarily blocked the Pentagon from designating Chinese biotechnology group WuXi AppTec as a “Chinese military company”, finding that defence officials repeatedly misread the evidence used to justify the decision.

US District Chief Judge James Boasberg granted WuXi a preliminary injunction barring the Department of Defence from enforcing or otherwise giving effect to the designation while the company’s lawsuit proceeds.

“A scarlet letter sends a clear message: keep away,” Boasberg wrote in a 35-page opinion, pointing to customers and suppliers that had cancelled contracts, ended long-standing relationships or moved business to WuXi’s competitors following the designation.
item.content:encoded:
A US federal judge on Friday temporarily blocked the Pentagon from designating Chinese biotechnology group WuXi AppTec as a “Chinese military company”, finding that defence officials repeatedly misread the evidence used to justify the decision.

US District Chief Judge James Boasberg granted WuXi a preliminary injunction barring the Department of Defence from enforcing or otherwise giving effect to the designation while the company’s lawsuit proceeds.

“A scarlet letter sends a clear message: keep away,” Boasberg wrote in a 35-page opinion, pointing to customers and suppliers that had cancelled contracts, ended long-standing relationships or moved business to WuXi’s competitors following the designation.

A Pentagon spokesperson declined to address the ruling or whether the department planned to appeal.

“As a matter of policy, the Department does not comment on ongoing litigation,” the spokesperson said in response to questions from the South China Morning Post.

“We welcome the court’s decision to grant the preliminary injunction we petitioned for,” a WuXi AppTec spokesperson told the Post. “This ruling relieves us from the immediate adverse consequences of the erroneous 1260H designation during the litigation process.”

The spokesperson said WuXi believed the facts presented in its court filings would prevail following “an objective and fair judicial review”, adding that its operations remained “fully functional”.

The ruling represents an early legal victory for one of China’s largest pharmaceutical research and manufacturing service providers and a setback for Washington’s expanding use of national-security restrictions against major Chinese commercial companies.

But the decision does not permanently remove WuXi from the Pentagon’s Section 1260H list or prevent the department from designating the company again using evidence and reasoning that satisfy the law.

The order does not affect Alibaba, Baidu, BYD or other Chinese companies placed on the Pentagon list.

However, analysts say Boasberg’s rejection of unsupported or inaccurately characterised evidence could strengthen similar legal challenges to designations based on indirect state or military affiliations.

Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, has separately sued the Pentagon over its addition to the list.

Judge questioned Pentagon's reasoning

WuXi was added to the list in June after the Pentagon alleged that it was indirectly owned by China’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission, or Sasac, and indirectly affiliated with the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defence and the People’s Liberation Army (SASTIND).

Boasberg found that each of those three rationales was likely deficient under the Administrative Procedure Act, which allows courts to set aside government actions found to be arbitrary or capricious.

The Pentagon’s ownership finding rested largely on an investment in WuXi by a fund connected to the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, a state-owned aerospace and defence conglomerate overseen by Sasac.

According to the judge, defence officials confused the percentage of the fund’s assets invested in WuXi with the percentage of WuXi owned by the fund.

A source cited by the Pentagon said WuXi shares represented 5.32 per cent of the fund’s net asset value. The department interpreted that figure to mean the fund owned 5.32 per cent of WuXi.

“This is flat-out wrong,” Boasberg wrote.

“If a household puts 5 per cent of its modest savings into a blue-chip stock, that does not mean it owns 5 per cent of the company.”

WuXi told the court that the fund’s actual investment was worth around US$200,000 and represented about 0.001 per cent of the company’s equity. Boasberg said he did not need to accept those figures to conclude that the Pentagon had mischaracterised its own sources.

“These errors do not inspire confidence in the fastidiousness of the agency’s decision-making process,” he wrote.

The court found similar problems with the Pentagon’s claims that WuXi was affiliated with China’s defence-industry regulator and the PLA.

Those conclusions were based on records of pharmaceutical studies involving hospitals affiliated with five universities supervised by the defence regulator, as well as one study involving the PLA General Hospital.

But the underlying records identified WuXi or its subsidiaries only as third-party laboratories hired to process samples. Other pharmaceutical companies had applied for government approval and selected the hospitals where the studies would take place.

The Pentagon nevertheless characterised WuXi as having received approval to conduct the studies in partnership with the universities and the PLA hospital.

The judge said the records did not establish such partnerships or explain why WuXi’s more limited laboratory role amounted to the “close formal or informal association” required by the statute.

Highlighting what he described as the breadth of the government’s reasoning, Boasberg noted that the same collection of records listed the University of Michigan as an applicant for a study conducted at a hospital affiliated with Peking University.

“If WuXi’s more remote role suffices to establish a close association with SASTIND, the report’s logic would make a member of the Big Ten a Chinese military company,” he wrote, referring to the US collegiate athletic conference where Michigan plays.

Boasberg stressed that courts owed considerable deference to government decisions involving national security and foreign affairs. But he said that deference could not compensate for evidence that did not support the Pentagon’s stated conclusions.

“The public interest in a list with teeth is thus inseparable from the public interest in a list that is accurate,” he wrote.

US operations in limbo

The judge also found that WuXi was suffering irreparable commercial harm from the designation.

The Shanghai-headquartered company operates six facilities and employs about 450 people in the United States. It serves more than 1,000 US customers, which accounted for roughly 70 per cent of its US$6.7 billion in global revenue last year, according to the opinion.

Since the designation, customers have suspended work, cancelled projects or begun transferring programmes to other suppliers, according to court documents. One online marketplace also made WuXi’s services unavailable for purchase without a customer-specific exception.

Because pharmaceutical development programmes can last for years and switching manufacturers may require new regulatory submissions and validation work, Boasberg found that customers moving to competitors were unlikely to return even if WuXi ultimately prevailed.

The designation also carried potential consequences under the Biosecure Act, which requires the White House budget office to publish an initial list of “biotechnology companies of concern” by December.

Being placed on the Section 1260H list is necessary, although not sufficient by itself, for inclusion on the Biosecure Act list. Companies ultimately covered by that law could be excluded from federally funded contracts and supply chains.

The Pentagon had asked Boasberg to stay any injunction during an appeal, but the judge rejected that request, saying the government had not identified any immediate and irreparable harm resulting from the temporary suspension of WuXi’s designation.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ subtitle-less ‘Spider-Man’ screening shows deaf inclusion is just lip service
item.description:
The release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day in the Philippines was supposed to be a shared cinematic moment for fans who had waited months for the latest instalment in the superhero franchise.

But for some deaf viewers, the experience was defined less by the action on screen than by what was missing: subtitles or captions that would allow them to follow the dialogue.

That frustration, captured in a viral Facebook post, has pointed to a wider accessibility gap in the country, where advocates say deaf audiences are still too often excluded from cinemas, entertainment and public information.
item.content:encoded:
The release of Spider-Man: Brand New Day in the Philippines was supposed to be a shared cinematic moment for fans who had waited months for the latest instalment in the superhero franchise.

But for some deaf viewers, the experience was defined less by the action on screen than by what was missing: subtitles or captions that would allow them to follow the dialogue.

That frustration, captured in a viral Facebook post, has pointed to a wider accessibility gap in the country, where advocates say deaf audiences are still too often excluded from cinemas, entertainment and public information.

In the post, a user named Cherry Ann described watching the film with her deaf friend and urged local movie distributors to consider adding subtitles to films.

“My friend is deaf, and we were so excited to watch the new Spider-Man movie … We thought that subtitles were going to be provided,” she wrote in the post, which was shared more than 11,000 times.

“It was painful to see that I could understand what was happening, while she was just staring at the screen, trying to figure out what was happening. Imagine sitting there for almost two hours when you cannot understand the dialogue and you don’t know why people are laughing or reacting inside the cinema,” she wrote.

“This isn’t a huge request, we are just asking for accessibility. Everyone deserves to enjoy movies, not just those who can hear.”

The scenario described in the viral post was not an isolated case.

“I saw my deaf friends who were excited to watch Spider-Man, but the movie had no subtitles. They were unhappy and found it difficult to understand the dialogue and important parts of the story,” said Chindee Cruz, a content creator and part-time deaf special education teacher. “They were very disappointed because they had been so excited to watch the movie, but without subtitles, they could not fully enjoy or understand it.”

Exclusion zone

Inaccessible screenings can also mean exclusion from shared social experiences, according to Hennie Parrocha, a graphic designer and Filipino Sign Language (FSL) advocate.

“I remember watching a movie with my family without subtitles. I could understand the characters’ facial expressions, actions and emotions but I couldn’t understand what they were saying or follow the story. I ended up having to ask my family what was happening,” Parrocha said. “If a movie doesn’t have subtitles, I usually choose not to watch it in theatres because I know I won’t fully understand or enjoy it.”

Deaf advocate Ahira Lotivio said many films were still produced without accessibility features such as FSL interpretation, captions or subtitles.

“For deaf audiences, this creates barriers because they may miss important dialogue, sound effects and emotional details that hearing audiences can easily access,” Lotivio said. “The situation highlights that accessibility should not be treated as an extra service but as a basic right for equal participation.”

The lack of accessible screenings is not new, according to advocates.

Deaf people were eager to understand what was happening in society “and wanted to enjoy the same entertainment that hearing people could access without barriers”, said Angelita Capanang, a Philippine Association of the Deaf board member.

The FSL interpreter for nearly 30 years recalled accompanying a deaf friend to watch the musical film Les Miserables in the 1990s, when media accessibility was an even greater concern. Because the film did not have subtitles or closed captions, her friend asked her to interpret the dialogue.

“It was extremely difficult because the theatre was dark and flashlights were not allowed inside. I did my best but naturally, much of the dialogue and music could not be conveyed effectively,” Capanang said.

Philippine Federation of the Deaf president Mariah Agbay called for a removal of such barriers and accessibility to be “systematically integrated” into public services, entertainment, education, and other sectors.

Limited implementation

Several laws have been adopted in the Philippines to support the inclusion of the deaf community in mainstream society.

The Filipino Sign Language Act was passed in 2018, declaring FSL the national sign language and requiring the use of interpreters in news and public affairs programmes as well as emergency announcements.

The Philippines also signed the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2007 and ratified it in 2008, while the 2016 Closed Captioning Act required television networks to provide closed captions for news and public affairs programmes.

But advocates said those measures remained limited in scope and implementation.

For one, Capanang said, the laws do not require movie producers and cinemas to provide closed captions or sign language interpretation.

Even when provided, not all captions are accurate or of high quality, according to Lotivio. “Some captions may be incomplete, delayed or unavailable. Stronger monitoring, enforcement and expansion of accessibility policies are needed to ensure deaf people can fully access media content,” she said.

Such gaps showed that the inclusion of persons with disabilities was often treated as a compliance issue rather than a human rights concern, Agbay said. “Policies may exist on paper, but they are not always supported by adequate funding, trained personnel, accessible communication, or meaningful consultation with persons with disabilities and their representative organisations.”

Advocates say accessibility should go beyond captions – because captions alone do not meet the needs of every deaf person.

“For many members of the deaf community, FSL is their first language, while written Filipino or English is their second. Providing both high-quality captions and FSL accessibility gives deaf people meaningful choices and ensures that information is presented in the language they understand best,” Agbay said.

Capanang said some deaf people had limited written vocabulary because they had not had the opportunity to attend school, making sign language their primary means of communication. She called for greater support to encourage cinemas and distributors to expand accessibility options, as well as stricter enforcement of accessibility laws.

The government, film industry and deaf organisations needed to collaborate to ensure no one is left behind, Agbay said. “By working together, [they] can create a media environment where everyone has equal access to information, culture and entertainment.”

item.title: [SCMP] Race for UN top job enters final stage: choice may ‘make or break’ organisation
item.description:
It is financially strapped, structurally flawed, infamously bureaucratic, reputationally damaged and riven with infighting.

So why would anyone want to take on the role of the next secretary general of the United Nations?

“I really think there should be some sort of psychiatric test for wanting this position,” said Richard Gowan, global issues and institutions director at the International Crisis Group (ICG). “The stakes are exceptionally high, and there is a strong sense around the UN that the next secretary general may make or break the organisation.”
item.content:encoded:
It is financially strapped, structurally flawed, infamously bureaucratic, reputationally damaged and riven with infighting.

So why would anyone want to take on the role of the next secretary general of the United Nations?

“I really think there should be some sort of psychiatric test for wanting this position,” said Richard Gowan, global issues and institutions director at the International Crisis Group (ICG). “The stakes are exceptionally high, and there is a strong sense around the UN that the next secretary general may make or break the organisation.”

The official start of the race to become the 10th UN chief in the organisation’s eight-decade history is under way, at an existential time for an organisation framed by noble ideals but dragged down by bickering and human failings.

While in theory the choice is made by its 193 member states, the real power is with the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (P5). The archaic several-month process that officially kicked off late last month includes secret ballots on coloured paper, with the largest voices going to major donors Beijing and Washington.

Once the P5 reaches a consensus, the others generally go along with it, and the new secretary general is usually in place for the five-year term by year’s end.

As member states assess which candidate will best protect their interests, the gossip-infused UN obsesses over every twist, which candidate is ahead, whether late entries will emerge, and what clues can be gleaned from the vague Chinese utterances and blunt American declarations.

“It’s everyone’s favourite parlour game around the UN,” said Elizabeth Cousens, president and chief executive of the UN Foundation, a civic group. “Every secretary general election is unpredictable, but this one comes at a particularly unpredictable time geopolitically.”

Shaping the selection is a concerning dilemma. Even as the Iran war rages, artificial intelligence upends societies and humanitarian crises intensify, UN peacekeeping has faltered and aid funding is drying up.

That ideally demands a strong, visionary leader capable of guiding the unwieldy global community through painful restructuring. But getting Washington and Beijing, along with Moscow, Paris and London, to agree – each with its red lines, parochial interests and rivalries – suggests a minimally objectionable candidate will prevail. Hardly the recipe for success.

“They’re all grey mouses of the system,” said one UN insider. “A lot of secretary generals have come in, made promises, moved a few deckchairs and lost their political capital.”

The hope, analysts say, is that a non-offensive winner finds their backbone once in office, as happened with past heads Dag Hammarskjold and U Thant.

Current Secretary General Antonio Guterres, who promised a “surge in diplomacy for peace” during his selection, has emerged as a cautious leader largely focused on humanitarian relief.

Critics also say he failed to seriously tackle cost-cutting, including expensive private school stipends and business-class travel.

While he is credited with forging a Russia-Ukraine Black Sea grain initiative in 2022, it was more in response to conflict than resolving the conflict itself, admittedly not an easy task.

One indication of the daunting challenges is the number of candidates, just seven compared to 13 at this stage in 2016, including some not supported by their home country. One withdrew after just two weeks; another just joined.

By UN convention, it “should” be a woman and the “turn” of someone from Latin America and the Caribbean, although these are not rules.

China has held its cards close, other than signalling support for women and Global South candidates.

“To sum up, commitment to the UN Charter, outstanding competency, integrity, impartiality, and the initiative to take responsibility,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in New York in May, outlining the characteristics needed for China’s preference.

What does Beijing seek?

Analysts say Beijing wants a candidate who will support more Chinese in top UN jobs, including China’s growing UN peacekeeping role, and back further integration of its Belt and Road Initiative, as well as its global security, development and civilisation initiatives into the UN architecture.

“The Chinese don’t want the UN interfering in their business, but the UN has been really meek on most things in the Asia-Pacific for quite a while,” Gowan said.

“They certainly don’t want anyone who presses them on their human rights record. That’s a given.”

The administration of US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, is looking for someone who is compliant with its unilateral approach to foreign policy, can improve the UN’s poor record on conflict resolution and can champion its aggressive financial reform agenda.

Washington’s US$4 billion arrears for core and peacekeeping operations, nearly half that budget, have sparked the UN’s crisis.

“Similar to China, the US has very entrenched interests on the world stage and doesn’t want the next secretary general to present themselves as someone who’s standing in the way,” said Daniel Forti, ICG’s UN affairs director.

“The Trump administration sees it as a ‘my way or the highway’ approach.”

US partiality is further fuelled by China hawks, Maga lawmakers and US social interest groups.

“The secretary general sets a tone,” Stefano Gennarini, vice-president with the conservative Centre for Family and Human Rights advocacy group, testified in Congress. “It’s fundamentally important that UN officials do not interfere in internal political debates about abortion or other controversial social policies.”

US-China interests overlap, however, in favouring serious structural transformation, even if Beijing talks in upbeat generalities and lets the US espouse brutal reform. Given the US’ responsibility for 22 per cent of the general budget and China’s for 20 per cent, every candidate has at least nodded to restructuring in their platforms.

“Many countries, including China, were thinking along the same lines anyway – that these reforms are way, way, way overdue,” said Dan Negrea, US ambassador to the UN Economic and Social Council.

Another change from past leadership transitions is that the Trump administration cares less than its predecessors did, giving China more opportunities in soft power.

“The US burned so many bridges, and China has taken over so completely and cleverly,” said Marc Limon, executive director, Universal Rights Group. “They’re not at loggerheads, but I don’t think they’re working together partly because the US is just useless. They think they can shout and everyone will do what they want.”

But both seem keen to avoid the selection process dragging on, given the Iran war, the energy crisis, economic problems and other pressing issues.

This contrasts with 1996, when the US vetoed the re-election of Egypt’s Boutros Boutros-Ghali against China’s wishes, ultimately resulting in Ghana’s Kofi Annan. And in 1981, after the Washington-supported Nazi-tainted Kurt Waldheim stood for an unprecedented third term, Beijing balked. That led to 16 contentious rounds of voting before Peru’s Javier Perez de Cuellar was picked as a compromise candidate.

Seven candidates in running

This year’s seven declared candidates include Michelle Bachelet, Chile’s former president and a former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights; Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, secretary general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development; and Rafael Mariano Grossi, a long-time Argentinian diplomat who heads the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The others are Macky Sall, Senegal’s former president; Maria Fernanda Espinosa Garces, Ecuador’s former defence and foreign minister and the UN’s former General Assembly head; Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana’s former foreign minister; and late entrant Olara Otunnu, Uganda’s former UN undersecretary general.

Five are from the Latin American and Caribbean region; four are women, and each has varied expertise, whether in human rights, global development, security and financial reform or small-state diplomacy.

Washington is generally seen as favouring Grossi given his ties to far-right Argentina. Some expect China to oppose Bachelet; others argue that Beijing appreciated her handling of Xinjiang as human rights head.

Betting app Kalshi gives Grynspan a 49 per cent chance of winning, compared to 42 per cent for Grossi and 8 per cent for Bachelet.

Trump’s long record as a showman has also spurred speculation that he could try and force through a preferred candidate using US funding leverage or pre-empt the process by announcing a winner at the G20 summit in Miami in mid-December to grab the credit and limelight.

Trump already floated Swiss football administrator Gianni Infantino for the job after he gave the attention-grabbing president a “Fifa peace prize”.

Expect stereotypes and sniping as race heats up

Amid the manoeuvring has come catty UN backbiting. That female candidates will not be respected handling security portfolios. That “woke” candidates will not survive Trump’s onslaught. That certain ages or religions are not ideal. That candidates who remain in their UN jobs while campaigning should be excluded.

The next leader will confront huge challenges. The UN has some 40,000 active tasks, reports, panels and working groups, many involving crises long since over, across 400 intergovernmental bodies, requiring some 27,000 meetings a year. UN initiatives are easy to launch but difficult to kill.

They also must grapple with two of the P5 – the United States and Russia – violating the UN Charter prohibiting use of force against another state, as Washington embraces “America first” policies.

And they will also face a World War II-era P5 that is badly out of step with the current geopolitical landscape, as India, Japan, Brazil, Nigeria and others clamour to join.

Under the selection process, candidates for the US$227,000 annual position are nominated to the Security Council and General Assembly, followed by interviews, town halls, visits to major capitals and several informal “straw polls” to gauge the preferences of Security Council members.

The first of these was held on July 30 and showed Grynspan as the early front-runner, followed by Rodrigue Birkett – with Grossi in third place.

“It’s supposed to be confidential, but they never are,” Gowan said. “It’s often out before the diplomats get back to their mission to write them up.”

These continue until one candidate gets nine of the 15 Security Council votes without a P5 veto, at which point the General Assembly can, in theory, reject them, although it never has.

The next winner of this poisoned chalice faces daunting odds and will need huge amounts of tact, wisdom, muscle and luck, analysts say.

“If they don’t use this crisis to make changes, then the UN will collapse,” Limon said.

“Like the League of Nations, people want to do good. But a lot of people earn ridiculous wages, golden handcuffs, and they don’t want to change.”

.

item.title: [SCMP] Thai teen kills at least 5 in school, after shooting grandparents at home
item.description:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.
item.content:encoded:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.

Police said 23 people were wounded in the incident.

The boy appeared to have shot his grandparents first before attending school as normal, said Royal Thai Police spokesman Police Lieutenant General Trairong Phiwphan. After class started, the boy opened fire inside his classroom before walking out and continuing to shoot.

Trairong said the teen fired more than 20 shots and over 30 rounds were found on him after he shot himself.

Several family members of the alleged shooter told police the boy usually kept to himself and was a good student. They said they were unaware of any troubles he faced at home or school.

Harrowing video footage shared on social media, apparently filmed by a pupil during the shooting, shows children in blue uniforms cowering under wooden desks, as five shots ring out while the school’s automatic public address system announces the time is 10am.

One pupil in the clip extends an arm out to comfort another who is crying as the shots are fired in what appears to be a methodical manner.

“It’s really awful, this shouldn’t have happened,” Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters. “I’m not just sad about the people who died, I’m sad that something like this could happen in our country at all.

“This is exactly what I’ve been saying – the reason the government doesn’t allow people to carry guns, doesn’t allow ownership, doesn’t allow licence renewals, is because of exactly this kind of thing.”

Anutin confirmed reports that the shooter was 14 years old and killed himself, according to Associated Press. He said the boy, who lived with his grandparents, had shown signs of stress related to school.

The gun, described by police as small and compact, was legally registered to the boy’s grandfather, Anutin said.

The prime minister on Friday also vowed to introduce a new firearms control law.

Anutin, who previously tightened gun ‌laws when he was interior minister, will now propose a law to restrict the carrying of firearms by the public.

“The new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns,” he told reporters on Friday, but did not provide any specifics for the envisaged legislation, including whether it would tighten gun ownership requirements.

Images shared by police showed what appeared to be the gunman’s weapon, a semi-automatic pistol with multiple rounds packed in a pouch, as questions emerged over his mental health and the motive behind the attack. Several pupils suggested the shooter had been bullied.

“Our school doesn’t check our bags when entering school,” Kittipat Choolert, 16, told This Week in Asia. “He fired several shots, I was two buildings away from him and I heard the gunshots, the entire school heard it and we were in shock.”

Tearful students in school uniforms held each other outside the school.

“I’m still in shock,” 16-year-old Thatchai Jaiyen told Agence France-Presse, expressing disbelief that a kind former teacher of his had been killed.

“She was such a good person. I thought that if she had encountered the shooter, she might have been able to reason with him. I never expected that the child would actually shoot her,” he said, his voice trailing away.

Student Purin Khumchoo said he felt depressed and bad for the people who were killed.

“The two teachers who were killed were lovely, and many students became better people because of them,” he said.

Emergency worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, 47, described arriving during the shooting and his team treating students with injuries to the back, ‌chest and arms. They found a teacher dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room a female teacher with chest and arm wounds.

Kiatikhun said he was called to treat the teenage shooter after hearing a final shot. “We rushed up ‌and found ‌that the perpetrator had shot himself in the right side of the head and collapsed. When we got up there, we checked his pulse, he still had one, so we started CPR.”

The school suspended all classes for next week and instructed staff to work from home during that time.

It is the latest shooting to stun a nation where millions of firearms are in circulation, many unlicensed and unregistered and where shootings are commonplace, but mass killings involving children are rare.

Last weekend, Anutin was at the scene of the killing of five people in Chonburi, including Russian siblings, one shot by an alleged robber.

In February, a teacher ‌died and a ‌student was injured in southern Thailand’s Hat Yai district after a gunman opened fire at a school.

In 2023, a shooting by a 14-year-old boy killed two – a Chinese and a Myanmar citizen – at Siam Paragon, one of Thailand’s most famous downtown malls.

It was a tragedy that spurred calls for stricter gun controls, yet killings have continued, with regular police raids unearthing large caches of heavy weapons and pistols.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia, second only to Pakistan but far surpassing its Southeast Asian neighbours.

Data collected in 2017 by the groups Small Arms Survey and GunPolicy.org in their last extensive international study found civilian gun ownership in Thailand was about 15.1 guns per 100 people, compared with fewer than one per 100 in neighbouring Malaysia.

Thailand had 3.49 deaths by firearms per 100,000 people, according to 2023 statistics published by World Population Review.

“I think we need to [look at] why we still haven’t learned from everything that’s happened,” Krisanaphong Poothakool, a leading criminologist and adviser to the Royal Thai Police on police reform, told Channel One News.

“Why do firearms in Thailand seem so easy to access? The fact that children and youth have access to guns and gun sets is really not something normal in Thai society.”

In the worst episode of its kind in living memory, Panya Khamrab, a 34-year-old former policeman with a history of drug abuse, massacred 37 people – 24 of them children – in a shooting and stabbing rampage at a day care centre in the northeastern province of Nong Bua Lam Phu in 2022.

Additional reporting by Associated Press, Reuters and Agence France-Presse

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond call centres? Philippines reopens Manila for outsourcing edge
item.description:
The Philippines is reopening Metro Manila to new outsourcing hubs as it tries to defend its place in the global services market and win more complex work from multinational companies.

Officials, industry executives and property analysts say the move could help the country compete for higher-value offshore functions – from software engineering and finance to healthcare documentation, data work and AI-related services – by making more modern, incentive-eligible office space available in the capital.

But the decision has also revived a concern raised when new IT parks in the capital were restricted seven years ago: whether allowing more investment back into Manila could weaken the push to build outsourcing hubs in provincial cities such as Cebu, Davao and Clark.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines is reopening Metro Manila to new outsourcing hubs as it tries to defend its place in the global services market and win more complex work from multinational companies.

Officials, industry executives and property analysts say the move could help the country compete for higher-value offshore functions – from software engineering and finance to healthcare documentation, data work and AI-related services – by making more modern, incentive-eligible office space available in the capital.

But the decision has also revived a concern raised when new IT parks in the capital were restricted seven years ago: whether allowing more investment back into Manila could weaken the push to build outsourcing hubs in provincial cities such as Cebu, Davao and Clark.

On July 23, President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr issued Administrative Order No. 45 (AO 45) allowing the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (Peza) to accept and evaluate applications for new information technology parks and centres in the National Capital Region.

Peza oversees special economic zones where eligible companies can apply for incentives, making its accreditation an important factor for outsourcing firms and multinational service hubs choosing where to locate.

The order partially lifts a 2019 moratorium which aimed to steer more economic activity into the provinces.

Tereso Panga, Peza’s director general, told This Week in Asia the reopening of Manila would not divert provincial investment.

“Instead, a larger Metro Manila investment pipeline can serve as a gateway for second and succeeding expansions into Central Luzon, Calabarzon [an agglomeration of Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal and Quezon provinces on Luzon island] and other emerging growth centres”, he said.

According to Panga, Peza has observed that global companies commonly establish their first Philippine operations in locations with deep talent pools, mature infrastructure and established business ecosystems.

Those initial Metro Manila investments could later lead to expansion in other parts of the country, he said, citing the growth of information technology and business process management (IT-BPM) activity in Cebu, Iloilo and Davao.

The Philippines’ IT-BPM industry includes outsourced services for global companies ranging from customer support and back-office work to software engineering, data and AI-related services, healthcare documentation and financial analysis.

“The Peza board is directed to formulate and issue the guidelines necessary to effectively implement the policy and ensure that the thrust to accelerate countryside development continues,” Panga said.

Marcos’ order resolves a long-standing policy constraint, helping Peza respond to the changing requirements of the IT-BPM industry while opening opportunities for property developers, according to Panga.

The IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines, which represents the sector nationally, welcomed the order as a “timely and pragmatic policy” that would strengthen the country’s competitiveness for new investment.

“In today’s highly competitive investment environment, speed and flexibility matter,” said Jack Madrid, the association’s president and chief executive.

“Administrative Order No 45 gives investors greater confidence that the Philippines can respond to evolving business requirements while preserving our long-term commitment to countryside development.”

Belinda Torres, president of ICT-Davao, the regional IT-BPM association, said her association welcomed the changes. Global investors increasingly viewed the Philippines as a “portfolio of locations” to support different stages of growth, rather than limiting their choices between Metro Manila and provincial hubs, Torres said.

“Providing investors with greater flexibility in choosing where to locate their operations makes the Philippines an even more attractive destination for long-term investment,” Torres said.

She cited Davao’s strengths as a hub for digital investment, such as investor confidence in its stable business environment and lower exposure to major natural disasters.

“The future is no longer about asking which city will attract the next investment. It is about ensuring that every investment into the Philippines finds the right environment to grow. Davao is well-positioned to be one of those environments,” she said.

This Week in Asia has also reached out to the IT-BPM association in Cebu for comment.

Panga said Peza saw growing demand from markets including Australia and Japan for outsourced business services, digital operations, engineering and other knowledge-based activities beyond the country’s traditional IT-BPM base.

Five projects in Metro Manila have already received Peza board approval and are awaiting presidential proclamations that will formally designate their sites as special economic zones.

They are Altaire and The Yuchengco Centre in Makati City, One Trium Tower in Muntinlupa City, ARCA South 1 in Taguig City and Parqal in Paranaque City.

Sites designated as special economic zones allow eligible tenant companies to apply for Peza registration and tax incentives, though developers that build or operate the facilities will not receive fiscal benefits.

The authority said the five projects could be proclaimed within the year if they met all requirements, but did not disclose their planned office space, investment values, prospective tenants or projected employment.

This Week in Asia has asked Ayala Land, which is developing ARCA South 1, for comments.

Property consultancy Colliers said Marcos’ order could help resolve a widening supply mismatch in Metro Manila’s office market, noting that companies requiring at least 5,000 square metres faced a more limited range of suitable registered offices.

Peza said last month that 44 per cent of available accredited office space was considered ageing.

Kevin Jara, a director in Colliers Philippines’ Office Services division, said older Peza buildings “may face greater pressure to reprice, upgrade or reposition” as companies increasingly prioritised sustainability and operating efficiency.

He cited Quezon City, Mandaluyong and the Bay Area, which offered more Peza-compliant choices for global capability centres (GCC) and IT-BPM companies, as the most likely beneficiaries of AO 45.

A GCC is an overseas hub that handles functions such as technology, finance and customer support for a multinational company.

Quezon City has about 317,700 square metres of Peza-proclaimed office stock, according to Colliers’ second-quarter data. Mandaluyong has roughly 276,000 square metres of proclaimed and potential supply, while the Bay Area could add about 242,000 square metres of potential space.

Jara said those districts could provide scalable alternatives for companies constrained by limited Peza-accredited options in Fort Bonifacio and Makati’s central business district.

“AO 45’s largest impact will likely be felt in districts where the pipeline can translate more quickly into broader tenant choice and more competitive leasing alternatives,” he said.

Kath Taburada, research manager at Colliers Philippines, said the order could also upgrade the quality of Metro Manila’s office market.

Since the 2019 moratorium, the capital added about 4.3 million square metres of office supply, but only around 40 per cent was Peza-proclaimed, she said.

“AO 45 is not simply adding more space; it is helping unlock newer office stock that was previously unable to fully serve Peza-registered occupiers.”

The supply would serve both third-party outsourcing firms and GCCs, Taburada said, but the stronger strategic opportunity lay with the latter because they typically needed larger offices, stronger infrastructure, skilled talent and room for long-term growth.

item.title: [SCMP] What China’s expanded funding for HIV/Aids in Africa means as US cuts health aid
item.description:
China is expanding its role in the fight against HIV/Aids in Africa by funding new projects and backing local medicine manufacturing as part of its signature health initiative, the Health Silk Road.

Beijing’s larger presence comes as traditional Western aid wanes following the closure of the US Agency for International Development and sweeping cuts to the World Health Organization and the President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar).

Pepfar was a major bilateral American initiative providing life-saving antiretroviral treatment and healthcare support for millions of people in developing countries.
item.content:encoded:
China is expanding its role in the fight against HIV/Aids in Africa by funding new projects and backing local medicine manufacturing as part of its signature health initiative, the Health Silk Road.

Beijing’s larger presence comes as traditional Western aid wanes following the closure of the US Agency for International Development and sweeping cuts to the World Health Organization and the President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar).

Pepfar was a major bilateral American initiative providing life-saving antiretroviral treatment and healthcare support for millions of people in developing countries.

Instead, Washington has signed bilateral health agreements with some African countries, though a few such as Zambia and Zimbabwe declined to sign the deals over worries about data sovereignty and sensitive health information sharing.

Following a recent trip to China, UNAids executive director Winnie Byanyima revealed that China’s Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund was backing HIV prevention projects in Lesotho, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe.

South Africa, which has about eight million people living with HIV, received a US$3.49 million Chinese grant last year to fund prevention programmes targeting more than 50,000 young people and harm-reduction services for people who inject drugs.

In Uganda, Chinese funding supports the Triple Elimination Project to end mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B.

Byanyima said the China International Development Cooperation Agency (CIDCA) had invited UNAids to submit further project funding proposals for regions facing distinct HIV challenges.

“Grateful for China’s strong commitment to multilateralism and understanding that global epidemics must be fought together,” Byanyima said in July after the trip.

The funding ties into Beijing’s broader health diplomacy under the Health Silk Road initiative, which has previously seen China fund programmes addressing Ebola and malaria across the continent.

According to the Chinese Loans to Africa Database at Boston University’s Global Development Policy Centre, China committed US$1.3 billion in health financing to Africa between 2000 and 2024.

Beijing also funded and built the US$80 million Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) headquarters and reference laboratories in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, as a gift for Africa to help fight diseases.

Those amounts came alongside direct government grants through agencies such as the CIDCA and the deployment of thousands of medical experts over decades.

Shenglan Tang, co-director of the Global Health Research Centre at Duke Kunshan University in China, said that as traditional donors, particularly the US, reassessed their foreign aid priorities, important financing gaps were emerging in global health.

“China appears increasingly willing to provide targeted support in areas where it believes it can add value, especially through South-South cooperation, technical collaboration and capacity building,” Tang said.

He observed that the recent support provided through China’s Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund, as well as the invitation for additional UNAids concept notes, suggested that “China is becoming more willing to finance selected global health initiatives”.

However, Tang described what was happening as an incremental evolution rather than a major transformation.

“China’s financial contribution to HIV remains modest compared with that of Pepfar and the Global Fund, but its role may become increasingly important when reductions in traditional donor funding may continue,” he said.

Meeting with officials in China in July, Byanyima voiced enthusiasm for partnering with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology to strengthen local and regional manufacturing of health commodities in Africa.

“I appreciate China’s willingness to share the dividends of the development of its health sector in the interest of the shared future for all humanity,” Byanyima said.

However, David Shinn, a China-Africa expert and former US diplomat in Africa, said China remained a minor player in HIV/Aids treatment compared with the US, which continued to provide billions globally despite local funding shifts.

“Although the US did stop funding in South Africa, it continues to provide about US$5 billion globally each year for the prevention and treatment of HIV/Aids, much of it going to Africa,” Shinn said.

He added that a close look at “China’s contributions demonstrates they are small but strategically located and heavily publicised”.

“China’s strength continues to be in the sending of medical teams to most African countries, a contribution that is rare from Western countries.”

According to Zhou Taidong, vice-president of the China Centre for International Knowledge on Development, affiliated with the Development Research Centre of the State Council, supporting HIV prevention under the Beijing-proposed Global Development Initiative aligns with broader health security.

Rather than treating HIV in isolation, China linked it to wider system resilience, Zhou said.

“China’s model increasingly focuses on building productive capacity, including pharmaceutical manufacturing, vaccine production, [Africa] CDC laboratories, hospital construction and digital health infrastructure.”

This approach, he added, “reflects China’s broader development philosophy that sustainable health outcomes require industrial capability as well as financing”.

“China’s role in HIV and broader health security is likely to become more capacity-oriented than purely aid-oriented.”

Rather than replacing traditional Western donors in financing service delivery, China could be expected to focus on complementary contributions such as health infrastructure, workforce development, technology transfer, pharmaceutical manufacturing and partnerships under South-South cooperation, Zhou said.

Tang, who is also a professor of medicine and global health at Duke University in the US, noted that African countries increasingly viewed local pharmaceutical production as an essential industrial development strategy following coronavirus pandemic-related supply disruptions.

Accordingly, China was regarded as offering affordable technologies and scalable capacity for technology transfer and investment partnerships, he said.

“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed Africa’s heavy dependence on imported medicines and vaccines, strengthening political commitment to regional manufacturing, as we have seen now in many African countries.”

Furthermore, China possessed extensive manufacturing capacity, relatively affordable production technologies and experience in scaling pharmaceutical production, Tang said.

“These strengths make it an attractive partner for technology transfer, investment and industrial cooperation.”

More Chinese pharmaceutical manufacturers had worked with their African counterparts to achieve a win-win outcome in this regard, he said.

Overall, Tang expected China’s role in global health, including HIV, to “continue expanding gradually”, while adding that it was “unlikely to replace the scale of traditional Western financing in the foreseeable future”.

item.title: [SCMP] The human faces of China’s belt and road strategy, through Liu Heung-shing’s lens
item.description:
It is barely light when Liu Heung-shing starts the day in his art-filled Happy Valley apartment. But then, the photojournalist has always believed in getting to the story before everyone else.

Liu, 74, wakes at 5am to spend three hours reading the news, coffee in hand. Despite being “long retired”, the Pulitzer Prize-winning photographer takes note of where he might want to visit next.

“There are so many ways to tell a story. Sometimes, the most difficult decision is when not to press the shutter, rather than when to press the shutter,” he says, while cooking and sipping a glass of Chablis. He has invited me to his home for dinner and to discuss his most recent book, Old Road New Connections: China Builds a Different World, for which his shutter charted a global odyssey following the tentacles of China’s Belt and Road Initiative. If the initiative sounds abstract in policy papers – six economic corridors, hundreds of billions in cumulative investment, more than 150 participating countries and 230 cooperation agreements – Liu’s book is an attempt to humanise that scale.
item.content:encoded:
It is barely light when Liu Heung-shing starts the day in his art-filled Happy Valley apartment. But then, the photojournalist has always believed in getting to the story before everyone else.

Liu, 74, wakes at 5am to spend three hours reading the news, coffee in hand. Despite being “long retired”, the Pulitzer Prize-winning photographer takes note of where he might want to visit next.

“There are so many ways to tell a story. Sometimes, the most difficult decision is when not to press the shutter, rather than when to press the shutter,” he says, while cooking and sipping a glass of Chablis. He has invited me to his home for dinner and to discuss his most recent book, Old Road New Connections: China Builds a Different World, for which his shutter charted a global odyssey following the tentacles of China’s Belt and Road Initiative. If the initiative sounds abstract in policy papers – six economic corridors, hundreds of billions in cumulative investment, more than 150 participating countries and 230 cooperation agreements – Liu’s book is an attempt to humanise that scale.

“I knew it was also a human story of Chinese going around the world, doing things, changing things and putting a uniquely Chinese stamp on different parts of the world.”

In many ways, the project is typical Liu: ambitious, self‑assigned and pursued with a mixture of stubbornness and curiosity.

“I think I’m somebody whose brain works 24 hours a day,” he laughs.

He likes to say that his books all begin with a simple editorial question: “If this is going to be one of the defining stories of the 21st century, and nobody has framed it properly yet, what can I do?”

Born in Hong Kong in 1951, Liu spent his early childhood in Fuzhou, Fujian province, with his mother, witnessing famine during the Great Leap Forward. His family eventually returned to Hong Kong.

In 1969, Liu left for New York, in the United States, where he studied politics at Hunter College. He remembers the year clearly because it was then that he saw Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin perform up close at the Woodstock festival.

More specific education came when his mentor, Albanian‑born photographer Gjon Mili, took him to the 28th floor of the Time & Life Building, which was where the photographers at Life magazine and other Time Inc titles were based.

“On that floor,” Liu says, “the world unfolded through photography.”

It was for Time Inc that Liu first returned to mainland China, in 1976, to photograph a nation coming to terms with the death of Mao Zedong.

As a foreign correspondent in China until the early 90s, he documented the pivotal decades that followed. Later, as the executive vice-president of News Corp China, Liu shuttled between tycoon Rupert Murdoch and party cadres.

Fundamentally, the photographer divides his understanding of modern China into three eras: China 1.0, the Maoist times he glimpsed as a child; China 2.0, launched by Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 reforms; and China 3.0, the country that is developing at breakneck speed, with the belt and road a defining initiative.

“This book is my exploration of that new world,” he writes in Old Road New Connections. “I used my camera to capture a resurgent nation spreading its wings.”

Doing so involved more than 270,000km of travel, “roughly the distance of seven times around the globe”, on multiple self-funded journeys over a three-year period. He covered five continents, 21 countries and 54 regions, spending a great deal of time in factories, mines, ports, deserts and train drivers’ cabins, as well as on the road, and that was after months of negotiation for access to the businesses, state-owned and otherwise, operating along the routes.

The resulting book turns one of this century’s most ambitious infrastructure projects into something unexpectedly intimate and personal: a portrait of a world quietly reordering at China’s direction.

“It’s capturing the contradictions sometimes, the smallest details that lend poetic meaning to life,” says Liu. “That is much more enduring than what’s in the latest news cycle.”

Following new lines of steel in Indonesia, he rode the Jakarta-Bandung high‑speed Whoosh, photographing Chinese and Indonesian operators shoulder to shoulder in the cab as Southeast Asia’s first bullet train, launched in 2023, zipped at 350km/h past villages and roads still heaving with traffic jams.

“You can show [a picture of] a high‑speed train once,” he says. “You show it twice, it’s already a repeat. After that, what interests me is who’s riding it, who’s driving it, who’s being moved and who finds their village cut in half.”

His journey through western China began on the old Silk Road: Xian’s terracotta warriors; camel caravans re‑enacted in Dunhuang. In complete contrast, he then visited the country’s first 100-megawatt molten‑salt solar thermal power station, which uses 12,000 mirrors and looks like a sci‑fi sun.

Some of Liu’s favourite photos from this project emerged along the sand ridges of the Gobi: young dancers from the Beijing Modern Dance Company performing in the desert, their body language, movement and skin tones coalescing with the sand dunes.

In Thailand, he watched workers construct concrete pillars that will one day connect Kunming, in China’s Yunnan province, to Bangkok and then Malaysia and Singapore, a rail artery replacing old Maritime Silk Road routes.

In Kazakhstan’s Aktau port, Liu slept uncomfortably “in a small converted shipping container”, he recalls, while sharing a worksite with engineers of the Citic Environmental Group, who were trying – not without problems – to hand over a water-treatment plant to a local team.

He met a couple in the old city of Kashgar, in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region; Hadiya Msham Abdulla from Tanzania studied at Fujian Medical University and now runs a cafe with her Uygur partner, Dilshat Tursun. As their staff made a latte for Liu, the couple proudly introduced him to their baby daughter.

“What is the most important factor in storytelling? I believe it’s trust,” he says. “I’m a humanist to the core, because I’m interested in everything. I’m interested in why this woman wants to look beautiful. I’m interested in athletes, how this man can run so fast.”

He’s also interested in the Kenyan manager at the Mombasa-Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway control centre who dispatches instructions in fluent Mandarin. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, Liu and his camera descended down a suffocating 1,150-metre-deep underground lift into the Kamoa-Kakula copper mine, which has Chinese investors. He snapped portraits of local miners, South African technicians and Angolan labourers working side by side with Chinese engineers.

Elsewhere in Africa, he encountered a Chinese lion conservationist, Xing Ba, in the Masai Mara wildlife reserve and a young Chinese engineer who has no plans to “go back” – Africa, for her, had become home.

His photographs from Iran date from just before the current conflict in the Middle East. While in the country, his interpreter asked him when more much-needed trains would be coming from China for Tehran’s metro. China helped build several of the city’s lines.

Liu captured a ladies’ Zumba class in Xinjiang; Brazilian cowboys; and a courier making AliExpress deliveries on horseback in a satellite town outside Moscow, Russia. He even peeked inside a Shanghai factory producing satellites deployed in the US-China space race.

A post-dinner snoop around his apartment finds a small framed picture of Liu’s, above his desk. It’s of Richard Nixon holding a bucket of Tsingtao beers and play-acting as a waiter on a Hangzhou-to-Shanghai train. The former US president was acting goofy on returning to China in 1982, to commemorate the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Shanghai Communiqué, which paved the way to normalising bilateral relations between China and the US.

On another wall is a picture that helped earn Liu his shared Pulitzer – as well as a punch from a KGB guard inside the Kremlin: a 1991 shot for Associated Press of Mikhail Gorbachev announcing his resignation and the dissolution of the Soviet Union. It shows the departing president sitting at a table, his shoulders slightly slumped, a blur of paper – an empire dissolving between one breath and the next.

“I was the only foreign photojournalist inside the great hall at the time,” recalls Liu. “I was really running around like crazy that day.”

His contributions to culture grew in 2015, when he founded the Shanghai Centre of Photography, which quickly became a mainstay of the West Bund art district before closing in December 2023. Running a non-profit, fundraising and training 10-plus staff proved rewarding but ultimately too taxing. He now divides his time between Hong Kong, Europe and mainland China.

With Old Road New Connections, Liu shows he is still more interested in being on the road than at the podium. Although conceived as a China 3.0 travelogue of sorts, a book on how China’s infrastructure push translates into lived experience is perhaps a logical addendum to a lifelong project of bearing witness to world-defining tipping points.

His photographs and anecdotes do not resolve into a neat verdict on the belt and road, or China’s far-spanning cross-border development. Instead, they register the speed of progress and the human ways by which capital and culture, Chinese or otherwise, flow. It’s not the panoramas of bridges, trains or ports that are most poignant, but the images of people absorbed in daily life as the world around them is being rewired.

“If the 21st century is to be China’s, as the last was America’s, I wanted to see the making of that century where it was happening, no matter how far away,” he writes.

“I’ve photographed so many people, in so many stories, in so many different countries, but I’m still interested,” he says, finishing the Chablis, “because my next picture could just be my best.”

Old Road New Connections: China Builds a Different World will be officially launched at Liu Heung-shing’s talk with Bernard Chan, chairman of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority board, on Thursday July 16, at the 36th Hong Kong Book Fair, which runs until July 21, at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asian scammers’ new disguise: your leader’s face
item.description:
There is a bogus version of Singapore’s prime minister that exists only to steal money. It connected to a Zoom call, thanked a stranger for his time and helped relieve him of US$3.8 million – with the real Lawrence Wong, for a time, none the wiser about what had happened.

The victim had received a WhatsApp message purporting to be from the secretary to the cabinet, inviting him to a private meeting.

What followed was not some doctored photo or a 15-second clip designed to fool a distracted doomscroll. It was an entire fabricated summit, complete with assembled officials including Wong, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, cabinet minister Indranee Rajah and foreign dignitaries, all rendered convincingly enough to believe they were discussing funding tied to the Strait of Hormuz.
item.content:encoded:
There is a bogus version of Singapore’s prime minister that exists only to steal money. It connected to a Zoom call, thanked a stranger for his time and helped relieve him of US$3.8 million – with the real Lawrence Wong, for a time, none the wiser about what had happened.

The victim had received a WhatsApp message purporting to be from the secretary to the cabinet, inviting him to a private meeting.

What followed was not some doctored photo or a 15-second clip designed to fool a distracted doomscroll. It was an entire fabricated summit, complete with assembled officials including Wong, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, cabinet minister Indranee Rajah and foreign dignitaries, all rendered convincingly enough to believe they were discussing funding tied to the Strait of Hormuz.

The synthetic Wong closed the meeting by thanking the victim for attending. Then a fake lawyer took the call and S$4.9 million (US$3.8 million) vanished into an account that no longer exists.

Southeast Asia’s scam industry has found a powerful new weapon, and it isn’t malware, cunning or even greed – it’s borrowed faces.

Criminals are increasingly cloning the region’s most trusted leaders using generative AI, wrapping fraud in the unimpeachable authority of a president’s voice or a prime minister’s visage and cashing in on the thing no security system can patch: human trust.

In Indonesia, a similar con surfaced within days of Prabowo Subianto’s 2024 election win, when an Instagram clip began circulating in which he appeared to ask viewers: “Who hasn’t received aid from me? What are your needs right now?”

The incoming president had said no such thing. But the voice was his, the face was his and for many, that was enough. Across 20 provinces, an unknown number of Indonesians each wired scammers “administrative fees” of up to 1 million rupiah (US$55), chasing government aid that was never coming and never had been.

In the Philippines, the fraud wore Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s face, superimposed onto footage endorsing an online trading scheme with a polish good enough to convince one dentist to hand over 93 million pesos (US$1.5 million) before the illusion broke.

Three countries. Three cons. One unsettling realisation: artificial intelligence has stopped merely helping scammers write better emails. It has started manufacturing their credibility from scratch.
