“If you’re not trained to look at it and you don’t have the discernment to know that it’s impossible for the president to be endorsing investment schemes, you will believe it,” said Art Samaniego, a Manila-based tech journalist and co-founder of ScamWatch Pilipinas. “Because you can clearly see the president’s face and he appears to be speaking.”

Old con, new face

An Interpol report released in June identified AI-driven crime as one of Southeast Asia’s most urgent emerging threats, warning of criminal networks that are growing leaner and more organised as technology races ahead of regulation.

From January 2024 to March 2025, it found “phishing” attacks – where scammers send fake emails, messages, or links to trick victims into sharing sensitive data – and related swindles were the costliest form of cybercrime across Asia and the South Pacific, with a third of countries logging more than 10,000 cases apiece.

“These include the use of deepfake videos to impersonate public figures, celebrities, or business executives,” it said. “Such schemes have resulted in significant financial losses and have targeted both individuals and institutions.”

On criminal forums and Telegram channels, chatter about deepfakes surged 600 per cent in just one five-month period in 2024, the report found.

But strip away the technology and the con itself is nothing new. All the AI does, experts say, is play on the same old human weaknesses – fear, hope, desperation, deference to power – but with a more believable face.

“Many people are raised to respect authority,” said Jun Angelo Sunglao, a clinical psychologist who chairs the Psychological Association of the Philippines’ mental health support group.

“So if someone calls and can impersonate someone we inherently perceive as good or trustworthy, our default instinct is to comply, not to doubt them.”

The elderly made for some of the easiest targets, Samaniego said, as many had been conditioned over long lifetimes to trust a phone call at face value.

But no one is immune from scammers, especially as the technology becomes more advanced. Voice cloning adds a crueller dimension still, mimicking the reassuring tones – or panicked cries – of a loved one.

“Hearing someone you care for cry for help triggers an immediate fight-or-flight response, completely shutting down your rational thinking,” Sunglao said. “You act on pure emotion.”

Nobody understands that better than a Filipino domestic worker identified only as Maria, who reportedly believed she had found love with a Dubai prince on a dating app.

He wrote constantly. He placed video calls, warm and attentive, present in every way that mattered. But he was never real.

By the time Maria saw through the facade, she had sent 100,000 pesos – a year’s wages – for a “marriage certificate” and a fictitious “royal membership card” meant to secure her a job in Dubai, Agence France-Presse reported earlier this month.

“They prey on isolated individuals,” Sunglao said of the scammers. “Slowly building a deep emotional connection with the goal of scamming them out of money.”

AI has not changed the criminals’ cruelty. It has simply given it a face worth falling for.

Tricking the experts

Jeremy Douglas, deputy director of operations at the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, confirmed to This Week in Asia that AI and other tech tools were increasingly being integrated into scam operations across Southeast Asia and further afield.

“It’s classic organised crime behaviour, innovating to accelerate business and stay ahead of law enforcement,” he said. “The use of deepfake images and videos, and mimicking or copying voice intonation and patterns of partners and contacts are on the rise and we can expect more sophisticated use going forward.”

Neal Jetton, who leads Interpol’s cybercrime directorate, pointed to estimates that global cybercrime losses hit US$10.5 trillion in 2025, with a 142 per cent rise forecast by the end of this decade.

“Cybercrime exists wherever anyone is using a smartphone or laptop … it is a global problem,” Jetton said, adding that AI had become “one of the main drivers”.

What makes the scams so effective, according to Interpol, is their reliance on social engineering techniques, exploiting human trust rather than technical vulnerabilities.

This has transformed so-called romance baiting into a booming subsector all of its own, part of a cyberfraud economy the UN Office on Drugs and Crime estimates has cost the world up to US$37 billion and counting.

The method rarely changes: weeks or months of patient, tender contact, before the big ask arrives.

Analysts are careful not to overstate the novelty, however. AI has not built a new criminal underworld, it has retooled an old one – at speed.

“These capabilities are enabling organised crime syndicates to radically change scam and associated money-laundering businesses,” Douglas said, adding that such operations were “professionalising, using fewer people to run or perpetuate scams” and sometimes switching jurisdictions or shifting from the notorious large scam compounds “into a model of networked locations”.

Samaniego has watched and reported on the retooling happening in real time.

“Before, if an email had wrong grammar, you could automatically tell it was a scam,” he said. “Now you can no longer identify it that way, because their grammar has become so good, because they’re using AI to create fake links and fake websites.”

“AI is not replacing cybercriminals, it’s making them more efficient … Their efficiency has doubled or tripled.”

AI is not replacing cybercriminals, it’s making them more efficient

Art Samaniego, ScamWatch Pilipinas

Even seasoned professionals occasionally fall foul of the scammers’ tactics.

Jetton recalled hearing of a cybercrime expert who clicked on a fraudulent email disguised as an Uber receipt, simply because he had recently used the e-hailing app.

“Awareness campaigns are helping, but we’re still seeing the human element – desperation, need, naivety. And the phishing emails are so good now,” he said, citing a Microsoft report that found a human was 4½ times more likely to click on a phishing email created by AI.

John Wojcik, senior threat researcher for Asia at cybersecurity firm Infoblox, said there had been “rapid acceleration” in the kinds of AI tools that scammers were using.

“From deepfakes, lifelike chatbots and complex, nuanced machine translation, to automated scam outreach, domain registration and phishing attacks, it’s clear this technology is being rolled out at scale within this criminal ecosystem,” he said, fed by a surge in “malware-as-a-service” kits sold on the dark web.

Doubting what you see

There is no silver bullet solution, Jetton concedes – only what he calls a “whole-of-society effort”.

And as AI-generated content edges towards the indistinguishable, old methods of detecting fakes, such as listening for a stilted phrase or watching for an unnatural blink, are fast losing relevance.

“As AI reaches human-level output, traditional visual or audio cues are becoming unreliable,” Samaniego said.

The only defence that still held, he said, was verification through a separate channel entirely.

“If you receive an urgent or high-stakes request, even if it looks or sounds exactly like someone you know, do not respond to the message or caller directly,” Samaniego said.

“If someone claiming to be your friend asks for money on social media, call him. If he texts, use other channels. Best if you can verify in person.”

His best advice for countering the scammers? Forcing them “off script”.

“AI models and scam scripts are excellent at handling expected flows but often falter when faced with unpredictable, human-centric interruptions,” he said. “Ask a question that other people won’t know the answer to.”

Sunglao’s solution, meanwhile, was more community-focused.

“If a suspicious investment opportunity or a sudden emergency request comes up, run it by a trusted peer first,” he said. “Talking it out disrupts the high-pressure environment the scammer relies on.”

For ScamWatch Pilipinas’ Samaniego, pre-emptive measures such as strong cyber literacy are the best defence.

“Hearing or seeing someone talk online is no longer sufficient proof that what you’re seeing is genuine or real,” he said. “Because of AI, we all need new ways to verify identity.”

What his cybersecurity advocacy movement wanted, Samaniego said, was for people to already be educated “before the scam occurs” – so they never had the misfortune to become victims in the first place.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump signs new orders targeting birthright citizenship and ‘birth tourism’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday seeking to narrow birthright citizenship and intensify a crackdown on “birth tourism”, making a new attempt to restrict automatic citizenship after his original policy was rejected by the Supreme Court.

Trump announced the measures unexpectedly during a White House event, describing the Supreme Court’s June 30 ruling as “very unfortunate” and arguing that wealthy foreigners had built businesses around securing US citizenship for their children.

“They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen,” Trump said.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday seeking to narrow birthright citizenship and intensify a crackdown on “birth tourism”, making a new attempt to restrict automatic citizenship after his original policy was rejected by the Supreme Court.

Trump announced the measures unexpectedly during a White House event, describing the Supreme Court’s June 30 ruling as “very unfortunate” and arguing that wealthy foreigners had built businesses around securing US citizenship for their children.

“They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen,” Trump said.

The measures are likely to renew a politically and legally contentious debate that has increasingly focused on China, with Trump and Republican lawmakers repeatedly alleging that wealthy Chinese nationals and commercial operators have exploited US citizenship laws.

The first order directs federal agencies not to recognise the US citizenship of certain US-born children when neither parent is an American citizen.

It applies when either parent is classified as an “alien enemy”, a category the order defines to include members of designated foreign terrorist organisations and individuals designated as global terrorists.

It also covers children whose parents include foreign government employees, a category encompassing ambassadors, foreign embassy or consular staff, people employed by foreign governments in an official capacity and some employees of international organisations.

The order additionally seeks to deny citizenship when either parent paid to arrange for a mother to be present in the United States or one of its territories to give birth, including through a commercial surrogacy arrangement.

It also covers children born in US territories or territorial waters where citizenship is not already conferred by federal law.

The order describes these categories as “non-exhaustive”, leaving open the possibility that the administration could attempt to identify others. It directs relevant federal agencies to issue implementation guidance within 30 days.

The second order directs the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security to take action against “birth tourism”, which it defines as entering the US on a non-immigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth – or helping another foreign national do so.

Measures authorised by the order may include denying or revoking visas, permanently barring people from entering the country, removing those found to have engaged in the practice, and taking action against individuals or organisations facilitating it in the US or overseas.

The order allows the secretaries of state and homeland security to grant exemptions on humanitarian or national-interest grounds.

The measures test the scope of the 14th Amendment, which provides that all people born or naturalised in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are US citizens.

“The practice of birth tourism is, as of the signing of this order, hereby banned,” said Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff for policy and widely considered the chief architect of Trump’s hardline immigration agenda.

Miller said people would no longer be allowed to obtain US visas for what he described as the fraudulent purpose of giving birth in the country.

US rules already allow consular officials to deny tourist visas when they believe a person’s primary purpose for travelling is to give birth in the United States so that the child will acquire citizenship.

The new orders go further by applying to entry on any non-immigrant visa, authorising permanent exclusion and removal, and targeting people and organisations accused of facilitating such travel.

Giving birth while visiting the country is not itself a crime. Previous prosecutions involving alleged birth-tourism schemes have generally relied on charges including visa fraud, conspiracy and money laundering.

Together, the orders appear to expand the crackdown by attempting to deny citizenship in certain cases and expanding enforcement against companies and individuals accused of arranging such travel.

Trump’s original executive order, signed on his first day back in office in January 2025, directed federal agencies to deny citizenship documents to children born in the US when their mothers were undocumented or temporarily present and their fathers were neither citizens nor permanent residents.

On June 30, the Supreme Court rejected that policy in a 6-3 ruling, holding that children born in the US to parents who were unlawfully or temporarily present were citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment.

Trump said on Thursday that the administration was now “ending it in a different way”.

White House staff secretary Will Scharf said the administration was confident the narrower measures would withstand judicial scrutiny.

“There’s absolutely nothing in here that runs afoul of any of the Supreme Court’s opinions on the subject,” Scharf said, adding that the White House would release a detailed fact sheet.

Trump claimed that “hundreds of thousands” of people had taken advantage of birth tourism, but did not provide evidence supporting the figure.

Estimates vary widely, in part because the federal government does not maintain a data set measuring how many women enter the country primarily to give birth.

Trump has repeatedly singled out China in his arguments against birthright citizenship, although he did not name the country during Thursday’s announcement.

After the Supreme Court ruling, he sarcastically congratulated Chinese President Xi Jinping and China for what he called their “massive Birthright Citizenship WIN”.

In March, Trump argued that the constitutional guarantee was “not about rich people from China, and the rest of the World, who want their children … to ridiculously become citizens of the United States of America”.

Republican-led congressional committees have also scrutinised companies accused of helping foreign clients give birth in the US.

The House Oversight Committee said earlier this year that expectant mothers travelling for that purpose came predominantly from China and Russia, raising what it described as national security and election integrity concerns.

The Justice Department has meanwhile instructed federal prosecutors to prioritise investigations into alleged birth-tourism schemes.

Cases cited by the department include those involving Chinese operators who charged clients tens of thousands of dollars to travel to the US and give birth.

Available statistics, however, suggest births to non-US residents from China represent a small fraction of total US births.

The National Centre for Health Statistics recorded 113 births to non-US residents from China in 2023, out of around 3.7 million births nationwide. The data do not indicate why the women travelled to the US or whether they misrepresented their intentions.

item.title: [SCMP] US presses China over alleged scam bosses despite growing police cooperation
item.description:
US President Donald Trump has personally pressed Chinese President Xi Jinping over transnational criminal organisations involved in Southeast Asia’s sprawling online scam industry, a senior State Department official said on Thursday.

Michael DeSombre, assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that Washington was raising concerns about both fentanyl trafficking and scam centres “at the highest levels” with Beijing.

“President Trump has raised transnational criminal organisations with President Xi,” DeSombre said during a hearing on Washington’s response to global scam operations.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has personally pressed Chinese President Xi Jinping over transnational criminal organisations involved in Southeast Asia’s sprawling online scam industry, a senior State Department official said on Thursday.

Michael DeSombre, assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that Washington was raising concerns about both fentanyl trafficking and scam centres “at the highest levels” with Beijing.

“President Trump has raised transnational criminal organisations with President Xi,” DeSombre said during a hearing on Washington’s response to global scam operations.

He said the US had urged Beijing to demonstrate that it was not helping alleged Chinese crime bosses evade international accountability.

“We’ve encouraged China to demonstrate that it is not abetting these crimes by allowing Chinese crime bosses to be held accountable internationally,” DeSombre said.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

DeSombre's comments come as the Federal Bureau of Investigation has expanded cooperation with Chinese authorities on cyberfraud and other transnational crimes, including through exchanges of law-enforcement personnel and joint operations.

The unusual partnership has created a delicate balance for Washington: US officials are seeking Beijing’s help dismantling criminal networks while questioning whether China is doing enough to hold their leaders accountable for crimes committed against Americans.

Pressure on Beijing

Although major scam compounds are concentrated in Southeast Asian countries including Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, US officials and international investigators have linked many of the operations to Chinese transnational criminal groups.

The compounds frequently rely on trafficked workers who are lured with fraudulent job offers and then forced under threats of violence to conduct online scams.

Senator Jim Risch, the Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the compounds had become a multibillion-dollar criminal industry involving human trafficking, money laundering, drugs and arms.

“As these scam centres evolve to use AI and other technologies to stay ahead of law enforcement, it is more important than ever that we mount an effective response,” Risch said.

Fraudsters increasingly use artificial intelligence to create realistic voices, messages and online identities, allowing them to impersonate relatives, employers and government officials. Such technology has been deployed in romance scams, fraudulent job offers, investment schemes and sextortion.

Americans reported losing more than US$12.5 billion to fraud in 2024, according to the Federal Trade Commission, although authorities say the actual total is likely considerably higher because many victims do not report their losses.

DeSombre said a preliminary US estimate placed reported American losses to Southeast Asia-based scam groups alone at US$12.5 billion in 2025. The State Department expected its final estimate to be “significantly higher”, according to his written testimony.

Lawmakers questioned whether Beijing was concentrating its enforcement efforts on operations targeting Chinese citizens while doing less to stop the victimisation of Americans and other foreigners.

“What about the idea that China is selectively enforcing the law on these scam operators that are targeting Chinese citizens, but not really worrying about Americans or other foreigners?” asked Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican from Nebraska.

DeSombre said Washington was urging governments in the region not to return suspected criminal leaders to China before they could be held accountable elsewhere for alleged crimes against foreign victims.

A prominent example is Chen Zhi, the founder and chairman of Cambodia-based Prince Holding Group. Cambodia extradited Chen to China in January after arresting him at Beijing’s request.

US prosecutors have separately charged Chen with wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracies, alleging that he directed forced-labour scam compounds in Cambodia. He has not faced those charges in a US court.

The US Justice Department also filed a civil action seeking the forfeiture of roughly 127,000 bitcoin linked to the alleged operation and valued at about US$15 billion when the action was announced. The department described it as the largest forfeiture action in its history.

China has conducted its own sweeping crackdown on online fraud, working with Southeast Asian governments on raids and the repatriation of suspects.

Analysts say Beijing’s campaign sharply reduced scams targeting Chinese citizens but also accelerated a shift by many syndicates towards American and other foreign victims.

One common form of investment fraud is known as “pig butchering”, derived from the Chinese term shazhupan . Scammers cultivate a victim’s trust over an extended period before persuading the person to transfer money into fraudulent investments.

Expanding cooperation

Despite Washington’s criticism, cooperation between Chinese and American law enforcement agencies has grown substantially over the past year.

FBI Director Kash Patel recently told Reuters that the bureau and China’s Ministry of Public Security had established working groups covering cyberfraud, fentanyl, crimes against children and fugitives.

The cooperation has included reciprocal visits by officials, intelligence sharing and joint operations. Patel said Chinese officers had visited FBI facilities in the United States, while American agents had travelled to China to work on cases, according to reports.

Patel visited Beijing in July and met Chinese Public Security Minister Wang Xiaohong, with both sides pledging to deepen what Chinese state media described as “practical cooperation” against transnational crime.

The closer relationship has nevertheless prompted concerns among former US law-enforcement officials about the counter-intelligence risks of allowing Chinese security personnel inside FBI facilities and sharing investigative information with them. Patel has said the exchanges are narrowly limited and that foreign visitors are vetted.

Trump signed an executive order in March directing federal agencies to develop a plan to disrupt cybercrime, fraud and predatory financial schemes targeting Americans.

The administration has also formed a 13-country Counter-Scams Contact Group to coordinate law enforcement, asset seizures, sanctions and information sharing. China is not among the countries listed as members of the group.

Congress is considering the bipartisan Scam Compound Accountability and Mobilisation Act, introduced by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat from New Hampshire.

The legislation would establish a government strategy against overseas scam compounds and human trafficking, authorise sanctions against people and entities supporting the networks, and improve help for victims.

“The good news is that the United States has begun responding to this threat,” Shaheen said. “If these criminal organisations operate across borders, our response has to operate across borders.”

item.title: [SCMP] US sanctions Cuba’s military representative in Beijing over China procurement
item.description:
The United States sanctioned Cuba’s senior military representative in Beijing on Thursday, accusing him of helping procure military-related equipment from China for the island’s armed forces.

Waldo Perez Cortes, Cuba’s military, naval and air attache in Beijing, was among six Cuban nationals and five entities added to the US Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list.

The US State Department said Perez Cortes was an official of Cuba’s Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces, known as MINFAR, who had been “involved in the procurement of military-related equipment from China to Cuba”.
item.content:encoded:
The United States sanctioned Cuba’s senior military representative in Beijing on Thursday, accusing him of helping procure military-related equipment from China for the island’s armed forces.

Waldo Perez Cortes, Cuba’s military, naval and air attache in Beijing, was among six Cuban nationals and five entities added to the US Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list.

The US State Department said Perez Cortes was an official of Cuba’s Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces, known as MINFAR, who had been “involved in the procurement of military-related equipment from China to Cuba”.

It did not identify the equipment, Chinese suppliers or transactions allegedly involved.

Cuban state news agency Prensa Latina has identified Perez Cortes as a senior colonel serving as Cuba’s military, naval and air attache in Beijing.

Perez Cortes has appeared publicly alongside senior officers from China’s People’s Liberation Army and spoken about Beijing’s support for Cuba’s defence capabilities.

At a reception in Beijing in November 2025, he said Cuba received help from several friendly countries, including China, as it worked to strengthen its defensive capacity, according to Prensa Latina.

Lieutenant General Wu Aimin and military, naval and air attaches accredited to China attended the event, the Cuban news agency reported.

The US State Department declined to make further comments beyond the official statement of the announcement. The South China Morning Post has also contacted the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment on the allegations and sanctions.

The sanctions package also targeted several Cuban officials and state enterprises accused of obtaining military equipment from China and Russia.

Among them was Heriberto Sanchez Alleyne, director general of the state-owned importer Tecnoimport. The State Department accused Sanchez of procuring military-related equipment and services from China and Russia.

Tecnoimport, a subsidiary of Cuba’s military-controlled Grupo de Administracion Empresarial SA, or GAESA, imported military equipment on behalf of MINFAR, according to the department. Washington alleged that the company had acquired military-related equipment from China and Russia.

Another sanctioned company, Duna SA, was accused of importing military-related equipment from the two countries.

Also sanctioned was Monica Milian Gomez, whom the State Department identified as Cuba’s military attache to Russia. The department accused her of involvement in transferring military-related equipment from Russia to Cuba.

Jose Antonio Remon Rodriguez, head of MINFAR’s Foreign Relations Directorate, was accused of involvement in transferring military-related equipment from China and Russia to Cuba.

Oscar Enrique Biosca Gallego, head of MINFAR’s Economic Directorate, allegedly participated in efforts to procure military-related equipment from both countries.

The other newly sanctioned officials included Roberto Jesus Viciana Mousset, director general of Cuba’s Military Industries Union, and Sanchez.

Actions taken under Trump order that broadened US sanctions powers

Defence Minister Alvaro Lopez Miera and Roberto Legra Sotolongo, chief of the general staff and first deputy minister of MINFAR, were also designated under the new Cuba-related sanctions authority. Both were already sanctioned under a separate US human-rights programme.

The State Department accused Lopez Miera of advancing Cuba’s foreign military cooperation and Legra of attempting to procure weapons systems from Russia.

The entities targeted included Cuba’s Military Industries Union, known by its Spanish initials UIM, and four companies involved in military equipment, technical products and trade: Tecnoimport, Tecnotex, Duna SA and the Yuri Gagarin Military Industrial Enterprise.

The State Department described UIM as a military holding company responsible for producing and repairing weapons and equipment for Cuba’s armed forces. It accused the company of working with Russian defence entities to modernise Russian-origin weapons systems.

The Yuri Gagarin enterprise was accused of maintaining and repairing Cuba’s Russian-made military aircraft, while Tecnotex allegedly took part in efforts to refurbish the country’s Russian-origin helicopter fleet.

The action was taken under an executive order signed by US President Donald Trump in May that broadened Washington’s authority to sanction foreign individuals and organisations associated with key sectors of Cuba’s economy or the Cuban government.

Perez Cortes and five other MINFAR officials were designated under a provision covering leaders and officials of the Cuban government or newly blocked entities.

Four of the companies were designated for operating in Cuba’s defence sector, while Tecnotex was targeted for acting on behalf of the Cuban government.

US accuses Cuba of being staging ground for China, Russia, Iran plans

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio accused Cuba of serving as a staging ground from which China, Russia and Iran could conduct operations against the United States.

“Today, the Trump administration is taking further action to protect our national security by sanctioning entities and individuals who facilitate Havana’s military relationships and the shipments of arms to the Cuban regime,” Rubio said.

Any property belonging to those designated that is in the United States or under the control of US persons must be frozen and reported to Treasury. American individuals and companies are generally prohibited from conducting transactions involving them.

Foreign individuals and financial institutions may also risk US sanctions if they transact with the designated parties or operate in specified sectors of Cuba’s economy, according to the State Department.

The sanctions come amid heightened scrutiny in Washington of Cuba’s security relationships with China and Russia.

A State Department report released last month alleged that three of 18 foreign-linked intelligence facilities in Cuba were operated by China, while other sites had connections to Russia. Beijing and Havana have repeatedly rejected US allegations about Chinese intelligence activity on the island.

The Trump administration has intensified economic pressure on Cuba this year, targeting senior officials, military-controlled businesses, banks, mining companies, energy suppliers and other state enterprises.

Washington says the campaign is intended to deny resources to Cuba’s political and military leadership. Havana has denounced the measures as economic coercion that worsens shortages and harms ordinary Cubans.

Beijing has repeatedly opposed Washington’s pressure campaign against Havana. China’s foreign ministry said last week that the US should stop its threats of force, unilateral sanctions and blockade against Cuba, adding that China would continue supporting the country in defending its sovereignty and opposing external interference.

item.title: [SCMP] China vs Japan: the battle for the global microphone to reshape post-war identity
item.description:
No longer confined to disputed islands or historical memory, the rivalry between Beijing and Tokyo has evolved into a fight for the global microphone, as both countries try to define each other’s international identity.

Amid an escalating diplomatic crisis, China is intensifying its rhetoric against what it calls Japan’s “new militarism”, using World War II-era history to rally regional and global sympathy for its position.

In stark contrast, Japan has rejected the label as “false claims”, casting itself as a defender of regional security, a peace-loving country and a victim of “coercion”.
item.content:encoded:
No longer confined to disputed islands or historical memory, the rivalry between Beijing and Tokyo has evolved into a fight for the global microphone, as both countries try to define each other’s international identity.

Amid an escalating diplomatic crisis, China is intensifying its rhetoric against what it calls Japan’s “new militarism”, using World War II-era history to rally regional and global sympathy for its position.

In stark contrast, Japan has rejected the label as “false claims”, casting itself as a defender of regional security, a peace-loving country and a victim of “coercion”.

Tokyo has argued that Beijing’s expanding arsenal, “opaque” military build-ups and “challenges to the established rules” should worry the international community.

While China’s denunciation of Japan’s new militarism is still being tested for traction abroad, many countries between the Asia-Pacific region and Europe have continued to deepen their defence cooperation with Tokyo.

“China faces a profoundly distorted global narrative that has largely obscured the fascist atrocities committed by Japan against China and other nations during World War II that have never been fully reckoned with at the international level,” said Shen Yi, executive director of the Centre for National Security Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai.

“The gap in collective memory has provided fertile ground for Japan’s new militarism to resurface.”

To address this, Shen said, Beijing should expand historical research and global communications through films, literature and academic outreach to present second world war realities.

Such efforts must adapt to today’s communications landscape, he added, suggesting the use of AI technologies to present historical facts through visual means.

Addressing the Shangri-La Dialogue in May, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi dismissed China’s accusations of new militarism against Japan as “nothing further from the truth”.

Koizumi said “it is only natural” for every country to update their defence capabilities to deal with new challenges.

In the clash of narratives, “China is pointing out more than just the rise of new militarism in Japan; the core agenda-setting is about safeguarding the post-World War II international order”, Shen said.

This approach required upholding the legal framework established by the 1943 Cairo Declaration and the 1945 Potsdam Proclamation, he added, including the total elimination of Japanese militarism, the strict delimitation of the territorial scope of Japanese sovereignty and the preservation of Japan’s pacifist constitutional order.

According to Shen, Tokyo has spent decades diminishing global awareness of its wartime atrocities, seeking to sever its modern identity from its aggressor past to cultivate an image of a “new Japan”.

A Western-centric global World War II narrative that had long marginalised non-Western victims, particularly those in Asia, inadvertently facilitated this effort, he said.

For its part, Tokyo has sought to deflect discussions about its wartime past on public occasions.

A Japanese scholar said that responding to Beijing’s accusations by citing Japan’s post-war pacifism risked validating the historical parameters set by China.

“Getting dragged into an exhausting, asymmetrical debate over past grievances is a losing proposition,” wrote Masahiro Matsumura, a professor of international politics and national security at St Andrew’s University in Osaka, in a commentary in The Japan Times in July.

“Tokyo must devise a sophisticated strategy that neutralises this rhetoric,” said Matsumura, who also holds a research position at the Taiwan Centre for Security Studies and advocates for closer Japan-Taiwan security coordination.

“Japan must proactively engage and reassure its neighbours through transparent defence diplomacy, ensuring that Beijing cannot use the ghosts of the 20th century to drive a wedge between Japan, its Western allies and its vital East Asian neighbours.”

This year, Japan retained its standing as Southeast Asia’s most trusted major power, with 65.6 per cent of regional respondents expressing confidence in Tokyo, according to the Singapore-based ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute’s annual survey.

China’s score of 39.8 per cent was much lower than Japan’s, though trust in Beijing across Asean surpassed distrust for the first time since the survey started in 2019.

Southeast Asian countries naturally prioritised their immediate interests and therefore China should deepen cooperation with its neighbours, Shen said, making opposition to the resurgence of Japanese militarism a shared regional security agenda.

This would ensure that neighbouring countries fully understood the danger and stood ready to coordinate with China in safeguarding regional peace and stability, he added.

The public silence reflects the “Asean centrality” and the bloc’s commitment to avoiding taking sides in major-power disputes, according to Ge Hongliang, vice-dean of the Asean College at Guangxi Minzu University.

Ge said the position was rooted in the countries’ complex World War II experiences.

Countries like Myanmar were under Western colonial rule before Japan’s invasion, leading some early nationalist movements to view Japanese forces as tactical leverage to expel European colonial powers, he added.

Although the Japanese army later carried out widespread wartime abuses across Southeast Asia, post-war dynamics shifted rapidly.

As Washington redirected its Asia policy in service of Cold War containment, Tokyo launched the “Fukuda Doctrine” in 1977, pledging that Japan would never become a military power, Ge said.

The policy also committed to building “heart-to-heart” partnerships with Southeast Asian countries as equal economic partners, he added.

Decades of systematic economic diplomacy under this framework effectively neutralised anti-Japanese sentiment and rebuilt regional trust, Ge said.

However, he cautioned that Southeast Asia’s neutrality should not be mistaken for indifference towards Japan’s present security trajectory.

Tokyo’s dialogue on nuclear option adjustments directly conflicts with Asean’s long-standing push to strengthen the Southeast Asia nuclear weapon-free zone, a commitment signed in 1995 to keep the region free of nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction.

In July, Koizumi called for breaking Japan’s long-standing taboo on discussing nuclear weapons, which was widely seen as laying the groundwork to dismantle the country’s three non-nuclear principles.

The principles are Tokyo’s long-held commitment not to possess, produce or permit the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japanese territory.

“Southeast Asia’s silence is not unconditional,” Ge said. “If Japan’s new militarism crosses a line that directly destabilises the regional balance or threatens Southeast Asian security interests, Asean’s quiet neutrality will inevitably begin to fray.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why the UK is doubling down on Asean ties amid European reset
item.description:
Britain’s new Labour government is trying to reassure Southeast Asia that its push to rebuild ties with Europe will not come at the region’s expense, analysts have said, after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband made an Asean meeting in Manila his first overseas stop.

Appointed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham on July 20, Miliband attended the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Foreign Ministers’ Meeting about 48 hours after taking office – a choice observers said pointed less to a policy reset than to continuity in Britain’s post-Brexit engagement with the bloc.

Analysts said the visit also highlighted why Asean had become more important to London: trade and supply-chain links after Brexit, maritime and regional security, and a shared interest among middle powers in keeping diplomatic space open amid intensifying great-power pressure.
item.content:encoded:
Britain’s new Labour government is trying to reassure Southeast Asia that its push to rebuild ties with Europe will not come at the region’s expense, analysts have said, after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband made an Asean meeting in Manila his first overseas stop.

Appointed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham on July 20, Miliband attended the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Foreign Ministers’ Meeting about 48 hours after taking office – a choice observers said pointed less to a policy reset than to continuity in Britain’s post-Brexit engagement with the bloc.

Analysts said the visit also highlighted why Asean had become more important to London: trade and supply-chain links after Brexit, maritime and regional security, and a shared interest among middle powers in keeping diplomatic space open amid intensifying great-power pressure.

The Manila gathering also marked five years since the United Kingdom became a full dialogue partner of the bloc.

“I felt it was very, very important to come straight to the Asean Foreign Ministers’ Meeting as a sign of solidarity with Asean countries and of the importance we attach to this partnership,” Miliband said in remarks before the bloc’s foreign ministers.

He stressed his country’s “commitment to Asean and commitment for the long term”, which he said remained “just as strong for the UK’s new prime minister as it did for our previous prime minister and for me personally”.

The trip also saw the adoption of a new plan of action between the UK and Asean, which Miliband said would “guide our partnership through the next five years” through 2031, alongside a joint statement on the Asean Outlook on the Indo-Pacific that “reaffirms our commitment to upholding international law and addressing mutual challenges”.

“Whether on maritime security, energy security, economic resilience or emerging technologies, our future will increasingly be shaped by how we work together multilaterally,” Miliband said.

For Laura Southgate, a lecturer in politics and international relations at Aston University, the timing and destination of Miliband’s trip mattered as much as the official agenda.

“Ed Miliband’s presence at the Asean Foreign Ministers’ Meeting is an early indication of the priority the new Burnham government is attaching to Southeast Asia and the wider Indo-Pacific,” Southgate said.

“Miliband himself confirmed an ongoing commitment to Asean and its centrality, whilst also pledging deeper engagement moving forward.”

His decision to make the Asean meeting his first overseas visit was “a deliberate signal of this commitment”, Southgate said, but also suggested “continuity with the previous government rather than a complete change in UK policy”.

Bill Hayton, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Asia Programme, said the visit reflected Britain’s view that it shared common ground with Asean as a grouping of middle powers navigating a more uncertain global environment.

“The UK wants to demonstrate our international presence, not just being caught up with the EU,” Hayton said.

That balancing act has become more important because Britain’s relationship with Asean is now part of its attempt to show that closer ties with Europe do not mean retreating from the Indo-Pacific.

The UK became an Asean dialogue partner in 2021, a status that formalised its engagement with the bloc after Britain left the EU and sought a broader “Global Britain” role.

Observers said Brexit made strengthening relations with Southeast Asia a greater priority, though it was not the only reason for London’s approach.

“The UK had already begun strengthening relations with Southeast Asia before 2016, but Brexit added urgency by requiring a reassessment of British foreign policy and encouraging a more outward-facing ‘Global Britain’ strategy,” Southgate said.

Consequently, Asean and the wider Indo-Pacific became more important to the UK’s economic, security and global ambitions, she said, including through closer trade ties, membership of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and Asean dialogue partner status.

“However, Brexit accelerated rather than created this engagement,” she said. “The UK’s attention and resources remain divided between the Indo-Pacific and its commitments in Europe.”

Brexit remained “a big shaper” of Britain’s foreign policy because “we’re on our own now, so we have to craft much more of our own foreign policy”, Hayton said.

“Our trade policy is now entirely independent … Now that we are members of the CPTPP, we have an economic interest in closer ties with the other CPTPP members.”

The previous Conservative government had turned away from the EU and bet heavily on the Asia-Pacific region, Hayton said, while Burnham’s first days in office showed a clear intent to repair European ties without abandoning that wider focus.

Downing Street said Burnham used early calls with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa to stress the importance of a closer UK-EU relationship, including work towards a summit later this year.

“This government wants to rebuild its relations with the EU and Europe, but it’s keen to show that that doesn’t mean giving up on Asia,” Hayton said.

“They are still engaged, and the fact that the foreign secretary, just two or three days into office, still wanted to get to the AMM summit reflects that – they want to be part of it.”

Middle-power ties

At the same time, Britain’s engagement with Asean is increasingly shaped by its position as a middle power, even as its former colonial role continues to influence relations with parts of Southeast Asia, analysts say.

Southgate pointed out that the UK maintained strong bilateral ties with former British colonies such as Malaysia and Singapore, both Commonwealth members, and retained a regional footprint through the Five Power Defence Arrangements and a permanent military garrison in Brunei.

“However, its position as a middle power means that engagement now depends more on consultation, partnership and practical cooperation than on historical influence,” she said.

“It is therefore important that the UK remains sensitive to its colonial history and respects Asean’s priorities, agency and centrality.”

Miliband’s Asean meeting showed the UK viewed the bloc not only through strategic interests but also as a partner in upholding multilateralism and international law, Southgate said.

“The UK identified Asean as a critical strategic partner in 2021 because of its location, economic growth and integration, and role in regional stability and diplomacy,” she said.

At a time of conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine, alongside wider geopolitical and economic uncertainty, Southgate said Asean’s role in supporting dialogue, regional stability and resilient supply chains had become increasingly important.

Hayton said Britain was presenting itself as a middle power that could support multilateral ties and help preserve Southeast Asian autonomy amid pressure from larger powers, including China.

“We see Asean as an important regional organisation – not the only one you can interact with, but one of the more effective ones in the sense that it has such important convening power,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] The numbers game: why the US is losing ground to China in the first island chain
item.description:
As the People’s Liberation Army marks its 99th anniversary on August 1, one year from the deadline for its centenary goals, its evolution highlights the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the second part of a series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Beijing is pushing the envelope on its near-seas island arc.

Beijing has urged the People’s Liberation Army to transform into a “world-class military” by the mid-21st century, intent on piercing US-led chokepoints along an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines.

Known as the first island chain, they underpin a US-aligned security architecture that Chinese strategists see as both a constraint on the PLA’s freedom to manoeuvre in a conflict and the likeliest entry route for US and allied forces in a regional crisis.
item.content:encoded:
As the People’s Liberation Army marks its 99th anniversary on August 1, one year from the deadline for its centenary goals, its evolution highlights the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the second part of a series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Beijing is pushing the envelope on its near-seas island arc.

Beijing has urged the People’s Liberation Army to transform into a “world-class military” by the mid-21st century, intent on piercing US-led chokepoints along an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines.

Known as the first island chain, they underpin a US-aligned security architecture that Chinese strategists see as both a constraint on the PLA’s freedom to manoeuvre in a conflict and the likeliest entry route for US and allied forces in a regional crisis.

Long associated with Cold War-era strategy, the first island chain has become a principal arena of military competition between China and the United States, with the Pentagon’s latest China Military Power Report identifying it as central to Beijing’s regional strategy.

A year ahead of its 2027 centenary goal, the PLA has shown progress in areas that could challenge the US defence line – specifically its dual-carrier operations, large-scale arms production and improved nuclear deterrence beyond the island chain.

Meanwhile, the US and its allies have also ramped up their input, including the expansion of American base access in the Philippines and increasingly sophisticated defence drills involving Washington’s regional partners.

More than geography

Stretching from Japan’s home islands and the Ryukyu archipelago through Taiwan to the Philippines and Borneo, the first island chain forms the maritime boundary between mainland China’s near seas and the open Pacific Ocean.

It encompasses narrow waterways and air corridors, including the Miyako Strait, the Bashi Channel and the Luzon Strait – the few routes through which the PLA can reach the wider Pacific.

During the Cold War, the first island chain formed part of a broader US strategy to deter Soviet and Chinese expansion in the Pacific.

Today, it links a network of forward-deployed forces of American and allied forces that have become more closely integrated in recent years.

Japan has accelerated defence spending and strengthened its military posture along its southwestern islands with new anti-ship and air-defence capabilities, while the US has expanded rotational access to military facilities in the Philippines, including several sites facing Taiwan.

Trilateral cooperation involving Washington, Tokyo and Manila has likewise evolved from largely symbolic exercises into sophisticated naval, air and amphibious training, transforming what was once a collection of bilateral alliances into a more integrated regional security architecture.

According to Oriana Skylar Mastro, director of the Indo-Pacific Policy Lab at Stanford University’s Freeman Spogli Institute, expanded basing and overflight access represents a consequential shift.

K. Tristan Tang, a non-resident fellow at the National Bureau of Asian Research, a US think tank, echoed the sentiment, noting that large-scale joint military exercises like Balikatan and Resolute Dragon “increasingly rehearse multidomain sensing, command and control, coastal defence, integrated fires and the defence of key maritime terrain”.

Chinese strategists increasingly view the island chains as “barriers, springboards and benchmarks”, said Andrew Erickson, a professor of strategy at the US Naval War College’s China Maritime Studies Institute.

This perspective also stemmed from the PLA’s transformation, Erickson added, from a force focused mainly on coastal defence into one seeking to operate across and eventually beyond the first island chain.

That shift in thinking extends beyond military terminology.

Chinese discourse had begun framing the objective in explicitly offensive terms, with Beijing “increasingly talking about ‘breaking through the first island chain’”, said Zhao Tong, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

In Zhao’s assessment, the PLA now believes the military balance along the chain is gradually shifting in its favour and that it could steadily erode long-standing US military dominance to establish itself “as a power willing and able to advance its perceived core interests” through its expanding capabilities.

In that vein, Mastro observed that Chinese thinking about the first island chain went beyond pure defence.

“Part of the reason China wants freedom of manoeuvre in the first island chain is to defend against attack, but also to defend against responses to its own aggression,” she said.

“It’s offensive. It’s defensive. It’s about power projection. It’s about great-power competition.”

Going further, Tang argued that the first island chain had “become more, not less, strategically important over the past decade”.

As the PLA’s power-projection capabilities grew, he said, “the chain’s value as a defensive barrier has therefore increased for all sides, even as it has become a central operational arena where control of key straits and air and maritime corridors could be decisive in wartime”.

Beijing’s push

In recent years, the PLA has undergone significant military changes that could help it better respond to the first island chain, ranging from naval expansion and doctrine to joint operations and deterrence.

Zhao cited the PLA’s naval expansion as the single most important driver of that transformation, alongside China’s possession of the world’s largest arsenal of theatre-range missiles, enabling Beijing to threaten strategic targets across the region.

Looking ahead, he said Beijing also appeared to be eyeing “a substantial expansion of its nuclear-powered submarine fleet”.

By combining stealth, endurance and long-range strike capability, the force could challenge one of America’s most enduring military advantages, Zhao added.

Once focused largely on coastal defence, the PLA Navy has evolved into the world’s largest naval force by hull count, conducting increasingly sustained operations east of Taiwan and Japan in waters that until recently lay largely beyond its routine reach.

For Beijing, these deployments reflect a deliberate effort to build a navy capable of protecting its expanding overseas interests while operating in an ever more contested environment.

According to Mastro, the scale of Beijing’s operations has already gone a long way towards eroding Washington’s traditional advantages in the northern waters of the chain, namely the East China Sea and Taiwan Strait.

“China has many more bases. They have the mass,” she said, noting that Beijing could also produce ships, missiles and military equipment far faster than the US.

“The United States is losing that numbers game, and we have for quite some time.”

Yet, further south, Mastro sees the balance as less favourable for Beijing.

China could increasingly complicate US operations across the wider first island chain, but projecting and sustaining military power over greater distances remained far more demanding than denying access close to the Chinese mainland, she said.

“Keeping the United States out of Asia is much easier than projecting power across those distances,” Mastro added.

According to Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in the PLA, the calculation is much simpler. Zhou said the first island chain’s importance was slipping as China’s military capabilities expanded, even as Washington continued to reinforce its forward presence.

From coastal defence to power projection

Analysts have noted an important shift in Beijing’s strategic purposes in the region, from keeping adversaries away with anti-access and area denial (A2/AD) strategy to operating farther from home and remaining there.

The strategy is underscored by Beijing’s pursuit of carrier strike groups, amphibious assault ships and replenishment vessels, as well as a growing overseas logistics network.

In 2024, the Liaoning and Shandong aircraft carriers conducted the PLA Navy’s first dual-carrier operations, while transits through the Miyako Strait into the Philippine Sea have become more routine.

Those deployments allow the PLA to rehearse the difficult requirements of sustained blue-water warfare, from coordinating multiple carrier strike groups to integrating escorts, carrier aviation and logistics over extended distances.

The launch of the Fujian, China’s third and most advanced aircraft carrier, is expected to substantially expand the PLA Navy’s carrier aviation capabilities, while the KJ-600 airborne early-warning aircraft promises to extend fleet air defence well beyond the reach of shore-based radar.

Tang regarded the Fujian and the maturation of China’s carrier strike groups as the most consequential development to watch.

“China’s earlier ski-jump carriers faced limitations in sortie generation and carrier-based fixed-wing airborne early warning,” he said.

“The Fujian’s electromagnetic catapults and KJ-600 aircraft can extend the fleet’s sensor coverage and improve the efficiency of sustained air operations in the Philippine Sea.”

As those capabilities matured, Tang added, forces positioned along the first island chain might have to prepare for pressure “coming simultaneously from the Chinese mainland to the west and carrier forces operating to the east”.

Learning to fight as a joint force

A more fundamental change has been under way in joint combat. Instead of treating the navy, air force, rocket force and support elements as largely separate services, the PLA now trains and organises to fight as an integrated joint force.

The effort is instrumental to denying US and allied forces the ability to operate effectively around the first island chain.

Central to that approach is the concept of “system destruction warfare”: prioritising the disabling of an adversary’s sensors, communications, command networks and decision-making processes rather than destroying individual platforms one by one.

The philosophy is reflected across the PLA’s force structure.

Long-range ballistic and cruise missiles are intended to hold forward-deployed forces at risk, bomber patrols through the Miyako Strait and around Japan have become frequent, and Beijing continues to expand its reconnaissance, surveillance and command networks across multiple domains.

In addition, as US allies strengthen cooperation along the first island chain, Beijing has sought closer military coordination with its strategic partner Russia through expanded joint bomber patrols and naval exercises around Japan and across the western Pacific.

Mastro described the arrangement as an “alliance grey zone”, saying Russia could, for example, close portions of its far-eastern airspace or provide logistical support to help China sustain operations during a prolonged crisis.

As Zhao sees it, the value of defence coordination for Beijing lies less in Russia’s capability than in the signal of “strategic coordination, shared objectives and mutual resolve in countering US military influence”.

Mastro said Chinese strategists had told her privately that closer coordination with Moscow was intended to send a signal to Washington and Tokyo about the potential costs of deepening US-Japan defence cooperation.

Beijing has simultaneously strengthened its strategic deterrence to show it could complicate US defence considerations beyond the first island chain.

In 2024, China publicly launched an intercontinental ballistic missile into the Pacific for the first time in decades.

And last month, it tested a submarine-launched ballistic missile in international waters, signalling the operational readiness of its sea-based nuclear deterrent.

According to Tang, these capabilities reinforce deterrence in complementary ways – carrier strike groups extend China’s conventional operational reach beyond the first island chain, while the submarine-launched ballistic missile strengthens the credibility and survivability of its nuclear second-strike capability.

His research suggests the Central Military Commission, which commands the armed forces, concluded by late 2024 that the PLA had largely achieved its objectives for “near-seas comprehensive operations”, with training shifting to “far-seas mobile operations”.

That said, having such capabilities is different from successfully employing them in combat.

Zhao pointed to a question that could ultimately prove decisive: which side will make more effective use of emerging technologies such as drones, autonomous vessels and AI-enabled weapons?

China “appears to enjoy certain advantages stemming from its industrial base and capacity to manufacture and field systems at scale”, he said.

But the US and its allies “may retain important advantages in innovation, operational adaptability and a more agile defence ecosystem”.

The PLA still had “comparatively limited operational experience” testing its new capabilities in large-scale joint operations, Zhao added.

“The jury is still out on which side will ultimately gain the more decisive military leverage along the first island chain.”

item.title: [SCMP] The best guest shifts in Hong Kong and Macau amid Asia’s 50 Best Bars 2026
item.description:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24
item.content:encoded:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24

Green Room x Three x Co

Ranked the No 15 best bar in Asia last year, Kuala Lumpur’s Three X Co is heading all the way up to the 49th floor of Upper House to take over Green Room for one night only. Represented this time by bar manager Rachel Hor and senior bartender Chris Ang, Three X Co focuses on contemporary cocktails such as those from its IndiVDuality menu. The Quiet Quinn riffs on the martini with a Tanqueray 10 base, a chrysanthemum infusion and Yzaguirre Dry Reserva Spanish vermouth, topped with orange bitters and grapefruit zest.

Where: Green Room, 49/F, Upper House Hong Kong, Admiralty

When: 6.30pm-9.30pm

The Local Pour – Dara x Flair Up

Dara, celebrated for its modern Filipino dishes and vibrant neighbourhood atmosphere, is teaming up with “flairtender” Washam Limbu for a special collaboration titled The Local Pour.

Limbu is the co-founder of Flair Up and frequently participates in the Young Chef, Young Waiter, Young Mixologist (YYY) competitions. He took home the 2026 YYY Story Teller Global title and was named the Young Mixologist of the Year in 2025, when he was also crowned champion in the 2025 Ichiko Cocktail Competition Hong Kong event.

Guests can expect high-energy performance, artisanal craft cocktails and a commitment to locally produced ingredients.

Where: Dara, Shop 3, Soho 189, 189 Queen’s Road West, Sai Ying Pun

When: 7pm until sold out

Saturday, July 25

The Road Less Travelled – Wing Lei Bar x Nomad Lab x Barc x Kiki Lounge

Even though Wynn Palace and Wing Lei Bar start their festivities earlier in the week, one of our favourites on the itinerary has to be this one – gathering bars from Mongolia, Nepal and the Isle of Man.

All three bars are represented by their co-founders. Nomad Lab’s Awaraa Awarzed is coming in from Ulaanbaatar as the self-proclaimed “first cocktail lab in Mongolia”, while Barc’s Abhishek Tuladhar is arriving from Nepal. The latter won the 2025 Michter’s Art of Hospitality award from Asia’s 50 Best Bars last year. Rounding out the takeover is Drew Fleming from Kiki Lounge in Isle of Man, the winner of the Spirits Business Awards Bar of the Year in 2024.

Where: Wing Lei Bar, West Esplanade, G/F, Wynn Palace, Avenida da Nave Desportiva, Coloane-Taipa, Macau

When: 5pm-8pm

25:00 x Thaipioka

Bartenders Hope Narawut and Supawit Thinpitayanurat, also known as Miguel, are arriving from Bangkok to take over 25:00 Twenty Fifth Hour, representing Thaipioka, which focuses on equal parts cocktails and music. Back home, Thaipioka offers fruit-centric cocktails like the Kyoho Balsamic Negroni, adding vinegar, shiso bitters and kyoho grapes to the traditional profile, or the Orange Thai Milk Tea, which soups up the citrus drink with rum, coffee, caramel and fresh orange.

Where: 13/F, Luk Yu Building, 24-26 Stanley Street, Central

When: 9pm-1am

Sunday, July 26 (early)

C108 celebrates its second anniversary with Sora Bar

C108’s second anniversary on Old Bailey Street is coming hot on the heels of its updated menu earlier in the month. Taking centre stage for Sunday’s anniversary party is a guest shift by Jonas Vittur, director of bars at Rosewood Phnom Penh’s rooftop bar, Sora, and its head bartender Phirun Lek.

Last year, the sky bar was ranked No 65 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars list and won the Ketel One Sustainable Bar Award. C108 is also working with Good Stuff to have four DJs play music all night long.

Where: 15 Old Bailey Street, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

The Old Man x AABBCC

Start your Sunday night at the top of the alphabet as AABBCC arrives from New Delhi to take over The Old Man on Aberdeen Street. The “retro-futuristic archive” bar sends co-founders Jairaj Singh Solanki and Aditi Singh, who are bringing cocktails such as a twist on the Godfather with dandelion, a Bellini using cacao butter, a caprese salad rendered in alcohol form, and a drink called the Mushroomisu.

Solanki’s former concept, Lair, also based in New Delhi, was ranked the 8th best bar in Asia last year.

Where: The Old Man, LG/F, 37 Aberdeen Street, Soho, Central

When: 6pm until sold out

Sunday, July 26 (late)

Dio x Bar Woody

There’s so much happening on Sunday and Monday that it’ll be easy to catch an early shift and a late shift on either night. Bar Woody has made a name for itself in Chengdu by anchoring its concept on the complexity of wood and herbs, with its signature cocktails such as the Cedar, the Benzoin and Sandalwood. Now there is a chance to try those earthy sips at Dio on Sunday, when Bar Woody’s Keith Lo and Austin Guo serve their wood-forward creations supported by Mizunara, featuring The Hachi Shochu and Wakshio 424 Gin.

Where: Dio, 8 Aberdeen Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

The Diplomat x Offtrack

Singapore’s Offtrack, last year’s No 23 best bar in Asia and known for its high-energy music and equally excellent focus on cocktails and food, arrives in Hong Kong to take over The Diplomat for one night only. At home, Offtrack’s co-founder Aslam Zainal and his team serve straightforward, inventive drinks like the Cora Middleton, combining raspberry, white almond, rum, lime, hibiscus and egg white. It makes perfect sense for Zainal to stage a guest stint at one of Hong Kong’s best bars for martinis, Irish coffees and burgers.

Where: The Diplomat, LG/F, H Code, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

Monday, July 27 (early)

Quinary x Native x Milli x Chanel Adams

Hong Kong’s first home of molecular mixology, Quinary, is starting the party early on Monday with a triple-header featuring Singapore’s Native and Milli, alongside a special guest. Native is represented by co-founder Vijay Mudaliar and mixologist Amillie Chan, who are showcasing their unique approach to obscure and foraged ingredients, while Danny is bringing a menu of playful cocktails from Milli, a rooftop bar atop Singapore’s National Gallery. Rounding out the line-up is Chanel Adams, who most recently worked at the Mandarin Oriental Bangkok, and at Please Don’t Tell in Hong Kong before that.

Where: Quinary, 56-58 Hollywood Road, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

Tell Camellia x Gong-Gan

Gong-Gan, famed for its zero-waste philosophy, arrives from Seoul to take over tea-inspired cocktail joint Tell Camellia. Ranked No 74 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars this year, Gong-Gan is represented by co-founders Evan Noh and Willy Park. Their signature cocktails include the Si-Jang, featuring the premium Korean spirit Igangju alongside bourbon, lemon juice, roasted rice and banana beer.

Where: Tell Camellia, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm onwards

Monday, July 27 (late)

Kinsman x Bar Truce x Bar Notes

Wong Kar-wai-inspired Kinsman brings together Indonesia and South Korea in a double header featuring Bar Truce from Jakarta and Seoul’s Bar Notes. The former is grounded in Japanese mixology tradition with a twist, serving cocktails like the Ogura Dream as a clarified twist on the Alexander. Meanwhile, Bar Notes puts its focus on storytelling – its owner Ricky is also a freelance writer – serving concoctions like the Ssanghwa, inspired by the portmanteau “halmae-nial” – a combination of “halmae”, meaning granny, and “millennial”, referring to millennials enjoying foods normally associated with the elderly – containing rum, cream, egg and the eponymous bitter tea.

Where: Kinsman, 65 Peel Street, Central

When: Bar Truce: 8pm-10pm; Bar Notes: 10pm-12am

Socio x Modernhaus

One of Jakarta’s best – Modernhaus – arrives to take over Socio, Hong Kong’s main venue focused on upcycling community ingredients. Modernhaus was named the No 12 best bar in Asia last year and focuses on conceptual, minimalist cocktails. At home, they serve drinks like the Turmeric, which involves a turmeric gin, coconut chai milk, cream, salted tamarind and lemonade soda, and the Apple, which spotlights smoked manalagi apple brandy, koji, umami bitters and apple miso.

Where: Socio, 17 Staunton Street, Central

When: 8.30pm onwards

Tuesday, July 28

Campari x Wynn Palace Asia’s 50 Best Bars after-party

Tuesday is the day we’ve all been waiting for. After our region’s most excellent bars get their flowers, Wynn Palace is joining hands with Campari to host an all-out after-party in Macau. Responsible for the vibes are some of the region’s best. Look out for veterans of the list to host this get-together: Singapore’s Cat Bite Club (No 86, 2026); The Cocktail Club (No 12, 2024) and Carrots (No 34, 2025), both from Jakarta; Opium from Bangkok (No 43, 2025); and Bengaluru’s Soka (No 28, 2025).

Where: Palace Reserve Club, Wynn Palace, Avenida Da Nave Desportiva, Cotai, Macau

When: Post-ceremony till late

Wednesday, July 29

Argo Mega Friends Takeover

Argo plays host to an exceptional night of mixology as Argo Mega Friends returns with three new regional names. This collaboration brings together teams from three of Asia’s top-ranked bars. Bangkok’s Bar Us is represented by co-founders Aum Veerach and Taln Sudarat; Dry Wave Cocktail Studio sends founder Supawit “Palm” Muttarattana and bartender Ammie Suparada; and Taipei duo William Wu and Cloris Huang of The Public House round out the line-up.

Expect a vibrant atmosphere where these master mixologists serve up inventive, culinary-forward cocktails, such as Bar Us’ famous Jackfruit & Sticky Rice.

Where: Argo, Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong, 8 Finance Street, Central

When: 6pm-9.30pm

Terrible Baby x Moebius Milano

Moebius Milano, ranked No 7 on the World’s 50 Best Bars last year, is housed inside a Milanese textile warehouse where Michelin-starred gastronomy, live jazz and avant-garde mixology collide.

For one night only, Moebius’ owner Lorenzo Querci and bartender Andrea Giraldo are taking over Eaton HK’s Terrible Baby. On the menu are cocktails like the Cocco & Salvia Negroni, which contains Bulldog gin and Del Professore Vermouth Rosso, as well as the aperitif Raspberry Lavorato Secco, which contains Campari and Rabarbaro Zucca.

Where: Terrible Baby, 4/F, Eaton Hong Kong, 380 Nathan Road, Kowloon

When: 7pm till sold out

item.title: [SCMP] How US became trapped in ‘dreadful situation’ of its own making over Iran war
item.description:
The United States is staring a historic “strategic defeat” in the face five months after launching the Iran war at Israel’s behest, according to Middle East observers.

The Islamic Republic is unlikely to fully relinquish its new-found hegemony over the Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump’s rhetorical mix of daily ultimatums and optimism about a deal, they say. Doing so would be giving up its leverage over the global economy – by far its greatest weapon in a war it cannot win militarily.

Having concluded that its June 17 memorandum of understanding with the US is all but dead, Iran is prepared to absorb all the military punishment the Trump administration can dish out.
item.content:encoded:
The United States is staring a historic “strategic defeat” in the face five months after launching the Iran war at Israel’s behest, according to Middle East observers.

The Islamic Republic is unlikely to fully relinquish its new-found hegemony over the Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump’s rhetorical mix of daily ultimatums and optimism about a deal, they say. Doing so would be giving up its leverage over the global economy – by far its greatest weapon in a war it cannot win militarily.

Having concluded that its June 17 memorandum of understanding with the US is all but dead, Iran is prepared to absorb all the military punishment the Trump administration can dish out.

Far from capitulating, the Revolutionary Guards and their Axis of Resistance allies across the Middle East have continued to escalate the conflict, targeting energy infrastructure and supply chains in the Red Sea, Suez Canal and the eastern Mediterranean. Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Egypt have all been targeted, and Syria could be next.

Late on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said negotiations with Oman on a proposed reopening of the strait were “forward-looking” and a deal would be struck “if certain third parties do not obstruct this process”.

While not mentioned, it was obvious who this “third party” would be. Iranian state television earlier reported that the reopening would be contingent “on a change in US behaviour”.

‘Extremely difficult predicament’

The Trump administration finds itself “in an extremely difficult predicament of its own making”, according to Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics, a Washington risk consultancy.

Washington faced a choice between pursuing a war that the US “is very unlikely to win or accepting a diplomatic settlement that would carry significant political costs for President Trump”, he said.

In Tehran, on the other hand, there is a “growing belief that only military escalation can restore deterrence”, and that diplomacy with the current US administration will “probably not produce an outcome that serves Iran’s interests”.

“Taken together, these dynamics leave little reason for optimism that the crisis will de-escalate any time soon,” Cafiero said.

Trump was “desperate”, said Hussein Ibish, senior resident scholar at the Washington-based Arab Gulf States Institute. The president had “manoeuvred himself into a dreadful situation” where anything he did pointed to “one of two bad outcomes”: acquiescing to Iranian power in the strait, or waging a years-long on-and-off air war.

A climbdown would be a “huge strategic defeat” for the US. Ibish said it would be the “first major step of the decline of the US dramatically as a global power” – undermining its standing in a way reminiscent of the decline of British and French power after they joined forces with Israel to briefly seize control of the Suez Canal in 1956.

But intensifying the war would create a “new structure of open-ended, kinetic and aggressive containment against Iran” turning it into “another forever war, even without boots on the ground”, Ibish said.

The groundwork for such a conflict is already being laid in the Middle East. Iraq, the region’s second largest oil exporter, is now a launch pad for drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia and Jordan by militias which, while officially part of the country’s armed forces, are armed and led by the Guards – much like the Lebanese Hezbollah.

In a departure from its policy of neutrality, Saudi Arabia responded to drone attacks against its energy infrastructure on July 29 by carrying out a joint air operation with the US against pro-Iran militias across Iraq.

Similarly, Riyadh and Yemen’s Houthi rebels have exchanged tit-for-tat air strikes with growing frequency since the Iran-allied militia imposed an embargo on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea on July 20.

Following the latest clash on Wednesday, the Houthis escalated their aggression by sinking an Indian ship trying to sail past the port of Hodeidah, which the militia controls. After four years of relative peace between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, the civil war in Yemen looks on the brink of resuming.

Stuck in the middle

This all underscored “just how vulnerable” the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states – Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain – were to a regional conflict involving an emboldened Islamic Republic viewing them as complicit in the Iran war, Cafiero said.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s intervention on Sunday to persuade Trump not to carry out his threatened escalation against Tehran did not merely seek to prevent more Iranian attacks against the GCC, Cafiero said. Rather, it was rooted in the GCC’s recognition that regional order “ultimately requires a workable relationship with Tehran”.

The GCC states realised that by striking them, Iran was attacking the entire global economy and putting enormous pressure on the US to “end the war on whatever terms”, Ibish said.

“It is [the Iranians’] ace card, and they are not going to give it up, so the Gulf countries know they remain in the crosshairs now and into the foreseeable future,” Ibish said. This situation was “exactly the disaster they foresaw” but failed to stop.

The only way for GCC members to mitigate the blowback is to “develop and pursue their own bilateral dialogues with Tehran”, he said.
