At the same time, they have to keep Washington on their side to supply them with the “very expensive and complex” missile defence systems to counter Iran’s “much cheaper but very effective” drone technology.

With Iran and its Axis of Resistance partners bent on implementing their “unity of theatres” strategy, however, it may only be a matter of time before the GCC states and their regional allies – Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan and Turkey – join forces to deter and, if necessary, retaliate.

The seeds of such an alliance were planted on July 30, when Saudi Arabia unveiled plans to establish a multinational maritime defence coalition ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab Strait and Gulf of Aden.

“As this crisis has prolonged and expanded since late February, Riyadh’s approach has evolved,” Cafiero said. While continuing to prioritise diplomacy, he said the kingdom has shown a “greater willingness” to use carefully calibrated military responses aimed at deterring attacks.

Despite wanting to avoid being drawn into the war with Iran “in a major way”, Ibish said the Gulf states at some point “are going to have to relent and get involved”.

“What the exact trigger is, nobody knows but them,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s retaliation against US shows depth of its trade war strategy, analysts say
item.description:
China’s latest export controls and sanctions against American companies in response to recent US measures underscore Beijing’s expanding economic toolkit and its growing willingness to deploy it, according to analysts.

“The multiple actions that China undertook underscore the breadth and depth of China’s retaliatory toolbox,” said Wendy Cutler, the senior vice-president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

She added that Beijing’s latest response stood in “sharp contrast” to its “ability and willingness” to retaliate during US President Donald Trump’s first term.
item.content:encoded:
China’s latest export controls and sanctions against American companies in response to recent US measures underscore Beijing’s expanding economic toolkit and its growing willingness to deploy it, according to analysts.

“The multiple actions that China undertook underscore the breadth and depth of China’s retaliatory toolbox,” said Wendy Cutler, the senior vice-president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

She added that Beijing’s latest response stood in “sharp contrast” to its “ability and willingness” to retaliate during US President Donald Trump’s first term.

The Chinese Ministry of Commerce on Wednesday announced a series of retaliatory measures, including tighter export controls on drones and related technologies, sanctions against seven US companies, and the launch of its first foreign trade-related national security investigation.

“China’s countermeasures have been restrained overall. China values the hard-won stability of China-US economic and trade relations. We hope the US side can work with China in the same direction,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.

The ministry highlighted that the measures were in response to recent US actions, including the sanctioning of 43 Chinese companies under a forced labour law and the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) bans on imports of new Chinese drones, robots, and power inverters.

The head of Arizona-based Compliance Testing LLC, one of the sanctioned entities, said China’s actions came as “a bit of a surprise” to him, but asserted that his firm’s work supports US security interests.

“This has to do with our national security,” Michael Schafer, the President of Compliance Testing LLC told the South China Morning Post.

“There are critical products which are manufactured and also tested in foreign adversary countries or non-reciprocal countries that we don’t have trading arrangements with.”

The firm is an FCC-recognised testing laboratory and telecommunications certification body that provides testing services for electronic products. It was targeted for assisting the federal agency in introducing measures that Beijing said endanger “China’s sovereignty, security and development interests”.

In April, the FCC advanced a proposal to ban Chinese labs from testing electronic devices, a move that has now drawn a response from Beijing. According to the FCC, around 75 per cent of all US electronics are tested in China.

China broadens its economic arsenal of legal, regulatory measures

Since 2020, China has broadened its economic toolkit, introducing a growing array of legal, regulatory and trade measures aimed at responding more forcefully to US restrictions and reducing the asymmetry in available policy tools.

Beijing’s legal architecture now includes laws and regulations such as the Export Control Law, Unreliable Entity List, Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law and Foreign Trade Law.

“They reveal that China’s countermeasures framework and toolkit have come of age,” said Sourabh Gupta, a resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies.

The most ambitious use of Beijing’s export controls came in April 2025, when China imposed sweeping restrictions on seven rare earths, triggering supply disruptions and temporary factory shutdowns around the world. A US-China truce in October last year helped avert a full-blown crisis.

“Beijing is signalling it has an expanding toolkit and is willing to use it, while leaving room to de-escalate,” Kyle Sullivan, vice-president at the US-China Business Council, wrote in a social media post.

Sullivan also pointed to the first use of the national security investigation mechanism under China’s Foreign Trade Law, targeting imported printing and copying office equipment that uses foreign-made software. US technology companies such as Microsoft and HP are among the major players in the printing software market.

“The broader package also looks more calibrated and coordinated than some past retaliation,” he added.

“It suggests China is building a more diversified toolkit for responding to US economic-security measures rather than relying on ad hoc retaliation.”

A senior US government official on Wednesday criticised China’s latest sanctions, warning that Beijing’s actions risk derailing efforts to stabilise economic ties between the world’s two largest economies.

“We are deeply disappointed that China has chosen to announce another round of escalatory measures,” the official said in a statement to the SCMP.

“Over the past two months, Beijing has taken a series of actions that undermine US economic interests and make it more difficult to achieve the stable and balanced economic relationship that both countries should seek.”

The official said that while the Trump administration and China’s leadership maintain a close relationship, “expanding the cycle of retaliation will not produce a durable solution.”

“President Trump will not allow American workers and manufacturers to continue bearing the costs of those practices,” the official added.

The US State Department also blamed China’s actions, saying they have disadvantaged US businesses and harmed American workers.

“China’s tactics put American businesses at a disadvantage and displace American workers,” a State Department spokesperson told the SCMP.

Tit-for-tat escalation fails to derail Trump-Xi summit in September

The latest measures mark another round of tit-for-tat escalation in recent days, with the US imposing tariffs and both Washington and Beijing expanding export controls and restrictions targeting companies.

While each side has blamed the other for the moves, they have so far avoided allowing the disputes to derail preparations for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the US in September.

Last week, China’s Vice-Premier He Lifeng held a video call with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to finalise economic deliverables for the visit, while also raising concerns about each other’s measures.

“It’s doubtful that the US will take further actions in response to the latest Chinese countermeasures,” Cutler said, but added that Washington’s response today had put Beijing on notice that “stabilisation should not be taken for granted.”

However, Sullivan highlighted that despite the breadth of China’s measures, the “response looks fairly restrained.”

“Beijing had considerably more painful options available and didn’t use them.”

Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies noted that China’s toolkit is “no longer just ornamental but is fit for purpose”.

“This past half-decade will come to be remembered many decades hence as the seminal moment that launched the modern age of China’s economic statecraft,” Gupta said.

item.title: [SCMP] China competition looms large in 2027 US defence bill
item.description:
Even as Congress remains divided over the latest US defence bill, lawmakers in both parties remain united on one issue: China.

The National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA), which sets US defence policy and authorises military spending each year, reflects a broad bipartisan consensus on expanding Washington’s military, technological and economic rivalry with Beijing.

While the House and Senate versions differ on a number of provisions, both include new measures on Taiwan, artificial intelligence, defence supply chains and preparations for a potential South China Sea crisis, underscoring how competition with Beijing has become embedded throughout US national security policy.
item.content:encoded:
Even as Congress remains divided over the latest US defence bill, lawmakers in both parties remain united on one issue: China.

The National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA), which sets US defence policy and authorises military spending each year, reflects a broad bipartisan consensus on expanding Washington’s military, technological and economic rivalry with Beijing.

While the House and Senate versions differ on a number of provisions, both include new measures on Taiwan, artificial intelligence, defence supply chains and preparations for a potential South China Sea crisis, underscoring how competition with Beijing has become embedded throughout US national security policy.

The House has already passed its version of the financial year 2027 NDAA, while the Senate is struggling to approve its own before next week’s August recess. The two chambers will then have to reconcile their differences before sending the legislation to US President Donald Trump for his signature.

This year’s tone is largely the same as in past bills, experts say, though with notable new additions targeting China across a wide range of issues, from defence procurement and supply chains to artificial intelligence, industrial policy and economic security.

Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund’s Indo-Pacific programme, said the NDAA had increasingly been used to bolster resilience against China while strengthening defence ties with allies and partners.

“Over the past decade, Congress has increasingly used the NDAA to emphasise strengthening deterrence in the Indo-Pacific,” she said, pointing out that the bill is especially aimed at “enhancing resilience against Chinese coercion, [and] enhancing Taiwan’s readiness and resilience”.

Taiwan and the US ‘war reserve’

Taiwan remains a feature of both versions of the NDAA, with the Senate version taking a stronger focus amid the potential for conflict with Beijing.

The Senate bill would establish a “War Reserve Stock Programme” for Taiwan – perhaps the provision to anger Beijing the most – authorising the pre-positioning of humanitarian supplies, ammunition, missiles and other military equipment to improve the island’s readiness in the event of a conflict.

“[The bill] marks the first time Congress is proposing the provision of direct statutory authority for such a programme, moving from a planning requirement to an operational capability,” Glaser said.

While the NDAA does not alter the long-standing US “one China” policy, she added, it reflects a clear bipartisan consensus that improving Taiwan’s ability to deter aggression is central to maintaining peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons.

Zack Cooper, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said the programme reflects an effort to help both Washington and Taipei better prepare “for a long-term conflict that would require deep war reserves.”

The Senate version would also extend and redesignate the “Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative” as the “First Island Chain Security Cooperation Initiative”, with the Philippines added to receive military support under the programme.

The Chinese embassy in Washington issued a sharply worded statement that China “strongly deplores and firmly opposes” these NDAA provisions, and any attempt to arm Taiwan “will face grave consequences”.

“The Taiwan-related provisions in the bill grossly interfere in China’s internal affairs, gravely undermine China’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, seriously disrupt peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, and send a profoundly wrong signal to ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist forces and the outside world,” the embassy spokesperson said in a statement.

The statement singled out named Taiwanese leader Lai Ching-te, arguing the real threat to peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait comes from his administration’s “Taiwan independence” separatist activities and interference by external forces.

“[The] Taiwan question allows no external interference, and China’s red lines must not be crossed,” the statement continued.

“The so-called enhancement of Taiwan’s defence capabilities will only embolden ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists, expose the people in Taiwan to the dangers of a powder keg, push the Taiwan Strait into a perilous situation, and inevitably heighten the risk of conflict and confrontation between China and the United States.”

Taiwan is the “most important” issue in Beijing’s relations with Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping told Trump in May.

And any perceived provocation – whether an arms sale approval or an initiative like the war reserve programme – could complicate preparations for Xi’s planned state visit to Washington this autumn.

Trump has separately paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, a move unrelated to the NDAA process but one that underscores how carefully the administration is managing the relationship ahead of Xi’s visit.

Supply chains and AI competition

One of the clearest themes in both versions of the NDAA is reducing the Pentagon’s reliance on Chinese products and suppliers.

A House Armed Services Committee fact sheet says the legislation seeks to “remove China from our defence supply chains”.

The House bill would prohibit the Department of Defence from acquiring Chinese-made humanoid robotic systems, photovoltaic cells, solar modules and inverters, as well as used sealift vessels built in China.

The House bill also includes workforce development initiatives to support the mining of critical minerals, aimed at reducing dependency on China.

The Senate bill would require an annual assessment of how advanced AI chips contribute to China’s military capabilities, and would prohibit defence contractors from sharing sensitive synthetic biology information with China.

Both versions seek to ban the use of Chinese-manufactured optical fibre and connected vehicles.

Cooper said the most consequential China-related provisions right now are the bills aimed at preventing China from acquiring advanced artificial intelligence chips, cloud compute and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

It remains unclear whether those export-control measures will survive into the final, reconciled version of the bill, he said, “but there is momentum in that direction”.

The Senate bill also includes a prohibition on Pentagon funding for film, television or other entertainment projects tied to the Chinese state.

Other provisions would strengthen research security and seek to prevent sensitive technologies from benefiting China’s military, including restrictions on collaboration with Chinese academic institutions and new “insider threat reporting” requirements for large AI contractors.

The Pentagon has also blacklisted several China-military-linked companies, triggering strong opposition from Beijing, which called Washington’s move an “overstretching” of the concept of national security and its use of “discriminatory lists” targeting Chinese businesses.

Some companies on the list, including Alibaba, have since sued the Department of Defence, seeking removal.

Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

South China Sea issue makes a comeback

The South China Sea may have drawn less attention in the halls of Congress than it did a decade ago, but the Senate version of the bill would require the Pentagon, within a year, to draft a crisis strategy for the sea identifying likely flashpoints and outlining phased response plans coordinated with federal agencies and foreign partners.

Evan Sankey, a fellow at the Cato Institute, said he was surprised by the provision.

“Ten years ago you heard a lot about the island-building in the South China Sea, and there was a lot of policy talk in the US over what to do about it,” Sankey said. “That issue has sort of fallen off.”

China’s “nine-dash line” claims overlap with the maritime claims of Vietnam, the Philippines and other South China Sea claimant states.

The disputes involve access to fishing grounds, potential oil and gas reserves, and strategic shipping lanes.

China also rejected a 2016 ruling by an international tribunal that was in favour of Manila, arguing that the ruling is “illegal” and the court did not have jurisdiction over sovereignty issues.

In July, the United States, Japan and the Philippines conducted joint military exercises and maritime drills aimed at strengthening regional security cooperation, moves Beijing said would “damage regional peace and stability”.

The same month, the US and its allies also concluded Rimpac, the world’s largest multinational maritime exercise, widely seen as reinforcing deterrence against China amid growing regional tensions.

The Senate bill also expands regional programmes beyond China-specific measures, deepening military partnerships with the Philippines and Australia and assessing Japan’s defence capabilities – an apparent move to boost the US’ Indo-Pacific presence and alliances.

Overall, Sankey said the NDAA sticks to its standard line on China: that Beijing is “a strategic competitor” with “ambitions to dominate Asia”.

The Senate has yet to begin debating the NDAA after Democrats blocked a procedural vote. A motion to reconsider remains pending. Sankey said he does not expect the NDAA to languish.

“Congress has a tendency to drag its feet on lots of stuff,” Sankey said. “But when it comes to the Pentagon, there will be pressure to get to pass something and get it signed by the president.”

item.title: [SCMP] US hawks push Trump on multibillion-dollar Taiwan arms deal ahead of Xi summit
item.description:
Washington has reopened discussions on billions in arms sales to Taiwan, casting a shadow over a leaders’ summit just weeks away – a meeting already burdened by bilateral trade frictions.

US President Donald Trump is expected to submit a US$14 billion Taiwan arms package to the US Congress soon, according to senior Republican lawmaker Michael McCaul on Tuesday.

“I am confident the president will forward soon another package to Congress with an additional US$14 billion in critical military defence articles,” the Texas congressman said at a security forum during his third visit to Taiwan, where he received an award from the island’s leader William Lai Ching-te.
item.content:encoded:
Washington has reopened discussions on billions in arms sales to Taiwan, casting a shadow over a leaders’ summit just weeks away – a meeting already burdened by bilateral trade frictions.

US President Donald Trump is expected to submit a US$14 billion Taiwan arms package to the US Congress soon, according to senior Republican lawmaker Michael McCaul on Tuesday.

“I am confident the president will forward soon another package to Congress with an additional US$14 billion in critical military defence articles,” the Texas congressman said at a security forum during his third visit to Taiwan, where he received an award from the island’s leader William Lai Ching-te.

Although observers doubt the deal will go through before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s trip to the US, they warn that Taiwan is a strict red line and any arms package could derail bilateral talks.

The package remains under review by the Trump administration and was described by the US president as “a very good negotiating chip” with Beijing during his high-stakes state visit to China in May.

In the same month, acting US Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said the US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan was paused to ensure American forces had enough weapons for the Iran war. McCaul added that US policy did not allow diplomatic relations with Beijing to “tie up arms sales to Taiwan”.

The amount would exceed that of a historic Taiwan arms package approved late last year – a move that prompted strong condemnation from Beijing, which held a two-day military exercise near the island soon after.

“Last December, Congress signed off on the largest foreign military sales package in history at US$11 billion – and we aren’t stopping there,” McCaul said.

The Chinese foreign ministry has yet to comment on McCaul’s remarks.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland.

The United States, like most countries, does not recognise self-governed Taiwan as an independent state, but is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is legally committed to supplying it with weapons.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said the underlying intent of McCaul’s remarks was largely domestic.

He said that reviving the topic of arms sales reflected pressure from China hawks in Congress and the administration, who see Trump as bogged down in Iran amid rising Republican discontent that could jeopardise the coming midterm elections.

“As for the Trump administration, it is currently beset by troubles at home and abroad. Therefore, to stabilise things within the Republican Party – especially to win over China hawks – it may also need to play the ‘Taiwan card’,” Wu said.

Zhang Chi, a senior researcher at the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong, said McCaul’s visit was aimed at “testing the waters” with both Beijing and Taipei.

Given McCaul’s close ties with Taiwan, Zhang said his remarks were “not surprising”, but they were delivered with “notable caution and diplomacy” without signalling any immediate action or deliverables.

“All of this underscores the central question: how will Trump handle the Taiwan issue as he attempts to build a ‘constructive strategic stability’ in US-China relations? Trump did learn a hard lesson on Taiwan early on … but it remains doubtful whether he fully grasps the issue,” Zhang said.

Trump and Xi agreed to the phrase “constructive strategic stability” to define the new framework of bilateral ties during their May summit in Beijing.

In that meeting, Xi called the Taiwan issue the “most critical matter” in relations with Washington, urging the US to handle the issue with “extreme caution”. He warned that if it did not, the two countries would clash and push bilateral ties “into a very dangerous situation”.

Trump said he and Xi “talked a lot” about the island during his trip, though the topic was omitted from the White House’s official statement about the meeting.

The American president told Fox News in May that the US would not fight a war over Taiwan. But he has sent mixed signals about future arms sales.

William Yang, a senior analyst for northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said it was unlikely that Trump would submit the arms sales to Congress ahead of Xi’s planned visit, as he would probably prioritise the summit.

“He has made it known that maintaining a cordial working relationship with Xi is one of his priorities when it comes to US-China relations,” he said.

Submitting the budget before Xi’s visit could risk delaying or cancelling the summit, Yang added.

“If the Trump administration thought they could use arms sales to Taiwan to impose pressure on Beijing, they could be miscalculating. In Beijing’s eyes, its position on Taiwan is non-negotiable.”

Zhang in Hong Kong stressed that there would be no guarantee that bilateral relations could maintain the current level if the “hard-won momentum” was disrupted again.

Both sides are paving the way for another leaders’ summit in Washington in September.

US Senator Steve Daines is expected to return to China for another round of talks ahead of Xi’s planned visit to help finalise the agenda and bridge differences, according to earlier reporting by the South China Morning Post.

Last month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi discussed the Chinese leader’s trip with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Manila.

When asked about the arms deal, Rubio said it was still under internal review because Washington had to take its own stockpile into consideration.

Ma Zhaoxu, China’s foreign vice-minister, made a two-day trip to the US in July and met US officials. The visit was widely viewed as an effort to lay the groundwork for Xi’s trip.

Meanwhile, trade tensions between China and the US have continued to fester.

On Wednesday, Beijing announced a barrage of counter-sanctions targeting a group of American entities and a tightening of export restrictions on the drone supply chain.

The move was a response to a series of moves by Washington, including the addition of 43 Chinese companies to its entity list over allegations of forced labour in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, as well as a ban by the US Federal Communications Commission on importing and selling new foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters.

Yang said these economic frictions would put the fragile trade truce under pressure, further testing the two countries’ ability to reach a consensus.

“In other words, both countries could find themselves falling back into the more escalatory competition mode if neither side is willing to soften their position,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s Palantir? Private tech firms surge into defence AI, aiming to match US giants
item.description:
The People’s Liberation Army is just a year away from its centenary goals in its evolution into a “world-class” fighting force. In this part of a series, Amber Wang looks at the growing influence of artificial intelligence in combat and the private firms stepping into the area.

Roughly two months before the United States launched air strikes on Iran, a little-known Chinese technology company was watching an unusual pattern emerge on its screens.

Drawing on open-source intelligence and artificial intelligence-powered analysis, Hangzhou-based Jingan Technology said it had detected an unusually large concentration of US surveillance assets across the Middle East.
item.content:encoded:
The People’s Liberation Army is just a year away from its centenary goals in its evolution into a “world-class” fighting force. In this part of a series, Amber Wang looks at the growing influence of artificial intelligence in combat and the private firms stepping into the area.

Roughly two months before the United States launched air strikes on Iran, a little-known Chinese technology company was watching an unusual pattern emerge on its screens.

Drawing on open-source intelligence and artificial intelligence-powered analysis, Hangzhou-based Jingan Technology said it had detected an unusually large concentration of US surveillance assets across the Middle East.

In a post published on its official account on January 6, Jingan suggested the build-up indicated that Washington “may already be in the midst of preparations for a potential military operation” – more than 50 days before the strikes took place.

Jingan has marketed its flagship product, the Jingqi Global Situational Awareness System, as a Chinese counterpart to operating systems such as Palantir Technologies’ Gotham and Anduril Industries’ Lattice.

While industry observers and military enthusiasts have cautioned against Jingan’s high-profile marketing claims, company materials and public disclosures suggest that its software has already been deployed within China’s public security system and state security apparatus, as well as some branches of the military.

Jingan is among a growing number of Chinese private tech firms entering the country’s rapidly expanding defence AI sector, driven by Beijing’s military-civil fusion strategy to integrate private companies into the defence industry.

Analysts say that some Chinese companies’ tech proficiency may be closing gaps with US counterparts like Palantir, but challenges remain for building an ecosystem capable of fully integrating such technology into operational decision-making.

According to Hu Bo, director of South China Sea Strategic Situation Probing Initiative (SCSPI), a leading Chinese think tank: “The gap doesn’t lie in the technology, but the United States is much further ahead in applying it, particularly in supporting decision-making.”

A turning point in modern warfare

Few defence software companies have attracted as much attention in recent years as US-based Palantir, which China’s defence sector follows closely.

Founded in 2003 in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, Palantir initially focused on providing large-scale intelligence analysis to combat terrorist attacks.

Now, its platforms are used across dozens of US government agencies including the Pentagon and several Nato allies, making Palantir one of the world’s most influential defence software companies.

The Pentagon has increasingly relied on Palantir’s Maven Smart System (MSS), with the company serving as an important contractor to gather intelligence, synthesise vast amounts of data and help commanders “make better and faster decisions”, according to US defence officials.

During the first 24 hours of the Iran conflict, the US used the MSS to help identify and strike more than 1,000 targets – a tenfold increase over what was possible before the system’s deployment – according to a June report by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

And in January, the US military used Claude during its special operation to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro from Caracas through Anthropic’s partnership with Palantir, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Palantir has also helped Ukraine with AI-enabled air defence and combat data analysis projects in its war with Russia.

Its AI-enabled systems are designed to fuse satellite imagery, sensor feeds, intelligence reports and operational data into a unified picture, enabling faster target identification, more responsive command decisions and shorter decision cycles than earlier generations of military software.

Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar has argued that the Iran conflict is likely to be remembered as the first major war in which artificial intelligence played a central operational role, marking a turning point in modern warfare.

In China, the country’s leadership has for years emphasised the “intelligentisation” of the People’s Liberation Army, alongside broader efforts to integrate emerging technologies into future combat capabilities.

However, exactly which AI models have been tested or deployed by the Chinese military – and the extent to which they have been incorporated into command-and-control systems – remains highly classified.

It is also impossible to know their performance on battlefields, as the country has not fought a full-scale war for more than four decades.

For Chinese military observers, recent global conflicts have reinforced an argument Beijing has advanced for years: future wars will be decided not only by weapons but also by the speed at which data can be transformed into operational decisions.

According to Yue Gang, a military analyst and retired PLA colonel: “The lesson here is that accelerating the intelligent transformation of the military is a matter of utmost urgency.”

Yue said recent armed conflicts showed how AI was becoming embedded throughout the battlefield, creating what he described as an “intelligent closed loop” linking intelligence, decision-making, strikes and support.

“In traditional warfare, the observe-orient-decide-act (Ooda) loop is measured in hours or even days. However, in modern conflicts, AI-assisted systems can compress this cycle to just seconds.”

“Data fusion, situational awareness and decision support represent the strategic high ground of future military competition,” he added.

At the same time, Yue warned, the reliability of AI-assisted target recognition was still a critical concern.

Other analysts voiced greater caution about the extent to which these systems have transformed the battlefield.

“When it comes to the actual impact of Palantir and Project Maven, the reality may not be as dramatic as media portrayals suggest. Human intelligence remains absolutely vital,” Hu of the SCSPI said.

While China broadly supports accelerating AI’s integration into the military, it also advocates a measured approach, arguing that humans should stay firmly “in the loop” and retain ultimate authority over the use of lethal force.

A Chinese Palantir?

As Palantir’s more prominent role on the battlefield has drawn global attention, Chinese entrepreneurs and investors have pointed to similar software as a strategic capability that China should develop.

But they are operating within a very different ecosystem, one shaped by Beijing’s military-civil fusion strategy, state-led procurement networks and the PLA’s evolving vision of intelligent warfare.

Today, hundreds of Chinese private technology companies are involved in defence projects, ranging from data fusion and autonomous systems to AI-assisted training and battlefield simulation.

Only a handful, however, have been described as China’s answer to Palantir.

Even then, analysts have expressed caution about their actual abilities and the extent to which their products have been adopted by the Chinese military.

One of the most prominent examples is Jingan Technology.

Founded in Hangzhou in 2021, the company was established by a group of engineers from leading Chinese tech firms with an initial focus on “urban security” applications such as summit security support, infrastructure protection and public security, according to company statements.

Like Palantir, the company’s name carries symbolic meaning. “Jingan” echoes a fictional Tang dynasty (618-907) public security institution popularised in a Chinese television drama.

The company has also recruited former personnel from the military, police and intelligence communities, according to its public introductions.

Jingan maintained a relatively low public profile until the outbreak of the Iran conflict, when it published a post claiming that its AI-powered analysis had predicted the US strikes more than 50 days in advance.

According to company materials, the system used in that analysis – its flagship “Jingqi” platform – is an AI-enabled command-and-control system that integrates satellite imagery, sensor feeds and multiple other data sources to provide real-time situational awareness, operational planning and decision support.

The company describes the platform as comparable to Anduril’s Lattice and Palantir’s Gotham. It has also been described by some Chinese media reports as “China’s Palantir”.

Similar to Palantir’s early development, Jingan initially focused on civilian security and policing rather than military applications.

According to company materials, its products have been deployed in cooperation with local public security bureaus, integrating thousands of police devices across multiple police stations in a major municipality.

Reported applications include responding to daily emergency incidents, supporting security operations for major public events and providing technical support during the coronavirus pandemic.

But over time, the company’s business appeared to have expanded into defence-related projects, and now the company introduces itself as a “defence tech” firm rather than its previous “urban security” label.

Publicly available information suggests Jingan has taken part in a project involving a radar monitoring station of the PLA’s former Strategic Support Force (SSF).

The SSF previously oversaw many of China’s space, cyber, electronic warfare and psychological operations arms before being dissolved in 2024, with its functions redistributed into the Information Support Force, the Aerospace Force and the Cyberspace Force.

Jingan’s customers include several of China’s biggest state-owned defence conglomerates, according to company materials.

Norinco, China Electronics Technology Group, China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation, China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation and China South Industries Group Corporation are among the customers, according to media reports.

The company has also gained momentum commercially.

In March, it announced the completion of a Series A+ funding round worth tens of millions of yuan, backed by a Chinese semiconductor manufacturer, bringing its total disclosed funding to about 300 million yuan (US$44.3 million).

Jingan is not alone.

Another Hangzhou-based company, MizarVision, which specialises in analysing commercial satellite imagery, has similarly attracted attention through its open-source intelligence analysis of American military deployments during the Iran conflict.

In May, the US Treasury added the company to its Specially Designated Nationals list, accusing it of publishing open-source imagery detailing American military activity during Operation Epic Fury.

Instead of challenging US sanctions in court, MizarVision took it as a badge of honour and highlighted the sanction in its recruitment campaign.

The South China Morning Post has contacted both Jingan and MizarVision for comment.

Another example is Beijing-based start-up EverReach AI.

During a defence technology exhibition in Beijing last year, the company showcased an AI-assisted military training platform using a flight map near the Taiwan Strait as one of its product demonstrations.

The presentation appeared to show how the system could support planning and evaluation of military exercises around Taiwan.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

A ‘very narrow’ path

Some investors view defence technology as one of China’s most promising long-term industries.

In 2022, Lu Di, CEO of Miracle Capital, described advanced defence technology as a pillar of national power.

“China is still in the early stages of developing this sector, but the potential is enormous,” Lu said at the time.

Despite rapid advances in China’s defence AI sector, some analysts argue that the gap with the US lies less in technological capability than in how AI is integrated into military operations.

“Their ultimate goal remains to serve the military, but the path is very narrow,” Hu said of the private defence tech firms’ ambitions.

The more significant gap was in operational integration, he added.

“Without large-scale military operations conducted by China, there is simply no operational environment in which to deploy and validate these applications.

“Where the US is applying this technology much more deeply than we are is in decision support and direct participation in decision-making,” Hu said.

Institutional challenges also persist within the PLA itself.

A commentary by the official PLA Daily in June pointed to enduring problems, including duplicated development of AI models across various military branches, limited interoperability and a lack of coordination between services.

Fu Qianshao, a Chinese military analyst, said future efforts should focus on integration.

“While every individual platform possesses its own ‘brain’, there ultimately needs to be a central command-and-control platform, a master brain, to coordinate overall decision-making,” Fu said.

China would also continue to draw lessons from America’s experience, he added, while pursuing its own technological road map.

“China’s AI development has its own characteristics, planning and path,” Fu said. “We are certainly working on it as well.”

The rise of companies such as Jingan reflects Beijing’s broader military-civil fusion strategy, which seeks to channel private-sector innovation into national defence.

But industry participants said business realities were another major obstacle.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, an employee at a leading Chinese tech company said the military’s control of costs and long procurement cycles had become major challenges for private defence tech firms seeking to become military contractors.

“The military is controlling procurement costs, while research and development requires substantial long-term investment,” the employee said.

The PLA has also made more of an effort to regulate the procurement sector.

In June, Xiamen-based AI company Yuanting Information Technology was barred from taking part in military procurement for three years after authorities found it had engaged in bid-rigging.

Many of the challenges mirror those faced by the Pentagon when it first sought to introduce AI into military operations.

Project Maven, launched in 2017, encountered years of bureaucratic resistance, procurement hurdles and organisational inertia before becoming one of the Pentagon’s flagship AI programmes.

As retired US Marine Corps Colonel Drew Cukor, who served as the founding chief of Project Maven, wrote in Fortune in May: “What made Maven different wasn’t the technology. It was the decision to treat AI not as an experiment to be managed but as an organisational transformation to be owned.”

For Chinese analysts, the lesson is not simply to replicate US technology but to build institutions that can integrate it while simultaneously regulating AI risks.

“We will continue developing our own capabilities while learning from the strengths of the United States and overcoming our own shortcomings,” Fu said.

Yue, the retired PLA colonel, argued that military-civil fusion was becoming the dominant model for China’s defence innovation.

China should continue to prioritise “human-in-the-loop” collaboration over complete machine autonomy, he said, while building an “independent and secure” military AI ecosystem alongside regulatory safeguards and risk-control mechanisms.

item.title: [SCMP] Are Indonesia’s Prabowo and ultra rich ‘9 Dragons’ on a collision course?
item.description:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s push to reorganise Southeast Asia’s largest economy around a stronger, more interventionist state has put him increasingly at odds, analysts say, with the country’s so-called Nine Dragons.

Known locally as Sembilan Naga, the label is a loose shorthand for some of Indonesia’s richest tycoon families – many of them Chinese Indonesian – with interests spanning banking, tobacco, property, palm oil, mining and consumer goods.

It has never referred to a formally confirmed group but is widely used in public discussion of powerful conglomerates associated with business empires such as Djarum, Salim Group, Lippo Group, Golden Agri-Resources, Barito Pacific and Agung Sedayu.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s push to reorganise Southeast Asia’s largest economy around a stronger, more interventionist state has put him increasingly at odds, analysts say, with the country’s so-called Nine Dragons.

Known locally as Sembilan Naga, the label is a loose shorthand for some of Indonesia’s richest tycoon families – many of them Chinese Indonesian – with interests spanning banking, tobacco, property, palm oil, mining and consumer goods.

It has never referred to a formally confirmed group but is widely used in public discussion of powerful conglomerates associated with business empires such as Djarum, Salim Group, Lippo Group, Golden Agri-Resources, Barito Pacific and Agung Sedayu.

Prabowo has not explicitly named the Nine Dragons as targets, but analysts say his warnings about wealth leaking overseas, his drive to centralise key exports and his effort to marshal tycoon money for state projects all suggest a broader bid to bring Indonesia’s old business elite under firmer state control.

“Prabowo may not mention names, but there’s no mistake he’s taking potshots at the dragons,” said Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow in the Indonesia Studies Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, whose research focuses on Indonesian state bureaucracy.

Yet the limits of Prabowo’s leverage run both ways: the tycoons remain deeply embedded in the Indonesian economy, while the president still needs private capital to help fund his flagship programmes.

“They [the tycoons] find themselves between a rock and a hard place: to submit to the president or to take their business somewhere else,” Made said.

But Vedi Hadiz, a political sociologist at the University of Melbourne and author of Reorganising Power in Indonesia: The Politics of Oligarchy in an Age of Markets, told This Week in Asia the second option was unlikely.

“At the core of it, most of their revenues come from their operations within the Indonesian economy.”

Prabowo’s push has also shed light on the rise of newer loyalists such as coal magnate Haji Isam, whose ascent analysts see as part of Prabowo’s effort to cultivate business figures more eager to align themselves with his state-led agenda.

“Prabowo’s end goal is to establish a more command-like and centralised political economy, in which he is at the apex of power,” Vedi said.

A more centralised political economy, analysts say, gives the administration greater leverage over business groups such as the Nine Dragons. However, they differ over whether Prabowo aims to break their influence or simply remake the terms of their relationship with the state.

State grip

At a plenary cabinet meeting at the State Palace in Jakarta on July 20, Prabowo framed the problem as one of national economic leakage, saying in remarks published by the State Secretariat that Indonesia was losing “hundreds of billions of dollars every year” through under-invoicing, falsified trade reports, transfer pricing and smuggling.

Under-invoicing involves under-reporting the value of exports to reduce duties or taxes, while transfer pricing can be used by related companies to shift profits to lower-tax jurisdictions.

“These are legitimate concerns by the president, as both practices are certainly done by our big exporters,” said Ricky Ho, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Jakarta-based Four Capital, a family office investment firm.

Prabowo’s response has been to give the state a greater role in export flows. This includes a one-door system for key commodities, overseen by Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI), a new arm of the state investment agency Danantara, and a Foreign Exchange Earnings mechanism (DHE) that requires non-oil-and-gas natural-resource exporters to retain export proceeds in Indonesia for at least 12 months.

The DSI system is being introduced in stages, with full implementation planned for 2027.

Ricky said the measures risked giving the state too much control over private cash flows, commercial contracts and export pricing – a shift that would fall most heavily on large commodity exporters.

For critics, the concern is not only the policy design but also the political message to conglomerates that rely heavily on Indonesia’s commodity exports and natural-resource concessions.

Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Jakarta-based think tank Centre of Economic and Law Studies, said both DSI and DHE could be read partly as a presidential warning.

“This was intended to put pressure on the tycoons to toe the line or have their business threatened,” he said.

Patriot money

Many of Indonesia’s biggest conglomerates expanded under Suharto’s New Order, when state contracts, licensing and regulatory protection helped bind politically connected business groups to the president’s patronage system.

For analysts such as Made, Prabowo’s approach carries echoes of that period.

“Prabowo appears to hanker for a return to the Suharto era and he doesn’t shy away from deploying state instruments to achieve his ends,” Made said.

One test of that relationship came through Patriot Bonds, a low-yield financing instrument unveiled in August 2025 and offered through a private placement to selected large business groups rather than to the public.

The bonds reportedly carried a 2 per cent annual yield, well below comparable government securities.

“Most of the tycoons were initially unenthusiastic, due to the low yield of the bonds,” Bhima said.

A circulated list of 46 alleged subscribers fuelled speculation that many of Indonesia’s best-known tycoons had joined the programme, though Danantara did not verify the names.

Mohamad Al-Arief, managing director of global relations and governance at Danantara, said the list was not official and the fund had not named any buyers, adding that participation in the private placement was voluntary.

The programme became more sensitive after legal protections were extended to buyers of Patriot Bonds and similar “Red and White” bonds – named after the colours of Indonesia’s flag – though officials later said those protections applied only to funds placed in the instruments, not to investors’ wider businesses or assets.

For analysts, the low yield, selective placement and limited disclosure around subscribers makes Patriot Bonds a potential test of political alignment and financial investment.

One episode that has fuelled those questions involves Djarum, the Hartono family conglomerate. In September 2025, Danantara said Djarum was among the groups interested in Patriot Bonds and the leaked list claimed that Budi Hartono had committed 3 trillion rupiah.

Two months later, the Attorney General’s Office placed Djarum president director Victor Rachmat Hartono under a travel ban during an investigation into alleged tax corruption between 2016 and 2020. The ban was lifted weeks later after prosecutors said he had cooperated.

Local investigative news outlet Tempo’s reporting asked whether the case was connected to the drive to mobilise elite capital through Patriot Bonds. In an editorial, the outlet said the episode had political and business overtones, warning that prosecutors must not become a tool for pressuring major companies.

The Attorney General’s Office denied a link and no direct evidence has emerged publicly. This Week in Asia has contacted Djarum for comment.

Rising loyalists

Bhima said the pressure on Indonesia’s older business elite formed part of a broader two-pronged strategy of state capitalism.

“He aims to bring the older generation of oligarchs to heel while at the same time pushing for the advancement of new loyalist tycoons like Haji Isam,” he said.

Born in 1977, Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, better known as Haji Isam, rose from a modest background to become one of Indonesia’s most politically connected businessmen.

His fortunes changed after he entered the coal industry in South Kalimantan in the early 2000s, before expanding into palm oil, shipping, logistics and aviation through Jhonlin Group.

Haji Isam has built ties across successive administrations, including by backing Joko Widodo’s 2019 re-election campaign and emerging as a visible business figure around Prabowo’s food-security agenda.

He has been prominently associated with Prabowo’s food-estate push in Merauke, South Papua, where the president has targeted 1 million hectares of new farmland as part of his self-sufficiency drive.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Jhonlin Group for comment.

Bhima said Prabowo’s effort to bring older tycoons under firmer control could carry economic costs, including weaker market trust and the risk of capital outflow.

Any outflow of private tycoon funds is difficult to quantify because such wealth is often held through layered corporate structures, offshore vehicles or family offices and may not show up clearly in public capital-flow data.

What is visible is broader market unease: Indonesian equities saw heavy foreign selling in 2026, with foreign investors net selling about US$3.89 billion by late June.

Vedi, however, said the recalibration of ties between Prabowo and Indonesia’s older tycoon networks was unlikely to end in an irreparable rupture.

No major Indonesian conglomerate, he argued, can survive without alliances with the political elite.

“The tycoons will sulk and get annoyed, kicking and screaming, but by and large they’ll cooperate.”

He characterised their relationship as a “symbiosis”, since Prabowo also needs the tycoons to help fund his flagship programmes.

“But in return for their loyalty, the president has to reciprocate by making sure some of their interests are accommodated.”

item.title: [SCMP] Arrest of ‘fake Filipino’ sharpens concerns over security risks in key sectors
item.description:
The detention of a Chinese national accused of posing as a Filipino for more than two decades has sharpened concerns in the Philippines that identity fraud could be used to gain access to sectors vital to national security.

Immigration authorities arrested Lawrence Ke Sy, president, largest incorporator and majority shareholder of Maxipro Development Corp., on June 27, although the arrest was only disclosed to the public on Monday.

Maxipro is a contractor involved in projects for the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP), the privately owned company responsible for operating, maintaining and developing the country’s state-owned power grid.
item.content:encoded:
The detention of a Chinese national accused of posing as a Filipino for more than two decades has sharpened concerns in the Philippines that identity fraud could be used to gain access to sectors vital to national security.

Immigration authorities arrested Lawrence Ke Sy, president, largest incorporator and majority shareholder of Maxipro Development Corp., on June 27, although the arrest was only disclosed to the public on Monday.

Maxipro is a contractor involved in projects for the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP), the privately owned company responsible for operating, maintaining and developing the country’s state-owned power grid.

Authorities did not disclose how Sy was captured but presented documents they said were fraudulently obtained to support his alleged claim to Philippine citizenship, including a Philippine passport, birth certificate, marriage certificate and records from the National Bureau of Investigation and the Land Transportation Office.

Investigators also uncovered an Alien Certificate of Registration Identity Card issued to Sy in 2009 that identified him as a Chinese national born in Fujian province.

“He was immediately taken into custody. He is now facing a case for undesirability for allegedly misrepresenting himself as a Filipino. Cases involving foreigners who use Philippine documents to pretend or misrepresent themselves as Filipinos are considered violations of immigration laws,” Bureau of Immigration spokeswoman Dana Sandoval was quoted by news outlet Bilyonaryo as saying.

According to the Bureau of Immigration, citing Securities and Exchange Commission records, Maxipro’s 2026 General Information Sheet showed Sy owned 88.8 per cent of the company’s shares, down from 98.8 per cent in 2025.

Maxipro’s website says it has completed 11 projects for NGCP and is undertaking six more.

Identity fraud as security threat

Experts say the operation leading to Sy’s arrest underscores a shift in how Philippine authorities approach national security, with identity fraud increasingly seen as a possible route into sensitive sectors.

Edmund Tayao, a law professor at San Beda Graduate School of Law in Manila and president of the Political Economic Elemental Researchers and Strategists think tank, said the concept was no longer limited to threats directly targeting the government or the Filipino people.

It now also encompassed less visible activities that could undermine the country’s critical infrastructure, key institutions and overall resilience, he said.

Danielito Jimenez, a doctor of civil law and founder of the advocacy platform The Pinoy Street Lawyer Official, said passport fraud – including the falsification of birth certificates – was increasingly being examined through a national security lens when it was used to conceal a person’s true identity or facilitate access to critical sectors.

“Clearly, when a fake Filipino identity is used to enter strategic industries like power, telecommunications, or other critical infrastructure, it should be a national security concern. Also, it can be used to circumvent constitutional limits on foreign ownership,” Jimenez told This Week in Asia.

Justin Kyle Malarayap, a visiting assistant professor at Arellano University in Manila, described authorities’ approach as a “strategic rebalance”.

Since the early 2000s, Manila had already linked passport fraud to national security concerns because foreign terrorists and terrorism financiers often came to the Philippines carrying tampered or falsified documents, Malarayap said.

“Therefore, leveraging lessons learned since the early 2000s, the tightening of security against falsified documentation may appear aggressive and coordinated to foreign observers, but it should not be viewed as targeting any particular nationality,” he said.

Recent high-profile cases illustrated why authorities had adopted a broader national security approach, Jimenez said.

He cited the case of Alice Guo that exposed how a questionable Filipino identity could be used to gain political power and infiltrate local government. Guo, also known as Guo Hua Ping, is a Chinese national who entered the Philippines in 2003 and later served as mayor of Bamban, Tarlac.

She came under scrutiny in 2024 after authorities linked her to a Philippine offshore gaming operator allegedly involved in fraud, human trafficking and illegal detention, then fled the country during a Senate investigation before being arrested in Indonesia.

In November last year, a court found her guilty of human trafficking and sentenced her to life imprisonment.

Another high-profile case involves mining tycoon Joseph Sy, who is accused of fraudulently obtaining Philippine citizenship and compromising national security through his honorary role in the Philippine Coast Guard.

Joseph Sy, who also uses the Chinese name Chen Zhong Zhen, was detained at Ninoy Aquino International Airport after investigators said his fingerprints matched those of a Chinese citizen previously issued a long-term visa.

The immigration bureau said Joseph Sy remained in its lawful custody while deportation proceedings and an investigation into his citizenship status were pending.

The Chinese embassy has not publicly commented on the cases involving Guo or Lawrence Ke Sy, but it previously expressed concern over what it described as the increasing number of arrests of Chinese nationals in the Philippines, urging authorities to handle such cases fairly and in accordance with Philippine law.

The military has called for cases involving foreign nationals engaged in critical infrastructure projects to be thoroughly investigated.

Retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, a spokesman for the Armed Forces of the Philippines, said authorities should determine whether foreign nationals involved in essential government infrastructure projects posed national security risks.

“Critical government infrastructure is called critical because it is essential for our survival as a people and as a nation,” Trinidad said, warning there could be significant security risks if hostile foreign powers controlled such infrastructure.

But analysts say Manila’s challenge is tightening scrutiny over sensitive sectors without treating foreign participation as a threat.

Jimenez said stronger national security measures need not come at the expense of foreign investment, arguing that the government could pursue both objectives simultaneously.

Authorities should focus on enforcing existing laws, verifying the true ownership of companies and imposing stricter screening on businesses operating in sectors critical to national security, he added.

Malarayap urged the government to address domestic vulnerabilities, saying that proper oversight should be coupled with ownership rules favouring Filipino investors, especially in sectors where companies operating in the Philippines had significant foreign ownership.

Jimenez called for stricter measures on passports, birth records and corporate ownership, especially in sectors critical to national security.

One possible measure, Jimenez said, was a law allowing the government to cancel or nullify fraudulently obtained birth certificates to enable authorities to resolve such cases more quickly instead of relying on lengthy court proceedings.

“Enforcement must, however, remain fair and evidence-based to avoid unfairly targeting legitimate foreign investors, naturalised Filipinos, or Chinese-Filipino communities. The goal should be protecting the country’s interests without undermining the rule of law or investor confidence,” Jimenez said.

item.title: [SCMP] New yacht travel scheme makes waves but can Hong Kong cash in on marine economy?
item.description:
For the first time, veteran sailor Thomas Wong Kam-chuen and his partners set sail from Hong Kong on their 46-foot yacht on a two-day trip earlier this month to a holiday island in Zhuhai, testing the waters for more leisure travel to mainland China.

After a five-hour voyage from the Causeway Bay typhoon shelter on a sunny weekend, they anchored their Danish-built yacht, DBX2, at Guishan Island, went ashore for a seafood lunch with beer and stayed overnight.

“Food is really economical. We had 11 people, and a seafood meal was only HK$112 [US$14] per person. If you eat seafood in Hong Kong, it is at least HK$600 to HK$700 a person,” said the 79-year-old structural engineer, who has 52 years of sailing experience.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, veteran sailor Thomas Wong Kam-chuen and his partners set sail from Hong Kong on their 46-foot yacht on a two-day trip earlier this month to a holiday island in Zhuhai, testing the waters for more leisure travel to mainland China.

After a five-hour voyage from the Causeway Bay typhoon shelter on a sunny weekend, they anchored their Danish-built yacht, DBX2, at Guishan Island, went ashore for a seafood lunch with beer and stayed overnight.

“Food is really economical. We had 11 people, and a seafood meal was only HK$112 [US$14] per person. If you eat seafood in Hong Kong, it is at least HK$600 to HK$700 a person,” said the 79-year-old structural engineer, who has 52 years of sailing experience.

DBX2 joined nine other vessels in a flotilla organised by the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club in collaboration with the Zhuhai Yacht Association, with the early batch of sailors navigating Greater Bay Area waters under a new individual yacht travel scheme.

The trip was made possible after Beijing approved the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme in June, allowing Hong Kong owners to sail their vessels to designated ports as part of a broader “yacht economy” strategy for the Greater Bay Area.

The bay area is a central government initiative to link Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in neighbouring Guangdong province into an integrated economic powerhouse.

Some boat owners and maritime experts note that the yacht scheme currently operates as one-way traffic, generating economic gains for mainland destinations. They have urged Hong Kong authorities to seize the opportunity to upgrade the city’s marine infrastructure to attract southbound yachts.

They have also called on the government to prioritise high-end maritime services – such as trading, financing and design – and to use an ongoing public consultation for Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan to capitalise on the marine economy.

“What we hope for in the future is to place Hong Kong’s yacht industry – including yacht exhibitions, design and trading – in Hong Kong,” said Professor Chen Jihong, director of the Shenzhen International Maritime Institute, who was involved in research and planning for the cross-border individual yacht scheme.

“In the future, Hong Kong can definitely play a greater role in high-end services and financial value addition.”

An ‘economically unbalanced’ voyage?

The scheme is currently limited to northbound Hong Kong yachts, pending mainland approval for yachts there to sail to the city under a southbound arrangement.

The northbound section operates under strict parameters, capping vessel capacity at 12 people and requiring captains to hold Chinese citizenship and have home-return permits and to submit digital clearance hours in advance. Home-return permits allow Hong Kong and Macau people to travel freely between their home city and the mainland.

Potentially, a vast market is waiting to be tapped. Wong Sai-fat, director of marine, citing estimates from multiple media and political party research reports published between April and June, earlier said that once the yacht economy reached maturity, it could generate annual economic benefits of HK$4.4 billion to HK$22.5 billion for Hong Kong.

From 2023 to 2025, an average of 77 yachts visited Hong Kong annually, 35 of which came from the mainland, according to InvestHK, the government’s investment promotion arm.

However, the new scheme is accelerating movement.

Liao Kai, president of the non-profit Zhuhai association, said 38 Hong Kong and Macau yachts had obtained temporary ship nationality certificates issued by mainland authorities as of mid-July.

Twenty of them applied specifically to visit Zhuhai. Without affecting their original ship registration, these certificates allow individual yacht travel within the waters of the nine mainland cities in the bay area.

“In just half a month, we have processed nearly half as many yachts as the roughly 60 that entered [Hainan] under a free travel scheme between Hainan, Hong Kong and Macau over the past six to eight years,” said Liao, whose association is registered under Zhuhai’s civil affairs bureau to advocate for cross-border yacht travel.

The Hainan scheme was implemented in 2019, allowing visiting yachts from Hong Kong and Macau to remain in the southern mainland island province for 30 days.

In Wong’s case, he and his partners paid about HK$5,000 in fees related to the application and preparation of certificates for the Guishan Island trip, excluding spending on meals and entertainment.

Located about three nautical miles (5.5km) southwest of Lantau Island, Guishan is known as a selfie hotspot for sunsets and seafood.

Whether the trip was worthwhile is open to debate.

“Do you think it’s worth it, doing so many procedures just to go for one night and two days? Even going somewhere as close as Guishan, travelling took about five hours each way – that’s 10 hours of sailing within less than 48 hours,” Wong said.

“Factoring in sleep time, the actual leisure time is very short. Those expenses – HK$5,000 – are basically mandatory, so if you only go for two days, it feels a bit economically unbalanced for a two-day trip.”

Still, some yacht owners, such as Simon Deng Wenjian, who visited Nansha in Guangzhou with friends earlier this month, felt the cost was acceptable.

Deng sailed his 53-foot yacht from the Gold Coast in Tuen Mun to Nansha Marina in about 5½ hours, noting that customs clearance at the passenger terminal was efficient and took about 20 minutes.

“Most of the things you do, like the AIS [automatic identification system, a marine tracking tool], are a one-off. If you deduct this cost, the actual cost of each trip is very low,” Deng said, adding that mainland marinas charged an agency and berthing fee of about 6,000 yuan (US$890) per trip.

Deng said prospective yacht owners deterred by high berthing costs might now choose to buy vessels in Hong Kong and register them there, using the travel scheme to sail them back to the mainland.

He said he believed this influx of new buyers purchasing tax-free vessels in Hong Kong would stimulate yacht sales and boost the city’s yachting industry.

To make the northbound scheme more attractive, Lawrence Chow, chairman of the Hong Kong Boating Industry Association, proposed that the city’s Marine Department expand its eSeaGo navigational chart app to cover Greater Bay Area waters so captains could chart their voyages.

Chow also pointed to a private website compiling information on northbound and southbound yacht travel so everyone could access the same information.

Liao said the Zhuhai association was exploring with the Guangdong provincial government the adoption of Hong Kong’s flexible capacity rules and the implementation of the English-language version of the application. Mainland maritime law strictly caps all yachts at 12 people including crew, regardless of the vessel’s size.

Bill Lau, founder of service company Voy Yachting, and Simon Kung, chief executive of Baypoint, both handle applications for yacht owners.

They said that due to complicated paperwork and unaligned systems, end-to-end processing took up to a month.

While Lau charges about HK$6,000 for standard processing, Kung noted that the high-end market commanded vastly different prices.

“For an 80-foot yacht, we are asking for HK$50,000 for the entire application fee,” Kung said. The charge covers paperwork, related fees for the first northbound journey, three days of management expenses with a mainland yacht club and berth rental in Zhuhai.

However, confusion remains among owners over an important issue.

“Many people think applying for the free travel scheme allows them to go for repairs or maintenance, which is not allowed. Actually, your yacht must enter and exit in the original condition,” Kung said.

Instead, owners must use a separate, recently launched bonded scheme in Zhuhai’s Jinwan district to bypass massive import taxes for heavy refits, he said.

Is Hong Kong ready for southbound yachts?

To prepare for the southbound scheme, the Marine Department has introduced several measures.

These include allowing visiting yacht operators to complete Hong Kong qualification exams on the mainland since June 12, submitting all health, immigration and port clearances through a one-stop electronic business system launched on June 29, and applying for five designated public anchorages without pre-booking private marina berths from July 8.

The anchorages are at Stanley Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Repulse Bay, Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung and Tai O.

To prepare mainland captains for Hong Kong’s busy waters, the department authorised two mainland centres in Shenzhen and Nansha to conduct local navigation exams and approved seven mainland institutions to offer certified courses.

As of July 24, 160 of 176 applicants had passed the exam or completed training since mid-June.

Once the southbound scheme was approved, mainland visitors could enjoy tax-free fine wines and imported seafood after arriving in Hong Kong by yacht, Kung and Liao said.

Pointing to the designated anchorage areas, Lau stressed the urgent need for better landing facilities and public shuttle boats to take passengers ashore.

“Getting on and off the boat is quite troublesome,” Lau said. “If you anchor in Stanley, how do you get ashore? When it’s so remote, there are no landing facilities.”

The Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club’s commodore, David Norton, who joined the Guishan voyage, said the club was organising another northbound trip in the coming month.

He said he believed the southbound scheme would not only cater to the ultra-rich, but also to sport sailors.

“The cost of mooring is like the cost of parking a car,” Norton said.

He added that a large number of people from fleets of smaller yachts generated far more economic activity onshore than a single superyacht.

However, the lack of an English-language system and Hong Kong’s congested harbours limited the scheme’s full potential, he added.

“Those sorts of facilities are things that the government should be working on – and they are working on it,” he said.

Beyond the yacht economy

Lawmaker Steven Ho Chun-yin said that the sector’s value extended far beyond basic tourism, aligning with calls to develop a supporting service industry chain covering yacht marketing, maintenance, certification and insurance.

“When superyachts come to Hong Kong, the owners are often here to discuss business, which drives our financial sector,” Ho said.

He said unlocking the sector’s potential required addressing institutional barriers to infrastructure investment.

He urged the government to allow operators to retain land for shipyards and improve amenities for sustainable investments, noting that 80 to 90 per cent of local firms held short-term tenancies of about seven years.

“Who would throw billions into a facility to only give it back in seven years?” Ho said.

He also called for more focus on the marine economy in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan.

Through the ongoing public consultation for the five-year plan, the government has signalled a willingness to gather views from all sectors of society to forge consensus on Hong Kong’s development road map.

“We need to establish a higher-level maritime economy committee,” Ho said. “Without a cross-departmental body, an individual department like the Marine Department will only focus on its own specific safety regulations.”

Hong Kong is facing a severe shortage of berthing spots, with 12,500 licensed yachts competing for only 4,300 available berths.

To ease the crunch, Lau, of the yacht service platform, suggested officially zoning existing typhoon shelters to separate leisure yachts from fishing boats and industrial barges.

“If the government regulates it well, it can be like a civilian yacht club,” he said.

Chen, of the institute, said he hoped the yacht industries in Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area could integrate at a higher level, with Hong Kong focusing on exhibitions, design and trading.

“Once this service matures in the Greater Bay Area, the model can fully be promoted to places like Shanghai, Qingdao and other coastal regions,” Chen said.

He noted that the yachting scheme was a vital piece of China’s goal to rise as a marine superpower in the national 15th five-year plan for 2026 to 2030.

Hong Kong could serve as the hub for high-end maritime services for all of China, including design, trade, manufacturing, refinancing and insurance, he added.

“Hong Kong can serve as a bridgehead, as a brilliant pearl,” Chen said. “In this way, we can break the current Western monopoly on these high-end services and value addition.

“Hong Kong’s [role] in China becoming a marine superpower, what is its function? It must be this high-value-added shipping service.”

item.title: [SCMP] Bachelet-led panel urges Latin America not to choose sides in US-China rivalry
item.description:
Latin American countries should resist pressure to choose between the United States and China and use their vast reserves of lithium, copper and other strategic resources to strengthen their negotiating power, according to a high-level commission co-chaired by former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet and former Colombian president Ivan Duque.

But the commission acknowledges that the region’s room for manoeuvre is sharply constrained in security, technology and critical infrastructure, areas in which Washington remains dominant and has sought to curb Beijing’s growing influence.

The report, released on Tuesday by the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, argues that countries can work with different partners on different issues – maintaining security relationships with Washington while diversifying trade and investment towards China and other economies.
item.content:encoded:
Latin American countries should resist pressure to choose between the United States and China and use their vast reserves of lithium, copper and other strategic resources to strengthen their negotiating power, according to a high-level commission co-chaired by former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet and former Colombian president Ivan Duque.

But the commission acknowledges that the region’s room for manoeuvre is sharply constrained in security, technology and critical infrastructure, areas in which Washington remains dominant and has sought to curb Beijing’s growing influence.

The report, released on Tuesday by the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, argues that countries can work with different partners on different issues – maintaining security relationships with Washington while diversifying trade and investment towards China and other economies.

Presenting the report in Santiago, Duque said Latin America needed “a geopolitical vision of our own, not dictated to us”, arguing that countries should not become trapped in fixed alignments or automatically take sides between rival powers.

Governments should instead retain the flexibility to align with different partners according to their strategic priorities, shared principles and opportunities for trade and investment, he said.

Bachelet said the region had gained leverage because intensifying competition among global powers had increased the value of its resources.

“The world has changed, and the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean have many things that the world needs,” she said.

The commission identifies Latin America’s natural resources as a potentially powerful negotiating tool.

The region holds an estimated 46 per cent of the world’s lithium reserves, 35 per cent of its copper, 28 per cent of its graphite and 23 per cent of its rare earths, according to the report.

It is also the world’s leading net food-exporting region, hosts nearly half of the planet’s terrestrial biodiversity and possesses about one-third of its freshwater resources.

China becomes a new option in Latin American negotiations

Qian Liu, a Chinese business executive who served on the commission, said Beijing’s increasing economic presence provided Latin American governments with another option as they negotiated with major powers.

“The rise of China is providing the world with a different option and opportunity, and competition is good,” said Liu, founder and chief executive of Wusawa.

China has become South America’s largest trading partner, she noted, while Chinese and other Asian companies have shown strong interest in expanding their operations in the region.
